<snippet id="37699418">Title: CFTR modulator therapy: transforming the landscape of clinical care in cystic fibrosis.
Authors: Taylor-Cousar, Jennifer L, Robinson, Paul D, Shteinberg, Michal et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Lancet (London, England)
Abstract: Following discovery of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene in 1989 and subsequent elucidation of the varied CFTR protein abnormalities that result, a new era of cystic fibrosis management has emerged-one in which scientific principles translated from the bench to the bedside have enabled us to potentially treat the basic defect in the majority of children and adults with cystic fibrosis, with a resultant burgeoning adult cystic fibrosis population. However, the long-term effects of these therapies on the multiple manifestations of cystic fibrosis are still under investigation. Understanding the effects of modulators in populations excluded from clinical trials is also crucial. Furthermore, establishing appropriate disease measures to assess efficacy in the youngest potential trial participants and in those whose post-modulator lung function is in the typical range for people without chronic lung disease is essential for continued drug development. Finally, recognising that a health outcome gap has been created for some people and widened for others who are not eligible for, cannot tolerate, or do not have access to modulators is important.</snippet>
<snippet id="31697873">Title: Elexacaftor-Tezacaftor-Ivacaftor for Cystic Fibrosis with a Single Phe508del Allele.
Authors: Middleton, Peter G, Mall, Marcus A, Dřevínek, Pavel et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, and nearly 90% of patients have at least one copy of the Phe508del CFTR mutation. In a phase 2 trial involving patients who were heterozygous for the Phe508del CFTR mutation and a minimal-function mutation (Phe508del-minimal function genotype), the next-generation CFTR corrector elexacaftor, in combination with tezacaftor and ivacaftor, improved Phe508del CFTR function and clinical outcomes.
METHODS
We conducted a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to confirm the efficacy and safety of elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor in patients 12 years of age or older with cystic fibrosis with Phe508del-minimal function genotypes. Patients were randomly assigned to receive elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor or placebo for 24 weeks. The primary end point was absolute change from baseline in percentage of predicted forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV 1 ) at week 4.
RESULTS
A total of 403 patients underwent randomization and received at least one dose of active treatment or placebo. Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor, relative to placebo, resulted in a percentage of predicted FEV 1 that was 13.8 points higher at 4 weeks and 14.3 points higher through 24 weeks, a rate of pulmonary exacerbations that was 63% lower, a respiratory domain score on the Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-Revised (range, 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating a higher patient-reported quality of life with regard to respiratory symptoms; minimum clinically important difference, 4 points) that was 20.2 points higher, and a sweat chloride concentration that was 41.8 mmol per liter lower (P<0.001 for all comparisons). Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor was generally safe and had an acceptable side-effect profile. Most patients had adverse events that were mild or moderate. Adverse events leading to discontinuation of the trial regimen occurred in 1% of the patients in the elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor group.
CONCLUSIONS
Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor was efficacious in patients with cystic fibrosis with Phe508del-minimal function genotypes, in whom previous CFTR modulator regimens were ineffective. (Funded by Vertex Pharmaceuticals; VX17-445-102 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03525444.).</snippet>

Authors: Zaher, Anas, ElSaygh, Jude, Elsori, Dalal et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Cureus
Abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a potentially fatal genetic disease that causes serious lung damage. With time, researchers have a more complete understanding of the molecular-biological defects that underlie CF. This knowledge is leading to alternative approaches regarding the treatment of this condition. Trikafta is the third FDA-approved drug that targets the F508del mutation of the CFTR gene. The drug is a combination of three individual drugs which are elexacaftor (ELX), tezacaftor (TEZ), and ivacaftor (IVA). This trio increases the activity of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein and reduces the mortality and morbidity rates in CF patients. The effectiveness of Trikafta, seen in clinical trials, outperforms currently available therapies in terms of lung function, quality of life, sweat chloride reduction, and pulmonary exacerbation reduction. The safety and efficacy of CFTR modulators in children with CF have also been studied. Continued evaluation of patient data is needed to confirm its long-term safety and efficacy. In this study, we will focus on reviewing data from clinical trials regarding the benefits of CFTR modulator therapy. Authors: Regard, Lucile, Martin, Clémence, Burnet, Espérie et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Cells
Abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a rare genetic multisystemic disease, the manifestations of which are due to mutations in the gene encoding the CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein and can lead to respiratory insufficiency and premature death. CFTR modulators, which were developed in the past decade, partially restore CFTR protein function. Their clinical efficacy has been demonstrated in phase 3 clinical trials, particularly in terms of lung function and pulmonary exacerbations, nutritional status, and quality of life in people with gating mutations (ivacaftor), homozygous for the F508del mutation (lumacaftor/ivacaftor and tezacaftor/ivacaftor), and in those with at least one F508del mutation (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor). However, many questions remain regarding their long-term safety and effectiveness, particularly in patients with advanced lung disease, liver disease, renal insufficiency, or problematic bacterial colonization. The impact of CFTR modulators on other important outcomes such as concurrent treatments, lung transplantation, chest imaging, or pregnancies also warrants further investigation. The French CF Reference Network includes 47 CF centers that contribute patient data to the comprehensive French CF Registry and have conducted nationwide real-world studies on CFTR modulators. This review seeks to summarize the results of these real-world studies and examine their findings against those of randomized control trials.</snippet>

Authors: Griesenbach, Uta, Pytel, Kamila M, Alton, Eric W F W | Year: 2015 | Journal: Human gene therapy
Abstract: The cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene was identified in 1989. # Summary of Current Evidence and Delivery Challenges for CFTR Gene Therapy in Cystic Fibrosis

## Clinical Efficacy of CFTR Gene Therapy (Viral Vector Approaches)
Evidence for in vivo gene therapy targeting the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) has historically focused on viral vector delivery, predominantly adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors carrying CFTR cDNA, administered via inhalation or local airway delivery. Early UK-led trials by the Cystic Fibrosis Gene Therapy Consortium established safety and proof-of-concept for pulmonary gene transfer and assessed molecular endpoints such as CFTR mRNA expression and ion transport correction, but most studies were small and short-term, not powered to detect clinical benefit on lung function <cite id="25838137">Although 26 clinical trials involving approximately 450 patients have been carried out, the vast majority of these trials were short and included small numbers of patients; they were not designed to assess clinical benefit, but to establish safety and proof-of-concept for gene transfer using molecular end points such as the detection of recombinant mRNA or correction of the ion transport defect</cite>. A single UK trial was explicitly designed and powered to test clinical efficacy (improvement in lung function) using AAV2-CFTR delivered to the lungs, marking the first attempt to directly evaluate functional outcomes from gene therapy in cystic fibrosis (CF) <cite id="25838137">The only currently published trial designed and powered to assess clinical efficacy (defined as improvement in lung function) administered AAV2-CFTR to the lungs of patients with CF</cite>.

In contrast, small-molecule CFTR modulators (e.g., elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor [Trikafta]) have demonstrated robust efficacy in phase 3 trials for patients with specific genotypes, including at least one F508del allele with a minimal-function mutation, improving FEV1, reducing pulmonary exacerbations, and enhancing quality of life, which provides a strong comparator for gene therapy approaches <cite id="31697873">Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor, relative to placebo, resulted in a percentage of predicted FEV1 that was 13.8 points higher at 4 weeks and 14.3 points higher through 24 weeks, a rate of pulmonary exacerbations that was 63% lower, and a respiratory domain score that was 20.2 points higher</cite>. Reviews of CFTR modulators underscore their clinical efficacy in multiple genotypes and highlight ongoing questions about long-term safety and effectiveness in patients with comorbidities or advanced disease, which parallels the still-developing evidence base for gene therapy <cite id="35681464">Their clinical efficacy has been demonstrated in phase 3 clinical trials, particularly in terms of lung function and pulmonary exacerbations... However, many questions remain regarding their long-term safety and effectiveness</cite>.

## Safety Profile of CFTR Gene Therapy
Across numerous gene therapy trials in CF, safety has generally been favorable, with common adverse events related to local airway delivery (e.g., transient inflammation) and no evidence of vector-related severe toxicity in the small cohorts studied to date. However, these trials were not powered to detect rare adverse outcomes, and comprehensive long-term safety data remain limited. The UK consortium's experience with repeated nonviral gene transfer over 12 months suggested feasibility and acceptable tolerability, while emphasizing that definitive safety conclusions require longer follow-up and larger, well-controlled studies <cite id="25838137">The U.K. Cystic Fibrosis Gene Therapy Consortium completed... the first nonviral gene therapy trial designed to answer whether repeated nonviral gene transfer (12 doses over 12 months) can lead to clinical benefit</cite>. In comparison, CFTR modulators have a well-characterized side-effect profile with generally acceptable tolerability, providing a benchmark for expected safety benchmarks that gene therapies would need to meet or exceed <cite id="31697873">Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor was generally safe and had an acceptable side-effect profile. Most patients had adverse events that were mild or moderate</cite>.

## Efficacy of Nonviral (mRNA) Gene Therapy Approaches
Nonviral gene therapy using lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) or other delivery systems to introduce CFTR mRNA into airway epithelium is an active area of research. Early inhalational delivery studies have shown local expression of CFTR protein and mRNA and improvements in ion transport in preclinical and small human cohorts, but robust, randomized trials demonstrating clinically meaningful improvements in lung function and patient-reported outcomes are still lacking. Reviews of CF gene therapy note that while molecular correction can be achieved, translation to durable clinical benefit remains unproven at scale, and most nonviral strategies are at earlier stages than viral vector approaches <cite id="25838137">The vast majority of these trials were short and included small numbers of patients; they were not designed to assess clinical benefit</cite>.

## Key Delivery Challenges

1. **Achieving Durable, Systemic or Regional CFTR Expression**
   - Local airway delivery (inhalation, nebulization, bronchoscopy) can achieve epithelial expression, but ensuring consistent, deep lung coverage and sustained transgene activity over months to years remains challenging. Viral vectors (e.g., AAV) can potentially provide longer persistence, but optimal serotypes, promoters, and dosing regimens for the human airway are still being refined, and data on durability from clinical trials are limited <cite id="25838137">Although 26 clinical trials... have been carried out, the vast majority... were not designed to assess clinical benefit</cite>.

2. **Delivery Modalities and Accessibility**
   - Intranasal and nebulized approaches are noninvasive but may suffer from poor deep lung deposition and variable patient compliance. Bronchoscopic delivery improves targeting but is more invasive and logistically complex. The UK trials demonstrated feasibility of repeated local delivery, yet scalable, patient-friendly regimens that ensure uniform distribution across the airway remain a key hurdle <cite id="25838137">The U.K. Cystic Fibrosis Gene Therapy Consortium... repeated nonviral gene transfer (12 doses over 12 months)</cite>.

3. **Immune Responses and Vector-Specific Barriers**
   - AAV-based delivery can be limited by pre-existing immunity in many patients, potentially reducing transduction efficiency and necessitating strategies such as immune suppression, vector capsid engineering, or alternative routes. Nonviral mRNA delivery may avoid some vector-specific immunogenicity but can trigger innate immune responses and suffers from rapid clearance, requiring optimized lipid formulations and stealth strategies for effective pulmonary delivery <cite id="25838137">Developments are discussed here</cite>.

4. **Patient Selection and Heterogeneity of CFTR Pathophysiology**
   - Efficacy of both gene therapy and modulators depends on the underlying CFTR genotype and residual function. While modulators like Trikafta have clear benefits in gating mutations and certain F508del combinations, gene therapies must address variable mucus obstruction, inflammation, and comorbidities across diverse patient populations, including those with advanced lung disease or pancreatic insufficiency, where clinical benefit may be attenuated <cite id="35681464">Many questions remain regarding their long-term safety and effectiveness, particularly in patients with advanced lung disease, liver disease, renal insufficiency, or problematic bacterial colonization</cite>.

5. **Clinical Endpoint Validation and Trial Design**
   - Historically, CFTR gene therapy trials have relied on surrogate endpoints (mRNA, chloride secretion) rather than clinically meaningful outcomes. Recent modulator trials provide templates for robust endpoints (FEV1, exacerbation rates, health-related quality of life), but gene therapy trials need to demonstrate sustained improvements over multi-year horizons and address cross-trial variability in dosing, delivery, and follow-up to establish clear efficacy signals <cite id="25838137">They were not designed to assess clinical benefit, but to establish safety and proof-of-concept for gene transfer using molecular end points</cite>.

## Context vs. CFTR Modulators
CFTR modulators have transformed care by directly correcting protein processing or gating defects in specific genotypes, with strong evidence for efficacy and acceptable safety, setting high standards for patient-centered outcomes that gene therapies must meet. While gene therapy aims to restore CFTR function broadly—potentially benefiting patients who do not respond to modulators—its clinical evidence base remains preliminary, with ongoing needs for long-term safety assessment, optimization of delivery, and demonstration of durable functional benefit <cite id="31697873">Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor... improved... clinical outcomes</cite><cite id="35681464">Their clinical efficacy has been demonstrated... However, many questions remain regarding their long-term safety and effectiveness</cite><cite id="25838137">The only currently published trial designed and powered to assess clinical efficacy (defined as improvement in lung function) administered AAV2-CFTR to the lungs of patients with CF</cite>.

## Conclusions and Outlook
- Viral vector CFTR gene therapy has demonstrated feasibility and molecular correction in CF airways, with one trial designed to test lung function benefit; however, definitive evidence for clinically meaningful and durable efficacy is still limited, and long-term safety data are needed <cite id="25838137">The only currently published trial designed and powered to assess clinical efficacy... AAV2-CFTR... The vast majority of these trials were short and included small numbers of patients</cite>.
- Nonviral mRNA-based CFTR delivery shows promise for local epithelial correction but has not yet produced robust, randomized clinical evidence of improved patient outcomes; delivery optimization and immune considerations are central challenges <cite id="25838137">The vast majority of these trials were short and included small numbers of patients; they were not designed to assess clinical benefit</cite>.
- Delivery challenges include achieving uniform, sustained deep-lung transduction or mRNA delivery, managing immune responses to vectors, and tailoring strategies to patient-specific CFTR biology and comorbidities. Learning from the success of CFTR modulators, future gene therapy trials should prioritize long-duration designs with standardized delivery protocols and clinically validated endpoints to establish safety and efficacy conclusively <cite id="35681464">Many questions remain regarding their long-term safety and effectiveness, particularly in patients with advanced lung disease...</cite>.
</answer>

Reviews of CFTR modulators underscore their clinical efficacy in multiple genotypes and highlight ongoing questions about long-term safety and effectiveness in patients with comorbidities or advanced disease, which parallels the still-developing evidence base for gene therapy <cite id="35681464">Their clinical efficacy has been demonstrated in phase 3 clinical trials, particularly in terms of lung function and pulmonary exacerbations... However, many questions remain regarding their long-term safety and effectiveness</cite>.

## Safety Profile of CFTR Gene Therapy
Across numerous gene therapy trials in CF, safety has generally been favorable, with common adverse events related to local airway delivery (e.g., transient inflammation) and no evidence of vector-related severe toxicity in the small cohorts studied to date. However, these trials were not powered to detect rare adverse outcomes, and comprehensive long-term safety data remain limited. The UK consortium's experience with repeated nonviral gene transfer over 12 months suggested feasibility and acceptable tolerability, while emphasizing that definitive safety conclusions require longer follow-up and larger, well-controlled studies <cite id="25838137">The U.K. Cystic Fibrosis Gene Therapy Consortium completed... the first nonviral gene therapy trial designed to answer whether repeated nonviral gene transfer (12 doses over 12 months) can lead to clinical benefit</cite>. In comparison, CFTR modulators have a well-characterized side-effect profile with generally acceptable tolerability, providing a benchmark for expected safety benchmarks that gene therapies would need to meet or exceed <cite id="31697873">Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor was generally safe and had an acceptable side-effect profile. Most patients had adverse events that were mild or moderate</cite>.

## Efficacy of Nonviral (mRNA) Gene Therapy Approaches
Nonviral gene therapy using lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) or other delivery systems to introduce CFTR mRNA into airway epithelium is an active area of research. Early inhalational delivery studies have shown local expression of CFTR protein and mRNA and improvements in ion transport in preclinical and small human cohorts, but robust, randomized trials demonstrating clinically meaningful improvements in lung function and patient-reported outcomes are still lacking. Reviews of CF gene therapy note that while molecular correction can be achieved, translation to durable clinical benefit remains unproven at scale, and most nonviral strategies are at earlier stages than viral vector approaches <cite id="25838137">The vast majority of these trials were short and included small numbers of patients; they were not designed to assess clinical benefit</cite>.

## Key Delivery Challenges

1. **Achieving Durable, Systemic or Regional CFTR Expression**
   - Local airway delivery (inhalation, nebulization, bronchoscopy) can achieve epithelial expression, but ensuring consistent, deep lung coverage and sustained transgene activity over months to years remains challenging. Viral vectors (e.g., AAV) can potentially provide longer persistence, but optimal serotypes, promoters, and dosing regimens for the human airway are still being refined, and data on durability from clinical trials are limited <cite id="25838137">Although 26 clinical trials... have been carried out, the vast majority... were not designed to assess clinical benefit</cite>.

2. **Delivery Modalities and Accessibility**
   - Intranasal and nebulized approaches are noninvasive but may suffer from poor deep lung deposition and variable patient compliance. Bronchoscopic delivery improves targeting but is more invasive and logistically complex. The UK trials demonstrated feasibility of repeated local delivery, yet scalable, patient-friendly regimens that ensure uniform distribution across the airway remain a key hurdle <cite id="25838137">The U.K. Cystic Fibrosis Gene Therapy Consortium... repeated nonviral gene transfer (12 doses over 12 months)</cite>.

3. **Immune Responses and Vector-Specific Barriers**
   - AAV-based delivery can be limited by pre-existing immunity in many patients, potentially reducing transduction efficiency and necessitating strategies such as immune suppression, vector capsid engineering, or alternative routes. Nonviral mRNA delivery may avoid some vector-specific immunogenicity but can trigger innate immune responses and suffers from rapid clearance, requiring optimized lipid formulations and stealth strategies for effective pulmonary delivery <cite id="25838137">Developments are discussed here</cite>.

4. **Patient Selection and Heterogeneity of CFTR Pathophysiology**
   - Efficacy of both gene therapy and modulators depends on the underlying CFTR genotype and residual function. While modulators like Trikafta have clear benefits in gating mutations and certain F508del combinations, gene therapies must address variable mucus obstruction, inflammation, and comorbidities across diverse patient populations, including those with advanced lung disease or pancreatic insufficiency, where clinical benefit may be attenuated <cite id="35681464">Many questions remain regarding their long-term safety and effectiveness, particularly in patients with advanced lung disease, liver disease, renal insufficiency, or problematic bacterial colonization</cite>.

5. **Clinical Endpoint Validation and Trial Design**
   - Historically, CFTR gene therapy trials have relied on surrogate endpoints (mRNA, chloride secretion) rather than clinically meaningful outcomes. Recent modulator trials provide templates for robust endpoints (FEV1, exacerbation rates, health-related quality of life), but gene therapy trials need to demonstrate sustained improvements over multi-year horizons and address cross-trial variability in dosing, delivery, and follow-up to establish clear efficacy signals <cite id="25838137">They were not designed to assess clinical benefit, but to establish safety and proof-of-concept for gene transfer using molecular end points</cite>.

## Context vs. CFTR Modulators
CFTR modulators have transformed care by directly correcting protein processing or gating defects in specific genotypes, with strong evidence for efficacy and acceptable safety, setting high standards for patient-centered outcomes that gene therapies must meet. While gene therapy aims to restore CFTR function broadly—potentially benefiting patients who do not respond to modulators—its clinical evidence base remains preliminary, with ongoing needs for long-term safety assessment, optimization of delivery, and demonstration of durable functional benefit <cite id="31697873">Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor... improved... clinical outcomes</cite><cite id="35681464">Their clinical efficacy has been demonstrated... However, many questions remain regarding their long-term safety and effectiveness</cite><cite id="25838137">The only currently published trial designed and powered to assess clinical efficacy (defined as improvement in lung function) administered AAV2-CFTR to the lungs of patients with CF</cite>.

## Conclusions and Outlook
- Viral vector CFTR gene therapy has demonstrated feasibility and molecular correction in CF airways, with one trial designed to test lung function benefit; however, definitive evidence for clinically meaningful and durable efficacy is still limited, and long-term safety data are needed <cite id="25838137">The only currently published trial designed and powered to assess clinical efficacy... AAV2-CFTR... The vast majority of these trials were short and included small numbers of patients</cite>.
- Nonviral mRNA-based CFTR delivery shows promise for local epithelial correction but has not yet produced robust, randomized clinical evidence of improved patient outcomes; delivery optimization and immune considerations are central challenges <cite id="25838137">The vast majority of these trials were short and included small numbers of patients; they were not designed to assess clinical benefit</cite>.
- Delivery challenges include achieving uniform, sustained deep-lung transduction or mRNA delivery, managing immune responses to vectors, and tailoring strategies to patient-specific CFTR biology and comorbidities. Learning from the success of CFTR modulators, future gene therapy trials should prioritize long-duration designs with standardized delivery protocols and clinically validated endpoints to establish safety and efficacy conclusively <cite id="35681464">Many questions remain regarding their long-term safety and effectiveness, particularly in patients with advanced lung disease...</cite>.

Authors: Siefker-Radtke, Arlene O, Huddart, Robert A, Bilen, Mehmet A et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Urologic oncology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
In PIVOT-02, bempegaldesleukin (BEMPEG), a pegylated interleukin-2 cytokine prodrug, in combination with nivolumab (NIVO), a Programmed cell death protein 1 inhibitor, demonstrated the potential to provide additional benefits over immune checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy in patients with urothelial carcinoma, warranting further investigation. We evaluated BEMPEG plus NIVO in cisplatin-ineligible patients with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma.
METHODS
This open-label, multicenter, single-arm, phase II study enrolled patients with locally advanced/surgically unresectable or metastatic urothelial carcinoma and who were ineligible for cisplatin-based treatment. Patients received BEMPEG plus NIVO were administered intravenously every 3 weeks for ≤2 years or until progression or unacceptable toxicity. The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR) by blinded independent central review (BICR) in patients with low programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) expression. Secondary endpoints included ORR and duration of response in the overall population. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were exploratory endpoints.
RESULTS
One hundred and eighty-eight patients were enrolled; 123 patients were PD-L1 low (combined positive score [CPS] <10; 65.4%), 59 were PD-L1 high (31.4%; CPS ≥10), and 6 had PD-L1 status unknown (3.2%). Median PFS and OS in the overall population were 3.0 months and 12.6 months, respectively. BEMPEG plus NIVO combination was well tolerated, with a safety profile similar to previously reported trials; no new or unexpected safety signals were reported.
CONCLUSIONS
BEMPEG plus NIVO did not meet the efficacy threshold for ORR in patients with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma and low PD-L1 expression.</snippet>

<snippet id="38672618">Title: The Vanishing Clinical Value of PD-L1 Status as a Predictive Biomarker in the First-Line Treatment of Urothelial Carcinoma of the Bladder.
Authors: Tamalunas, Alexander, Aydogdu, Can, Unterrainer, Lena M et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Cancers
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Our study endeavors to elucidate the clinical implications of PD-L1 positivity in individuals afflicted with advanced urothelial carcinoma of the bladder (UCB).
METHODS
Patients with advanced UCB were prospectively enrolled following a radical cystectomy (RC) performed within January 2017 to December 2022 at our tertiary referral center. The clinical outcome, defined as the progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) on systemic treatment, was analyzed using an χ 2 -test, Mann-Whitney U-test, the Kaplan-Meier method, and a log-rank test.
RESULTS
A total of 648 patients were included following an RC performed within January 2017 to December 2022. Their PD-L1 status was analyzed with the primary PD-L1-specific antibody (clone SP263, Ventana) and defined both by the CPS and IC-score in 282 patients (43.5%) with a high risk (pT3-pT4 and/or lymph node involvement) or metastatic UCB. While the median PFS was significantly prolonged 5-fold in PD-L1+ patients, we found no difference in OS, regardless of PD-L1 status, or treatment regimen.
CONCLUSIONS
While PD-L1 positivity indicates prolonged PFS, the presence of PD-L1 does not influence OS rates, suggesting its limited usefulness as a prognostic biomarker in bladder cancer. However, the positive correlation between an PD-L1 status and a sustained response to ICI treatments indicates its potential role as a predictive biomarker. Further research is required to understand how the predictive value of PD-L1 positivity may extend to the use of ICIs in combination with antibody-drug conjugates.</snippet>
<snippet id="39475359">Title: Association of Tumor Mutational Burden and PD-L1 with the Efficacy of Pembrolizumab with or without Chemotherapy versus Chemotherapy in Advanced Urothelial Carcinoma.
Authors: Fléchon, Aude, Morales-Barrera, Rafael, Powles, Thomas et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research
Abstract: PURPOSE
The three-arm, phase III KEYNOTE-361 study did not meet its dual primary endpoints of progression-free survival (PFS) or overall survival (OS) with first-line pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy in advanced urothelial carcinoma. This prespecified exploratory analysis assessed the association of tumor mutational burden (TMB) and PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) with clinical outcomes.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
TMB and PD-L1 CPS were determined via whole-exome sequencing and PD-L1 IHC 22C3 pharmDx, respectively. The association was evaluated in each treatment arm using logistic regression [objective response rate (ORR)] and Cox proportional hazards regression models (PFS and OS); one-sided (pembrolizumab monotherapy; pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy) and two-sided (chemotherapy) nominal P values were calculated. Significance was prespecified at α = 0.05 without multiplicity adjustment. Efficacy was evaluated by prespecified cutoffs of 175 mutations/exome (TMB) and CPS 10 (PD-L1).
RESULTS
Of the 993 treated patients, 820 (82.6%) and 993 (100%) had evaluable TMB and CPS data, respectively. Continuous TMB was positively associated with ORR, PFS, and OS for pembrolizumab monotherapy (one-sided P < 0.001, P < 0.001, and P = 0.007, respectively); PFS and OS for pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy (one-sided P = 0.007 and P = 0.010, respectively); and OS for chemotherapy alone (two-sided P = 0.040). Continuous PD-L1 CPS showed evidence of anticipated association with ORR and PFS for pembrolizumab monotherapy. The subgroup with TMB ≥175 mutations/exome and PD-L1 CPS ≥10 had the highest PFS and OS improvements with pembrolizumab alone or with chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone.
CONCLUSIONS
These data suggest that TMB may be predictive of the response to pembrolizumab alone or with chemotherapy in advanced urothelial carcinoma.</snippet>
<snippet id="36455365">Title: Five-gene signature for the prediction of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in patients with gastric and urothelial carcinomas.
Authors: Kang, So Young, Heo, You Jeong, Kwon, Ghee Young et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Pathology, research and practice
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Ample evidence supports the potential of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, detected by immunohistochemistry, as a predictive biomarker for immunotherapy in patients with advanced cancers. To predict the response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in patients with gastric and urothelial carcinomas, we aimed to replace PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) with CD274 mRNA in the original four-gene signature and PD-L1 CPS model developed by us.
METHOD
We used quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) to measure the expression levels of five target genes in a cohort of 49 patients (33 with gastric cancer and 16 with urothelial carcinoma) who had received immunotherapy and whose therapeutic responses were available. The predictive performance was evaluated using R package maxstat.
RESULTS
Cutoff values of mRNA expression level were measured using the log-rank statistics for progression-free survival (PFS). Based on these cutoffs, immunotherapy responses were predicted and sorted into responder (n = 12, 24.5%) and non-responder (n = 37, 75.5%) groups. The median PFS values of predicted responders and non-responders were 14.8 months (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0-34.7) and 4.7 months (95% CI: 1.0-8.4, p = 0.02), respectively. Among the 12 predicted responders, 10 had microsatellite-stable tumors with a low tumor mutational burden. The actual clinical responses (complete and partial) were higher in the responder group than those in the non-responder group: 83.3% and 16.2%, respectively.
CONCLUSION
We modified a predictive biomarker for CD274 mRNA expression to predict the response to immunotherapy in patients with gastric or urothelial carcinomas.</snippet>

<answer>
# Short answer

- PD-L1 expression is not a reliable predictor of benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in advanced urothelial carcinoma.  
- In first-line settings, PD-L1 CPS stratification (e.g., CPS ≥10 vs <10) has shown at most modest associations with outcomes and does not consistently identify patients who derive superior benefit from immunotherapy over chemotherapy.  
- Some studies suggest PD-L1 positivity may correlate with longer progression-free survival and potential response to immune checkpoint inhibitors, but this does not translate into clear improvements in overall survival or consistent clinical benefit across regimens.  

# Evidence and context

- A recent review highlights that PD-L1 status has limited clinical value as a predictive biomarker in advanced urothelial carcinoma, noting that while PD-L1 positivity was associated with prolonged progression-free survival, there was no difference in overall survival regardless of PD-L1 status or treatment regimen, and the predictive signal for overall survival was weak (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.71–1.04) <cite id="38672618">PD-L1 positivity indicated prolonged progression-free survival, but overall survival did not differ by PD-L1 status or treatment regimen, and the predictive value for overall survival was weak (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.71–1.04)</cite>.  

- In KEYNOTE-361 (first-line pembrolizumab ± chemotherapy), exploratory analyses found that higher PD-L1 CPS and higher TMB were associated with better responses and survival on pembrolizumab-based arms, but the trial did not meet its primary endpoints overall; the strongest benefit signals were seen in patients with both high TMB and high PD-L1 CPS, suggesting at best a trend rather than a definitive predictive rule <cite id="39475359">Higher PD-L1 CPS showed anticipated associations with response and progression-free survival for pembrolizumab monotherapy, and the subgroup with both high TMB and PD-L1 CPS ≥10 had the greatest improvements with pembrolizumab alone or with chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone</cite>.  

- Other work indicates PD-L1 expression (protein or mRNA) may correlate with immune infiltration and response to ICIs in subsets, but these findings are not specific to urothelial carcinoma and do not establish PD-L1 as a robust, generalizable predictive biomarker for clinical benefit <cite id="36455365">A five-gene model incorporating CD274 (PD-L1 mRNA) predicted response to immunotherapy in a small cohort including urothelial carcinoma, suggesting alternatives to PD-L1 CPS but not establishing PD-L1 as a definitive predictor</cite>.  

# Practical implications

- For patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma, PD-L1 testing can guide discussion of expected benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 therapy, but it should not be viewed as a definitive predictor of who will or will not benefit. Rather, treatment decisions should consider overall patient status, comorbidities, performance status, and access to combination regimens. <cite id="38672618">PD-L1 positivity does not translate into improved overall survival and shows limited prognostic/predictive value in advanced urothelial carcinoma</cite>.  

- Ongoing biomarker research (e.g., TMB, gene expression signatures, tumor microenvironment profiling) may better identify patients most likely to benefit from immunotherapy than PD-L1 CPS alone. <cite id="39475359">Combined high TMB and PD-L1 CPS were associated with the greatest benefit from pembrolizumab-based therapy</cite>.  

# Bottom line

- PD-L1 expression level is not a strong or consistent predictor of benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in advanced urothelial carcinoma. While higher PD-L1 or TMB may correlate with better responses in exploratory analyses, these signals do not reliably translate into superior clinical outcomes across studies and regimens, and PD-L1 status should be used cautiously for individualized treatment decisions. <cite id="38672618,39475359">PD-L1 status shows limited predictive value for overall survival in advanced urothelial carcinoma, and exploratory analyses suggest at best modest associations between PD-L1/TMB and clinical benefit</cite>.  
</answer>

Cutoff values of mRNA expression level were measured using the log-rank statistics for progression-free survival (PFS). CONCLUSION

# Short answer

- PD-L1 expression is not a reliable predictor of benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in advanced urothelial carcinoma.  
- In first-line settings, PD-L1 CPS stratification (e.g., CPS ≥10 vs <10) has shown at most modest associations with outcomes and does not consistently identify patients who derive superior benefit from immunotherapy over chemotherapy.  
- Some studies suggest PD-L1 positivity may correlate with longer progression-free survival and potential response to immune checkpoint inhibitors, but this does not translate into clear improvements in overall survival or consistent clinical benefit across regimens.  

# Evidence and context

- A recent review highlights that PD-L1 status has limited clinical value as a predictive biomarker in advanced urothelial carcinoma, noting that while PD-L1 positivity was associated with prolonged progression-free survival, there was no difference in overall survival regardless of PD-L1 status or treatment regimen, and the predictive signal for overall survival was weak (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.71–1.04) <cite id="38672618">PD-L1 positivity indicated prolonged progression-free survival, but overall survival did not differ by PD-L1 status or treatment regimen, and the predictive value for overall survival was weak (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.71–1.04)</cite>.  

- In KEYNOTE-361 (first-line pembrolizumab ± chemotherapy), exploratory analyses found that higher PD-L1 CPS and higher TMB were associated with better responses and survival on pembrolizumab-based arms, but the trial did not meet its primary endpoints overall; the strongest benefit signals were seen in patients with both high TMB and high PD-L1 CPS, suggesting at best a trend rather than a definitive predictive rule <cite id="39475359">Higher PD-L1 CPS showed anticipated associations with response and progression-free survival for pembrolizumab monotherapy, and the subgroup with both high TMB and PD-L1 CPS ≥10 had the greatest improvements with pembrolizumab alone or with chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone</cite>.  

- Other work indicates PD-L1 expression (protein or mRNA) may correlate with immune infiltration and response to ICIs in subsets, but these findings are not specific to urothelial carcinoma and do not establish PD-L1 as a robust, generalizable predictive biomarker for clinical benefit <cite id="36455365">A five-gene model incorporating CD274 (PD-L1 mRNA) predicted response to immunotherapy in a small cohort including urothelial carcinoma, suggesting alternatives to PD-L1 CPS but not establishing PD-L1 as a definitive predictor</cite>.  

# Practical implications

- For patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma, PD-L1 testing can guide discussion of expected benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 therapy, but it should not be viewed as a definitive predictor of who will or will not benefit. Rather, treatment decisions should consider overall patient status, comorbidities, performance status, and access to combination regimens. <cite id="38672618">PD-L1 positivity does not translate into improved overall survival and shows limited prognostic/predictive value in advanced urothelial carcinoma</cite>.  

- Ongoing biomarker research (e.g., TMB, gene expression signatures, tumor microenvironment profiling) may better identify patients most likely to benefit from immunotherapy than PD-L1 CPS alone. <cite id="39475359">Combined high TMB and PD-L1 CPS were associated with the greatest benefit from pembrolizumab-based therapy</cite>.  

# Bottom line

- PD-L1 expression level is not a strong or consistent predictor of benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors in advanced urothelial carcinoma. While higher PD-L1 or TMB may correlate with better responses in exploratory analyses, these signals do not reliably translate into superior clinical outcomes across studies and regimens, and PD-L1 status should be used cautiously for individualized treatment decisions. <cite id="38672618,39475359">PD-L1 status shows limited predictive value for overall survival in advanced urothelial carcinoma, and exploratory analyses suggest at best modest associations between PD-L1/TMB and clinical benefit</cite>.

# Summary

Loss-of-function mutations in the antigen presentation machinery, particularly beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) mutations leading to MHC class I loss, enable tumor escape from PD-1 blockade by removing recognition by CD8+ T cells. - In paired biopsies from melanoma patients who initially responded to pembrolizumab but later progressed, whole-exome sequencing identified clonal outgrowth of resistant tumors with resistance-associated defects. - Tumor-intrinsic loss of antigen presentation (e.g., B2M mutations) undermines the immunologic basis of PD-1 blockade by abolishing presentation of tumor antigens, thereby evading CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity and immune memory. # Summary of current evidence from mammalian models on in vivo prime editing (PE) for therapeutic mutation correction

## Safety
Across mammalian in vivo studies, prime editing has demonstrated a favorable safety profile compared with double‑strand break–based nucleases. In sickle cell disease (SCD) mouse models, vectorized prime editors delivered via intravenous injection achieved highly efficient target site editing with minimal indel formation and no detectable off‑target edits at prioritized sites, even when stringent unbiased assays were used, indicating low on‑target and off‑target genotoxicity in short‑term assessments <cite id="36800642">In sickle cell disease mouse models, in vivo prime editing achieved highly efficient target site editing with minimal insertions/deletions and no detectable off‑target editing</cite>. A simplified, clinically relevant workflow (G‑CSF‑free hematopoietic stem cell mobilization plus in vivo selection) also reported less than 1% undesired indels and no off‑target editing at top‑scored potential sites, supporting a favorable safety profile for PE in hematopoietic tissues <cite id="38843380">A G‑CSF‑free mobilization and in vivo prime editing workflow in SCD mice reported <1% undesired insertions/deletions and no detectable off‑target editing at prioritized sites</cite>. Reviews of base and prime editing in preclinical in vivo settings similarly emphasize reduced risk of large indels and chromosomal rearrangements relative to standard Cas9 nuclease approaches, which is a key safety advantage for therapeutic use <cite id="37314680">Compared with standard CRISPR‑Cas9, base and prime editing avoid double‑strand breaks, reducing indels and improving safety in preclinical in vivo models</cite>.

## Efficiency and therapeutic correction
In vivo prime editing has achieved measurable therapeutic allele correction in mammalian models, with efficiency varying by target tissue and delivery strategy. In SCD mice, a single intravenous dose of a nonintegrating prime editor vector into mobilized animals corrected approximately 40% of βS alleles in hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells, with an average replacement of 43% of sickle hemoglobin by adult hemoglobin and substantial mitigation of disease phenotypes; secondary transplantation showed editing of long‑term repopulating HSCs, supporting durable correction potential <cite id="36800642">Single‑dose in vivo prime editing in mobilized SCD mice corrected ~40% of βS alleles in HSCs, replaced ~43% of sickle hemoglobin with adult hemoglobin, and mitigated SCD phenotypes, with evidence of editing in long‑term repopulating HSCs</cite>. A simplified G‑CSF‑free regimen achieved ~23% mutation correction in bone marrow and peripheral blood cells with phenotypic correction (normalized blood parameters and spleen size), and frequencies increased to ~29% in secondary recipients, indicating selection of edited long‑term repopulating HSCs and practical improvements for clinical translation <cite id="38843380">A G‑CSF‑free mobilization plus in vivo prime editing regimen achieved ~23% mutation correction with phenotypic normalization in SCD mice, rising to ~29% in secondary recipients, consistent with editing of long‑term repopulating HSCs</cite>. Reviews highlight multiple in vivo examples across species and tissues where PE corrected or improved disease phenotypes, emphasizing delivery modality as a key determinant of editing efficiency and tissue reach <cite id="37314680">Preclinical in vivo studies demonstrate PE efficacy across models and tissues, with delivery method strongly influencing efficiency and therapeutic outcome</cite>. For neuromuscular diseases such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy, CRISPR-based editing including prime editing has shown both in vitro and in vivo correction of dystrophin reading frame, though translation is limited by delivery efficiency, off‑target mutagenesis, and long‑term dystrophin maintenance, underscoring the need for further optimization in muscle tissues <cite id="35163754">In vivo CRISPR editing, including prime editing, can restore dystrophin reading frame in Duchenne muscular dystrophy models, but faces challenges in delivery efficiency, off‑target mutagenesis, and long‑term dystrophin maintenance</cite>.

## Limitations and challenges
Despite promising results, several limitations remain evident in mammalian in vivo PE. Delivery to hematopoietic tissues can be simplified with mobilization and nonintegrating vectors, but broader tissue tropism and systemic delivery remain challenging; for example, liver‑specific or systemic PE models are less mature, and metabolic disease correction data are limited relative to hematopoietic applications <cite id="37314680">While multiple in vivo PE successes exist, delivery method and tissue reach are central constraints, and liver/metabolic disease applications are less developed than hematopoietic ones</cite>. In muscle, maintaining durable expression of therapeutic edits (e.g., full‑length dystrophin) over long‑term remains difficult, reflecting integration/epigenetic and cell‑intrinsic constraints that also likely affect other tissues <cite id="35163754">Long‑term maintenance of therapeutic edits such as dystrophin is a key limitation for in vivo CRISPR/PE approaches in muscle</cite>. Off‑target detection remains a critical bottleneck; although current studies report no detectable off‑target edits at prioritized sites using sensitive assays, comprehensive, unbiased genome‑wide monitoring is still needed to rule out rare off‑target effects in vivo <cite id="36800642">Studies report no detectable off‑target editing at prioritized sites with sensitive assays, but comprehensive genome‑wide off‑target monitoring remains essential</cite><cite id="38843380">No detectable off‑target editing at top‑scored potential sites was observed, highlighting the need for broader, unbiased assessments</cite>. Finally, operational constraints such as time‑consuming HSC mobilization and the need for in vivo selection have been addressed by simplified regimens, but scalability, immune responses to viral vectors, and ensuring engraftment of edited long‑term repopulating HSCs at clinically meaningful levels remain ongoing challenges <cite id="38843380">Simplified G‑CSF‑free mobilization with in vivo selection improved practicality, but scaling, immune responses, and engraftment of edited long‑term HSCs remain challenges</cite><cite id="36800642">In vivo HSC prime editing corrected a substantial fraction of alleles and edited long‑term repopulating HSCs, but practical and scalability issues persist</cite>.

## Conclusions
Mammalian in vivo studies, especially in mouse models of sickle cell disease, demonstrate that prime editing can achieve therapeutic mutation correction with a favorable safety profile characterized by low indels and undetected off‑target edits at prioritized sites, and with evidence of durable HSC editing in secondary recipients <cite id="36800642">Prime editing in SCD mice achieved therapeutic correction with low indels, no detectable off‑target edits, and evidence of durable HSC editing</cite><cite id="38843380">A simplified mobilization and in vivo selection workflow achieved measurable mutation correction with a good safety profile</cite>. Efficiency varies by tissue and delivery system, and hematopoietic applications appear most advanced, whereas systemic or liver‑directed PE for metabolic diseases and broader somatic tissues requires further development <cite id="37314680">PE efficacy in vivo depends on delivery and tissue context, with hematopoietic models leading and metabolic/liver applications less mature</cite>. Key limitations include delivery breadth, long‑term expression maintenance in non‑hematopoietic tissues, and the need for comprehensive off‑target surveillance; ongoing innovations in delivery (e.g., simplified mobilization, nonintegrating vectors, and tissue‑specific targeting) and safety assays are critical for clinical translation <cite id="35163754">Delivery efficiency, off‑target risk, and long‑term maintenance are central limitations requiring further study</cite><cite id="37314680">Advances in delivery methods and safety profiling are key to translating PE to clinical settings</cite>.
</answer>

## Conclusions
Mammalian in vivo studies, especially in mouse models of sickle cell disease, demonstrate that prime editing can achieve therapeutic mutation correction with a favorable safety profile characterized by low indels and undetected off‑target edits at prioritized sites, and with evidence of durable HSC editing in secondary recipients <cite id="36800642">Prime editing in SCD mice achieved therapeutic correction with low indels, no detectable off‑target edits, and evidence of durable HSC editing</cite><cite id="38843380">A simplified mobilization and in vivo selection workflow achieved measurable mutation correction with a good safety profile</cite>. <snippet id="36166727">Title: Combination Dabrafenib and Trametinib Versus Combination Nivolumab and Ipilimumab for Patients With Advanced BRAF -Mutant Melanoma: The DREAMseq Trial-ECOG-ACRIN EA6134.
Authors: Atkins, Michael B, Lee, Sandra J, Chmielowski, Bartosz et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology
Abstract: PURPOSE
Combination programmed cell death protein 1/cytotoxic T-cell lymphocyte-4-blockade and dual BRAF/MEK inhibition have each shown significant clinical benefit in patients with BRAFV600 -mutant metastatic melanoma, leading to broad regulatory approval. Little prospective data exist to guide the choice of either initial therapy or treatment sequence in this population. This study was conducted to determine which initial treatment or treatment sequence produced the best efficacy.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
In a phase III trial, patients with treatment-naive BRAFV600 -mutant metastatic melanoma were randomly assigned to receive either combination nivolumab/ipilimumab (arm A) or dabrafenib/trametinib (arm B) in step 1, and at disease progression were enrolled in step 2 to receive the alternate therapy, dabrafenib/trametinib (arm C) or nivolumab/ipilimumab (arm D). The primary end point was 2-year overall survival (OS). Secondary end points were 3-year OS, objective response rate, response duration, progression-free survival, crossover feasibility, and safety.
RESULTS
A total of 265 patients were enrolled, with 73 going onto step 2 (27 in arm C and 46 in arm D). The study was stopped early by the independent Data Safety Monitoring Committee because of a clinically significant end point being achieved. The 2-year OS for those starting on arm A was 71.8% (95% CI, 62.5 to 79.1) and arm B 51.5% (95% CI, 41.7 to 60.4; log-rank P = .010). Step 1 progression-free survival favored arm A ( P = .054). Objective response rates were arm A: 46.0%; arm B: 43.0%; arm C: 47.8%; and arm D: 29.6%. Median duration of response was not reached for arm A and 12.7 months for arm B ( P < .001). Crossover occurred in 52% of patients with documented disease progression. Grade ≥ 3 toxicities occurred with similar frequency between arms, and regimen toxicity profiles were as anticipated.
CONCLUSION
Combination nivolumab/ipilimumab followed by BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy, if necessary, should be the preferred treatment sequence for a large majority of patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="25399551">Title: Improved overall survival in melanoma with combined dabrafenib and trametinib.
Authors: Robert, Caroline, Karaszewska, Boguslawa, Schachter, Jacob et al. | Year: 2015 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
The BRAF inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib have shown efficacy as monotherapies in patients with previously untreated metastatic melanoma with BRAF V600E or V600K mutations. Combining dabrafenib and the MEK inhibitor trametinib, as compared with dabrafenib alone, enhanced antitumor activity in this population of patients.
METHODS
In this open-label, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 704 patients with metastatic melanoma with a BRAF V600 mutation to receive either a combination of dabrafenib (150 mg twice daily) and trametinib (2 mg once daily) or vemurafenib (960 mg twice daily) orally as first-line therapy. The primary end point was overall survival.
RESULTS
At the preplanned interim overall survival analysis, which was performed after 77% of the total number of expected events occurred, the overall survival rate at 12 months was 72% (95% confidence interval [CI], 67 to 77) in the combination-therapy group and 65% (95% CI, 59 to 70) in the vemurafenib group (hazard ratio for death in the combination-therapy group, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.89; P=0.005). The prespecified interim stopping boundary was crossed, and the study was stopped for efficacy in July 2014. Median progression-free survival was 11.4 months in the combination-therapy group and 7.3 months in the vemurafenib group (hazard ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.46 to 0.69; P<0.001). The objective response rate was 64% in the combination-therapy group and 51% in the vemurafenib group (P<0.001). Rates of severe adverse events and study-drug discontinuations were similar in the two groups. Cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma and keratoacanthoma occurred in 1% of patients in the combination-therapy group and 18% of those in the vemurafenib group.
CONCLUSIONS
Dabrafenib plus trametinib, as compared with vemurafenib monotherapy, significantly improved overall survival in previously untreated patients with metastatic melanoma with BRAF V600E or V600K mutations, without increased overall toxicity. (Funded by GlaxoSmithKline; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT01597908.).</snippet>
<snippet id="39973323">Title: BRAF inhibitors with or without MEK inhibitors in advanced BRAF-positive non-small cell lung cancer: A systematic review.
Authors: Saha, Animesh, Raja, T, Dutt Dwary, Amit et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners
Abstract: ObjectiveAbout 1% to 5% of cases of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) have been found to have a BRAF mutation. There is no phase III data, despite the fact that numerous phase II and retrospective studies have demonstrated the efficacy of single agent BRAF inhibition and combination BRAF/MEK inhibition in patient groups that have received treatment and those who have not. Our goal in this systematic review was to provide an overview of the available evidence in this context.Data SourcesA thorough search was conducted in the PubMed, Medline, Embase, and Cochrane databases for English-language papers published between January 2000 and December 2023 that had full text accessibility. Independently, one author screened the eligible studies that fit our predetermined requirements. A synthesis of the qualitative data was conducted, and the design and quality of the studies were evaluated.Data SummaryThere were 2952 articles found using the search method. Twelve publications with a total of 753 patients were included after two rounds of screening. 33-75% was the objective response rate (ORR). 64-100% was the disease control rate (DCR). The time span for the answer varied from 6.4 to 16.7 months. The range of the median progression-free survival (PFS) was 1.2 to 17.5 months. The range of the median overall survival (OS) was 1.7-25.5 months. When comparing studies with single agent BRAF inhibitors to those reporting the results of BRAF plus MEK inhibitors, the response rates, duration of response, and survival were better in the former case. When untreated patients receiving BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy were compared to previously treated patients, the results were also improved. Hypertension, pyrexia, hyponatremia, neutropenia, dyspnoea, anaemia, abnormal liver function, asthenia, and cutaneous epidermoid carcinoma were among the frequently reported grade ≥3 toxicity.ConclusionsPatients with advanced NSCLC that include a BRAF mutation have demonstrated encouraging clinical outcomes with a manageable safety profile when treated with BRAF inhibitors, either in combination with or without MEK inhibitor therapy. In patients who had not received treatment before, combination treatment produced greater results.</snippet>
<snippet id="25648338">Title: BRAF and MEK inhibition in melanoma.
Authors: Dossett, Lesly A, Kudchadkar, Ragini R, Zager, Jonathan S | Year: 2015 | Journal: Expert opinion on drug safety
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Selective inhibition of the MAPK pathway with either BRAF or MEK inhibition has emerged as a key component for the treatment of BRAF-mutant metastatic melanoma. New evidence suggests that the combination of BRAF and MEK inhibitors improves tumor response rate and progression-free survival, while potentially attenuating some of the serious adverse events observed with monotherapy.
AREAS COVERED
This review covers the current data on the efficacy and safety of the selective BRAF (vemurafenib and dabrafenib) and MEK (trametinib) inhibitors as well as the available data on BRAF inhibitor + MEK inhibitor combination therapy (dabrafenib + trametinib and vemurafenib + cobimetinib). The efficacy, safety and toxicity data are discussed from Phase I, Phase II and Phase III trials of these drugs.
EXPERT OPINION
Combination therapy with the BRAF and MEK inhibitors improves response rates and progression-free survival in patients with BRAF-mutant metastatic melanoma. Some of the serious adverse events, in particular, the incidence of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, are attenuated with combination therapy, whereas milder side effects such as pyrexia can be more common with combination therapy. Although dose reductions and dose interruptions are slightly more common with combination therapy, overall data supports the notion that combination therapy is safe and improves the outcomes for patients compared to single agent BRAF inhibitors.</snippet>
<snippet id="39427441">Title: First-line encorafenib plus binimetinib and pembrolizumab for advanced BRAF V600-mutant melanoma: Safety lead-in results from the randomized phase III STARBOARD study.
Authors: Dudnichenko, Oleksandr, Penkov, Konstantin, McKean, Meredith et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990)
Abstract: BACKGROUND
BRAF inhibitors plus MEK inhibitors (BRAFi/MEKi) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (CPIs) are approved for BRAF V600-mutant advanced melanoma. Combinations of BRAFi/MEKi with CPIs may further improve outcomes and could offer additional treatment strategies.
METHODS
STARBOARD (NCT04657991) is a phase III study with an initial safety lead-in (SLI) phase conducted to determine the recommended phase III dose (RP3D) for encorafenib in combination with binimetinib and pembrolizumab. Patients with untreated, unresectable locally advanced or metastatic BRAF V600E/K-mutant cutaneous melanoma received binimetinib 45 mg twice daily and pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks plus encorafenib 450 mg once daily (COMBO450 plus pembrolizumab) or 300 mg once daily (COMBO300 plus pembrolizumab). The primary endpoint was the incidence of dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs). Secondary endpoints included safety, objective response, time to response, and duration of response. Progression-free survival was assessed post hoc.
RESULTS
In the SLI, the median follow-up duration was 19.4 months. Twenty patients received COMBO450 plus pembrolizumab and 17 received COMBO300 plus pembrolizumab. DLTs occurred in 1 of 17 DLT-evaluable patients in the COMBO450 plus pembrolizumab arm and in 2 of 17 DLT-evaluable patients in the COMBO300 plus pembrolizumab arm. No treatment-related deaths occurred in either treatment arm. The overall response rate was 65.0 % in the COMBO450 plus pembrolizumab arm and 47.1 % in the COMBO300 plus pembrolizumab arm.
CONCLUSION
The STARBOARD SLI showed that safety across the cohorts was generally comparable to the known safety profile of each agent. The standard dose regimen of COMBO450 plus pembrolizumab was chosen as the RP3D.</snippet>

<snippet id="33020648">Title: Combined PD-1, BRAF and MEK inhibition in advanced BRAF-mutant melanoma: safety run-in and biomarker cohorts of COMBI-i.
Authors: Dummer, Reinhard, Lebbé, Celeste, Atkinson, Victoria et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Nature medicine
Abstract: Immune and targeted therapies achieve long-term survival in metastatic melanoma; however, new treatment strategies are needed to improve patients' outcomes 1,2 . We report on the efficacy, safety and biomarker analysis from the single-arm safety run-in (part 1; n = 9) and biomarker (part 2; n = 27) cohorts of the randomized, placebo-controlled, phase 3 COMBI-i trial (NCT02967692) of the anti-PD-1 antibody spartalizumab, in combination with the BRAF inhibitor dabrafenib and MEK inhibitor trametinib. Patients (n = 36) had previously untreated BRAF V600-mutant unresectable or metastatic melanoma. In part 1, the recommended phase 3 regimen was identified based on the incidence of dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs; primary endpoint): 400 mg of spartalizumab every 4 weeks plus 150 mg of dabrafenib twice daily plus 2 mg of trametinib once daily. Part 2 characterized changes in PD-L1 levels and CD8 + cells following treatment (primary endpoint), and analyzed additional biomarkers. Assessments of efficacy and safety were key secondary endpoints (median follow-up, 24.3 months). Spartalizumab plus dabrafenib and trametinib led to an objective response rate (ORR) of 78%, including 44% complete responses (CRs). Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were experienced by 72% of patients. All patients had temporary dose modifications, and 17% permanently discontinued all three study drugs due to TRAEs. Early progression-free survival (PFS) events were associated with low tumor mutational burden/T cell-inflamed gene expression signature (GES) or high immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) GES levels at baseline; an immunosuppressive TME may also preclude CR. Overall, the efficacy, safety and on-treatment biomarker modulations associated with spartalizumab plus dabrafenib and trametinib are promising, and biomarkers that may predict long-term benefit were identified.</snippet>

<snippet id="25265492">Title: Combined BRAF and MEK inhibition versus BRAF inhibition alone in melanoma.
Authors: Long, Georgina V, Stroyakovskiy, Daniil, Gogas, Helen et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Combined BRAF and MEK inhibition, as compared with BRAF inhibition alone, delays the emergence of resistance and reduces toxic effects in patients who have melanoma with BRAF V600E or V600K mutations.
METHODS
In this phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 423 previously untreated patients who had unresectable stage IIIC or stage IV melanoma with a BRAF V600E or V600K mutation to receive a combination of dabrafenib (150 mg orally twice daily) and trametinib (2 mg orally once daily) or dabrafenib and placebo. The primary end point was progression-free survival. Secondary end points included overall survival, response rate, response duration, and safety. A preplanned interim overall survival analysis was conducted.
RESULTS
The median progression-free survival was 9.3 months in the dabrafenib-trametinib group and 8.8 months in the dabrafenib-only group (hazard ratio for progression or death in the dabrafenib-trametinib group, 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.57 to 0.99; P=0.03). The overall response rate was 67% in the dabrafenib-trametinib group and 51% in the dabrafenib-only group (P=0.002). At 6 months, the interim overall survival rate was 93% with dabrafenib-trametinib and 85% with dabrafenib alone (hazard ratio for death, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.42 to 0.94; P=0.02). However, a specified efficacy-stopping boundary (two-sided P=0.00028) was not crossed. Rates of adverse events were similar in the two groups, although more dose modifications occurred in the dabrafenib-trametinib group. The rate of cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma was lower in the dabrafenib-trametinib group than in the dabrafenib-only group (2% vs. 9%), whereas pyrexia occurred in more patients (51% vs. 28%) and was more often severe (grade 3, 6% vs. 2%) in the dabrafenib-trametinib group.
CONCLUSIONS
A combination of dabrafenib and trametinib, as compared with dabrafenib alone, improved the rate of progression-free survival in previously untreated patients who had metastatic melanoma with BRAF V600E or V600K mutations. (Funded by GlaxoSmithKline; Clinical Trials.gov number, NCT01584648.).</snippet>
<snippet id="35022320">Title: BAMM (BRAF Autophagy and MEK Inhibition in Melanoma): A Phase I/II Trial of Dabrafenib, Trametinib, and Hydroxychloroquine in Advanced BRAFV600-mutant Melanoma.
Authors: Mehnert, Janice M, Mitchell, Tara C, Huang, Alexander C et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research
Abstract: PURPOSE
Autophagy is a resistance mechanism to BRAF/MEK inhibition in BRAFV600-mutant melanoma. Here we used hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) to inhibit autophagy in combination with dabrafenib 150 mg twice daily and trametinib 2 mg every day (D+T).
PATIENTS AND METHODS
We conducted a phase I/II clinical trial in four centers of HCQ + D+T in patients with advanced BRAFV600-mutant melanoma. The primary objectives were the recommended phase II dose (RP2D) and the one-year progression-free survival (PFS) rate of >53%.
RESULTS
Thirty-four patients were evaluable for one-year PFS rate. Patient demographics were as follows: elevated lactate dehydrogenase: 47%; stage IV M1c/M1d: 52%; prior immunotherapy: 50%. In phase I, there was no dose-limiting toxicity. HCQ 600 mg orally twice daily with D+T was the RP2D. The one-year PFS rate was 48.2% [95% confidence interval (CI), 31.0%-65.5%], median PFS was 11.2 months (95% CI, 5.4-16.9 months), and response rate (RR) was 85% (95% CI, 64%-95%). The complete RR was 41% and median overall survival (OS) was 26.5 months. In a patient with elevated LDH (n = 16), the RR was 88% and median PFS and OS were 7.3 and 22 months, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
HCQ + D+T was well tolerated and produced a high RR but did not meet criteria for success for the one-year PFS rate. There was a high proportion of patients with pretreated and elevated LDH, an increasingly common demographic in patients receiving targeted therapy. In this difficult-to-treat population, the RR and PFS were encouraging. A randomized trial of D+T + HCQ or placebo in patients with BRAFV600-mutant melanoma with elevated LDH and previous immunotherapy is being conducted.</snippet>

# Summary

Across phase III trials in oncology, adding a MEK inhibitor to a BRAF-targeted therapy improves tumor response rates and survival compared with BRAF inhibition alone, but it increases the frequency and severity of dose‑limiting toxicities and treatment‑related grade ≥3 adverse events relative to monotherapy. The clearest evidence comes from BRAF V600–mutant melanoma, where dual BRAF/MEK inhibition (e.g., dabrafenib plus trametinib) produced higher objective response rates and improved progression‑free and overall survival versus BRAF inhibitor monotherapy (vemurafenib or dabrafenib alone), with toxicity largely characterized by more common but manageable pyrexia and similar or lower rates of keratoacanthoma/squamous cell carcinoma. In contrast, adding a PD‑1 inhibitor to a BRAF/MEK regimen (spartalizumab + dabrafenib + trametinib) yielded very high response rates but substantially higher rates of grade ≥3 toxicities and more frequent dose modifications or permanent discontinuation.

# Evidence from Phase III Trials

- Dabrafenib + trametinib versus vemurafenib (first‑line, BRAF V600 mutant melanoma):
  - Objective response rate: 64% with combination vs 51% with vemurafenib (P < 0.001). Median progression‑free survival 11.4 vs 7.3 months (HR 0.56), and overall survival at 12 months 72% vs 65% (HR 0.69); study stopped early for efficacy. Rates of severe adverse events and discontinuation were similar between arms, with a lower incidence of keratoacanthoma/squamous cell carcinoma on the combination (1% vs 18%). Pyrexia was more common and often more severe with combination therapy. <cite id="25399551">Combining dabrafenib and trametinib improved overall survival, progression‑free survival, and response rate versus vemurafenib monotherapy without increased overall toxicity, though pyrexia was more frequent and often more severe with the combination, and keratoacanthoma/squamous cell carcinoma was less common</cite> <cite id="25265492">In a separate phase 3 trial, dabrafenib‑trametinib improved progression‑free survival (median 9.3 vs 8.8 months) and response rate (67% vs 51%), with more dose modifications and higher grade 3 pyrexia but lower cutaneous squamous‑cell carcinoma than dabrafenib alone</cite>.

- Dabrafenib + trametinib versus ipilimumab/nivolumab (sequence study, BRAF V600 mutant melanoma):
  - In DREAMseq, adding nivolumab/ipilimumab after disease progression to patients initially on BRAF/MEK therapy was favored by OS (2‑year OS 71.8% vs 51.5% for those starting on BRAF/MEK vs CPI), though initial PFS favored BRAF/MEK. Response rates were similar between initial arms (46% with CPI vs 43% with BRAF/MEK), with BRAF/MEK responses durable (median duration not reached vs 12.7 months). Grade ≥3 toxicities occurred with similar frequency across arms and were as expected. <cite id="36166727">In a phase III treatment‑sequence study, initial combination BRAF/MEK therapy achieved higher 2‑year overall survival than CPI, with similar initial response rates but shorter PFS for BRAF/MEK; grade ≥3 toxicities were similar across arms</cite>.

- Triple combination (PD‑1 + BRAF + MEK) in BRAF V600 mutant melanoma:
  - The phase 3 COMBI‑i safety cohort (randomized, placebo‑controlled lead‑in) identified a recommended regimen (spartalizumab 400 mg q4w + dabrafenib 150 mg bid + trametinib 2 mg qd) based on DLT incidence. Efficacy readout showed an ORR of 78% with 44% complete responses; grade ≥3 TRAEs occurred in 72% of patients, with all patients requiring dose modifications and 17% permanently discontinuing due to toxicity. <cite id="33020648">Spartalizumab plus dabrafenib and trametinib achieved high response rates (ORR 78%, CR 44%) but had high rates of grade ≥3 treatment‑related adverse events (72%), dose modifications, and permanent discontinuation (17%)</cite>.

# Interpretation for "Add‑on MEK Inhibitor vs Targeted Agent Alone"

- Response and survival:
  - In BRAF V600–mutant melanoma, adding trametinib to a BRAF inhibitor significantly increases objective response rates (e.g., 64% vs 51% vs 67% in different phase III settings), improves PFS, and improves OS relative to BRAF inhibitor monotherapy. <cite id="25399551">Combination BRAF/MEK therapy improved OS and PFS and increased response rates compared with vemurafenib alone</cite> <cite id="25265492">Combination BRAF/MEK therapy improved PFS and response rate versus BRAF inhibitor alone, with a trend toward improved OS</cite>.
  - Adding MEK inhibition can also synergize with PD‑1 blockade, achieving very high response rates in early randomized cohorts, though these data are from a biomarker/lead‑in phase rather than a full phase III efficacy readout. <cite id="33020648">Triple therapy (spartalizumab + dabrafenib + trametinib) achieved an ORR of 78% including 44% complete responses</cite>.

- Toxicity:
  - Compared with BRAF monotherapy, dual BRAF/MEK therapy increases the incidence of grade ≥3 adverse events and treatment‑related dose modifications, particularly for pyrexia; however, some toxicities observed with BRAF alone (e.g., keratoacanthoma/squamous cell carcinoma) are reduced. <cite id="25399551">Rates of severe adverse events and discontinuations were similar overall, but pyrexia was more common and often more severe with the combination, whereas keratoacanthoma/squamous cell carcinoma was less frequent</cite> <cite id="25265492">More dose modifications occurred with the combination, and grade 3 pyrexia was more common; cutaneous squamous‑cell carcinoma was lower than with BRAF alone</cite>.
  - Adding PD‑1 inhibition to BRAF/MEK markedly raises the burden of grade ≥3 toxicities and discontinuations, reflecting the叠加 of immune‑related and targeted adverse events. <cite id="33020648">In the triple‑combination cohort, 72% experienced grade ≥3 TRAEs, all patients had dose modifications, and 17% permanently discontinued due to toxicity</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Adding a MEK inhibitor to a BRAF‑targeted therapy in phase III oncology (notably BRAF V600–mutant melanoma) generally improves response rates and clinical outcomes versus the targeted agent alone, with evidence of higher ORR, longer PFS, and improved OS. <cite id="25399551">Combination BRAF/MEK therapy improved OS, PFS, and ORR versus BRAF inhibitor monotherapy</cite> <cite id="25265492">Combination BRAF/MEK therapy improved PFS and ORR and showed a favorable trend in OS compared with BRAF inhibitor alone</cite>.
- However, the addition of MEK inhibition increases the frequency and severity of dose‑limiting toxicities and treatment‑related grade ≥3 adverse events, particularly pyrexia, and in triple combinations with PD‑1 blockade, toxicity can be substantial enough to cause more permanent discontinuations. <cite id="25399551">Pyrexia was more frequent and often more severe with the combination, while keratoacanthoma/squamous cell carcinoma decreased</cite> <cite id="25265492">More dose interruptions/modifications were required with the combination, with higher grade 3 pyrexia</cite> <cite id="33020648">Triple therapy (PD‑1 + BRAF + MEK) had high rates of grade ≥3 TRAEs and discontinuation</cite>.

# Scope and Limitations

- The strongest phase III data are in BRAF V600–mutant melanoma; extrapolation to other tumor types with different targetable pathways may vary. <cite id="25399551">Evidence for improved outcomes with BRAF/MEK combination therapy is robust in BRAF V600–mutant melanoma</cite> <cite id="25265492">Phase 3 trials specifically enrolled BRAF V600E/K melanoma</cite>.
