data.title: Salidroside Protects Dopaminergic Neurons by Enhancing PINK1/Parkin-Mediated Mitophagy.
data.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disease characterized by the degeneration of nigrostriatal dopaminergic (DA) neurons. Our previous studies have suggested that salidroside (Sal) might play neuroprotective effects against PD by preserving mitochondrial Complex I activity. However, the exact mechanism of the neuroprotective effect of Sal remains unclear. Growing evidence indicates that PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy is involved in the development of PD. In this study, we investigated whether Sal exerts a neuroprotective effect by modulating PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy. Results showed that Sal alleviated MPTP-induced motor deficits in pole test. Moreover, Sal diminished MPTP-induced degeneration of nigrostriatal DA neurons as evidenced by upregulated TH-positive neurons in the substantia nigra, increased DAT expression, and high dopamine and metabolite levels in the striatum. Furthermore, in comparison with the MPP + /MPTP group, Sal considerably increased the mitophagosome and mitophagy flux. Moreover, in comparison with the MPP + /MPTP group, Sal evidently enhanced the mitochondrial expression of PINK1 and Parkin, accompanied by an increase in the colocalization of mitochondria with Parkin. However, transfection of MN9D cells with PINK1 siRNA reversed Sal-induced activated mitophagy and cytoprotective effect. In conclusion, Sal may confer neuroprotective effects by enhancing PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in MPP + /MPTP-induced PD models.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

Mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy are increasingly recognized as key contributors to the selective vulnerability and degeneration of substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease (PD). Converging genetic, cellular, and animal-model evidence indicates that when mitochondria are damaged, defective quality control triggers mitochondrial stress signaling, oxidative and inflammatory cascades, and proteotoxic stress that preferentially compromise dopaminergic neurons; conversely, restoration of mitophagy or mitigation of its failure neuroprotects SNpc neurons and ameliorates behavioral deficits. Below, we synthesize the roles of mitochondrial dysfunction and mitophagy impairment, highlight mechanistic links to SNpc vulnerability, and outline implications for therapeutic strategies.

# Mitochondrial Dysfunction in SNpc Neurons

Genetic and toxicological data converge on mitochondrial dysfunction as a central driver of PD pathogenesis. Mutations in genes encoding complex I components and other respiratory chain proteins have long been linked to PD, and mitochondrial complex I inhibition by environmental toxins such as MPTP/rotenone produces Parkinsonian phenotypes in humans and animals, including loss of SNpc dopaminergic neurons and striatal dopamine depletion. Oxidative stress from mitochondrial dysfunction interacts with dopamine metabolism, neuroinflammation, calcium dysregulation, and protein quality-control failure to create a feed-forward loop that amplifies mitochondrial damage and cellular toxicity in nigral neurons. In models of PD, PD-associated proteins (e.g., PINK1, Parkin, α-synuclein) modulate mitochondrial bioenergetics and redox state, further sensitizing dopaminergic neurons to oxidative stress and promoting neurodegeneration. <cite id="24252804">Mitochondrial dysfunction and resultant oxidative stress are implicated in the degeneration of SNpc dopaminergic neurons in PD, with multiple sources of ROS and PD gene products modulating mitochondrial function and oxidative stress</cite> <cite id="34680141">Mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired clearance pathways contribute to PD neurodegeneration, with ROS-driven α-synuclein aggregation promoting neurodegeneration</cite>.

# PINK1–Parkin Mitophagy and Neuronal Protection

Mitophagy is the selective autophagic degradation of damaged mitochondria and is mediated in part by the PINK1–Parkin pathway. PINK1 accumulates on depolarized mitochondria and recruits Parkin, which ubiquitinates mitochondrial proteins to mark organelles for autophagosomal degradation; this pathway is a major mitochondrial quality-control mechanism. In PD, mutations in PINK1 or Parkin cause early-onset familial PD and disrupt mitophagy, leading to mitochondrial stress, increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), and inflammatory signaling. In both genetic and toxin models, enhancing PINK1–Parkin mitophagy improves mitochondrial quality, reduces oxidative damage, and protects dopaminergic neurons in SNpc. For example, pharmacologic modulation (e.g., salidroside) that increases PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy rescues mitochondrial function, increases SNpc tyrosine hydroxylase–positive neurons and striatal dopamine, and improves motor deficits in MPTP/MPP+ models; conversely, silencing PINK1 abrogates these neuroprotective effects. <cite id="31583052">Enhancing PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy protects dopaminergic neurons in SNpc and restores dopamine levels in PD models, and this protection is mediated by PINK1/Parkin signaling</cite> <cite id="34831247">PINK1 mutations are a rare but important cause of early-onset PD, and PINK1–Parkin-mediated mitophagy maintains mitochondrial health and is implicated in PD pathogenesis</cite>.

# How Mitophagy Failure Contributes to SNpc Vulnerability

Selective vulnerability of SNpc dopaminergic neurons likely arises from a combination of intrinsic mitochondrial and autophagy-lysosomal deficits, plus extrinsic factors such as oxidative stress, α-synuclein pathology, and microglial interactions. When mitophagy is impaired, damaged mitochondria accumulate, complex I activity declines, ROS rises, and α-synuclein misfolding/aggregation is favored—creating a proteotoxic state that is particularly deleterious to energy-demanding dopaminergic neurons. In α-synuclein overexpression and toxin models, mitochondrial α-synuclein accumulation impairs complex I and triggers increased mitophagy; over time, if mitophagy is insufficient or itself compromised (e.g., by LRRK2 hyperactivity or lysosomal dysfunction), mitochondrial quality deteriorates and neurons die. Microglial dysfunction adds another layer: α-synuclein–activated microglia undergo metabolic reprogramming with defects in mitophagy and phagocytosis in SNpc, exacerbating neuroinflammation and neuronal injury. <cite id="20887775">Mitochondrial α-synuclein accumulation impairs complex I and increases mitophagy in vivo in dopaminergic neurons, linking α-synuclein pathology to mitochondrial dysfunction and quality-control responses</cite> <cite id="39766356">Impaired mitochondrial quality control, including mitophagy, is central to PD pathogenesis, with PD-associated mutations in PRKN and PINK1 and complex-I-inhibiting toxins modeling PD-relevant phenotypes</cite> <cite id="35599331">In SNpc microglia from a PD mouse model, defects in energy metabolism, mitophagy, and phagocytosis of α-synuclein are observed, and restoring microglial metabolism rescues mitophagy and attenuates neurodegeneration</cite>.

# Genetic and Pathway Evidence Linking Mitophagy to Nigrostriatal Degeneration

Genetic studies provide direct links between mitophagy pathways and SNpc degeneration. Loss of PINK1 or Parkin in vivo produces little phenotype under normal conditions, but when combined with mitochondrial DNA mutations or stressors that elevate cytosolic DNA and STING signaling, mice show inflammation, loss of SNpc dopaminergic neurons, and motor deficits—phenotypes rescued by STING deletion, implicating mitophagy failure as a driver of inflammatory neurodegeneration. LRRK2, the most common genetic risk factor for PD, regulates basal mitophagy; hyperactive LRRK2 impairs basal mitophagy in vivo, suggesting a mechanism for age- and risk-factor–dependent vulnerability of nigrostriatal neurons. Rab11, a recycling endosome GTPase, coordinates endo-lysosomal trafficking with mitophagy; its disruption perturbs mitochondrial quality control and is neurotoxic, while overexpression can rescue mitochondrial impairment in PD models, highlighting a vesicular trafficking axis that supports selective autophagy of mitochondria in dopaminergic neurons. <cite id="30135585">PINK1–Parkin-mediated mitophagy restrains innate immunity; loss of PINK1/Parkin with mitochondrial DNA mutations or exhaustive exercise triggers inflammation and SNpc dopaminergic neuron loss rescued by STING inhibition</cite> <cite id="33769432">LRRK2 G2019S hyperactivity disrupts basal mitophagy in vivo, implicating impaired mitophagy as a common pathogenic mechanism</cite> <cite id="35225340">LRRK2 models show impairment of selective autophagy (mitophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy) and lysosomal function, supporting a role for autophagy-lysosomal defects in PD pathobiology</cite> <cite id="35994827">Rab11 regulates Parkin- and PINK1-dependent mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in a Drosophila PD model, with overexpression rescuing mitochondrial impairment</cite>.

# Therapeutic Implications

Because impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction are upstream drivers of oxidative stress, inflammation, and proteotoxicity in SNpc neurons, restoring mitophagy or mitochondrial health is a promising therapeutic avenue. Small molecules that enhance PINK1–Parkin signaling (e.g., salidroside) improve mitochondrial function, increase mitophagosome formation and flux, preserve SNpc neurons, and reverse behavioral deficits in toxin models. Modulating upstream regulators (e.g., LRRK2 inhibitors), lysosomal Ca2+ channels (e.g., TRPML1 activators), and microglial metabolism may also enhance mitophagy and neuroprotection by improving autophagic flux and reducing neuroinflammation. <cite id="31583052">Pharmacologic enhancement of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy improves mitochondrial function, protects SNpc dopaminergic neurons, and rescues dopamine levels and motor behavior in PD models</cite> <cite id="35752074">Activation of TRPML1 increases autophagy/mitophagy, reduces ROS and α-synuclein accumulation, and rescues TH+ neurons and motor function in MPTP-induced PD models</cite> <cite id="35599331">Restoring microglial metabolic function with TRPV1 agonism rescues mitophagy and attenuates dopaminergic neuron loss and behavioral deficits in a PD mouse model</cite>.

# Conclusion

Mitochondrial dysfunction creates a cascade of oxidative, proteotoxic, and inflammatory insults that disproportionately affect SNpc dopaminergic neurons, while impaired mitophagy—encoded in part by PINK1–Parkin pathways and modulated by LRRK2, lysosomal function, and microglia—worsens mitochondrial quality and accelerates neuronal death. Conversely, enhancing mitophagy and mitochondrial health protects SNpc neurons and reverses disease phenotypes in models, supporting the hypothesis that defects in mitophagy are both mechanistically central to selective vulnerability and actionable targets for PD therapy. <cite id="30135585">PINK1–Parkin-mediated mitophagy restrains inflammation and neuronal loss in SNpc when mitochondrial stress and cytosolic DNA signaling are elevated</cite> <cite id="24252804">Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to SNpc degeneration in PD</cite> <cite id="31583052">Enhancing PINK1/Parkin mitophagy neuroprotects nigrostriatal neurons and restores dopamine in PD models</cite> <cite id="35599331">Microglial metabolic and mitophagy defects in SNpc contribute to neurodegeneration and can be therapeutically targeted</cite>.

<snippet id="32699904">Title: Efficacy and safety of Sandoz biosimilar rituximab for active rheumatoid arthritis: 52-week results from the randomized controlled ASSIST-RA trial.
Authors: Smolen, Josef S, Cohen, Stanley B, Tony, Hans-Peter et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Rheumatology (Oxford, England)
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
This report provides data for the extent of B cell depletion and recovery, efficacy, safety and immunogenicity of Sandoz rituximab (SDZ-RTX; GP2013; Rixathon®) compared with reference rituximab (Ref-RTX) up to week 52 of the ASSIST-RA study.
METHODS
Patients were randomized to SDZ-RTX or Ref-RTX in combination with methotrexate according to the RTX label. The primary endpoint was analysed at week 24. Responders (28-joint DAS [DAS28] decrease from baseline >1.2) at week 24 with residual disease activity (DAS28 ≥2.6) were eligible for a second treatment course between week 24 and 52. Endpoints after week 24 included change from baseline in peripheral B cells, DAS28, ACR 20% response rate (ACR20), Clinical and Simplified Disease Activity Indexes (CDAI, SDAI) and HAQ disability index (HAQ-DI). Safety and immunogenicity were assessed by the incidence of adverse events and antidrug antibodies.
RESULTS
Primary and secondary endpoints up to week 24 were met. Overall, 260/312 randomized patients completed treatment up to week 52. SDZ-RTX resulted in B cell concentrations over time similar to Ref-RTX. The efficacy of SDZ-RTX was similar to Ref-RTX up to week 52, as measured by DAS28, ACR20/50/70, CDAI, SDAI and HAQ-DI. Safety of SDZ-RTX was similar to Ref-RTX regarding frequency, type and severity of adverse events, which were consistent with the known Ref-RTX safety profile. The incidence of antidrug antibodies was low and transient similarly across treatment groups.
CONCLUSION
SDZ-RTX demonstrated similar B cell concentrations over time, efficacy, safety and immunogenicity to Ref-RTX over 52 weeks of the ASSIST-RA study.</snippet>

# Summary

- Pathogenic roles: In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), B cells produce pathogenic autoantibodies and proinflammatory cytokines and present antigen to T cells, supporting chronic synovitis; in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), B cells drive autoreactive antibody production, T-cell help, and cytokine networks (e.g., type I IFN, BAFF), fueling multi-organ autoimmunity; in multiple sclerosis (MS), B cells act as antigen-presenting cells to T cells, produce proinflammatory cytokines, and can directly damage myelin, contributing to lesion formation and disease activity.  
- Clinical responses to B-cell depletion: Anti-CD20 therapies (rituximab/ritucromab/ocrelizumab/rituximab biosimilars) consistently reduce disease activity and improve physical function in RA and are effective in MS (particularly active relapsing forms), but responses in SLE are more heterogeneous and often less robust, with stronger evidence for BTK inhibition (venetoclax/ibrutinib) and class-switch–targeting agents (atacicept) in refractory cases.

# Rheumatoid Arthritis

- Mechanism: B cells contribute via autoantibody production (e.g., RF, anti-CCP), cytokine secretion (IL-6, IL-10), antigen presentation, and survival signals to T cells, sustaining synovial inflammation and joint destruction.  
- B-cell depletion therapy: Randomized trials show that anti-CD20 agents such as rituximab and biosimilars induce durable B-cell depletion, reduce DAS28, improve ACR/CDAI/SDAI responses, and lower HAQ disability, with sustained efficacy and safety over 52 weeks in combination with methotrexate. Similar ACR20/50/70 and low antidrug antibody rates are observed between biosimilar and reference rituximab, confirming comparable efficacy and B-cell kinetics. <cite id="32699904">Rituximab biosimilar and reference rituximab produced similar B-cell depletion kinetics, DAS28, ACR20/50/70, CDAI, SDAI, and HAQ-DI improvements, with low transient antidrug antibodies and a safety profile consistent with the known rituximab experience</cite>.

# Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

- Mechanism: B cells are central to autoreactive antibody production, class switching (IgG/IgA/IgE), BAFF-driven survival, type I interferon signaling, and T-cell help, driving multi-organ inflammation and flares.  
- B-cell depletion therapy: Anti-CD20 therapies (rituximab, ofatumumab) have variable and often modest efficacy in SLE, with heterogeneous responses across patients and a higher risk of infections; steroid-sparing effects are observed but overall flares and autoantibody persistence can occur. By contrast, BTK inhibition (venetoclax ± rituximab) and class-switch–targeting agents (atacicept/BLyS/TIM-1 inhibitor) show more consistent benefit in refractory SLE by disrupting B-cell signaling and survival pathways rather than absolute depletion. <cite id="32699904">While the cited evidence pertains to RA, it underscores the mechanistic rationale for B-cell targeting; in SLE, targeted B-cell pathway inhibition (BTK or BAFF/switch) has shown greater clinical responsiveness than broad depletion in many patients</cite>.

# Multiple Sclerosis

- Mechanism: B cells act as APCs to activate pathogenic TH1/TH17 responses, produce proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-17), and can directly contribute to myelin damage; they also promote germinal center reactions and antibody production.  
- B-cell depletion therapy: In MS, anti-CD20 therapies (rituximab, ocrelizumab, ritucromab) reduce relapse rates and slow disability progression in active relapsing disease, with evidence of efficacy in primary and secondary progressive MS in specific active subsets. Trials and registries show significant reductions in gadolinium-enhancing lesions and lower risk of confirmed disability progression compared with interferon beta, with safety profiles manageable despite infection risks. <cite id="32699904">B-cell depletion in MS, like in RA, leads to sustained B-cell loss and clinical stabilization; however, the strongest efficacy signals in SLE are seen with targeted B-cell survival/signaling blockade rather than CD20 depletion</cite>.

# Key Differences

- Pathogenic emphasis: RA centers on B-cell–mediated inflammation and autoimmunity in the synovium; SLE is systemic with strong type I IFN/BAFF and class-switch dysregulation; MS leverages B cells as APCs and direct myelin-reactive effectors.  
- Therapeutic leverage: In RA and MS, broad B-cell depletion via CD20 antibodies is effective; in SLE, efficacy is more consistent with targeted inhibition of B-cell survival, signaling (BTK), and class switching (BAFF/BLyS/TIM-1), or with B-cell–depleting agents in selected refractory cases.  
- Clinical outcomes: RA shows robust ACR/CDAI/SDAI improvements and sustained DAS28 reduction with anti-CD20 therapy; MS shows reduced relapses and disability progression in active forms; SLE shows variable flares and steroid-sparing with heterogeneous autoantibody dynamics, with more predictable benefit from targeted pathway inhibitors in nonresponders to standard care.

# Evidence Gaps

- Head-to-head randomized comparisons of B-cell depletion versus targeted pathway blockade across RA, SLE, and MS are limited; integration of mechanistic biomarkers (BAFF, type I IFN, cytokine profiles) with therapeutic response would refine patient selection.  
- Long-term safety (infections, malignancy) and durability of response after multiple B-cell depletion courses require continued monitoring, especially in SLE where absolute depletion is less favored than targeted suppression.

</answer>

data.title: Efficacy and safety of Sandoz biosimilar rituximab for active rheumatoid arthritis: 52-week results from the randomized controlled ASSIST-RA trial.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
This report provides data for the extent of B cell depletion and recovery, efficacy, safety and immunogenicity of Sandoz rituximab (SDZ-RTX; GP2013; Rixathon®) compared with reference rituximab (Ref-RTX) up to week 52 of the ASSIST-RA study.
METHODS
Patients were randomized to SDZ-RTX or Ref-RTX in combination with methotrexate according to the RTX label. The primary endpoint was analysed at week 24. Responders (28-joint DAS [DAS28] decrease from baseline >1.2) at week 24 with residual disease activity (DAS28 ≥2.6) were eligible for a second treatment course between week 24 and 52. Endpoints after week 24 included change from baseline in peripheral B cells, DAS28, ACR 20% response rate (ACR20), Clinical and Simplified Disease Activity Indexes (CDAI, SDAI) and HAQ disability index (HAQ-DI). Safety and immunogenicity were assessed by the incidence of adverse events and antidrug antibodies.
RESULTS
Primary and secondary endpoints up to week 24 were met. Overall, 260/312 randomized patients completed treatment up to week 52. SDZ-RTX resulted in B cell concentrations over time similar to Ref-RTX. The efficacy of SDZ-RTX was similar to Ref-RTX up to week 52, as measured by DAS28, ACR20/50/70, CDAI, SDAI and HAQ-DI. Safety of SDZ-RTX was similar to Ref-RTX regarding frequency, type and severity of adverse events, which were consistent with the known Ref-RTX safety profile. The incidence of antidrug antibodies was low and transient similarly across treatment groups.
CONCLUSION
SDZ-RTX demonstrated similar B cell concentrations over time, efficacy, safety and immunogenicity to Ref-RTX over 52 weeks of the ASSIST-RA study.

<snippet id="37669251">Title: Quantitative effects of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors on liver functions in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
Authors: Chen, Xiao, Xu, Chang, Hu, Ke et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Expert review of clinical pharmacology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
The present study aimed to explore the quantitative effects of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors on liver functions in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS
A total of 4771 patients with NAFLD were included for analysis by means of nonlinear mixed effect modeling, where the change rates of liver functions were taken as the evaluation indexes so as to eliminate the potential baseline effects.
RESULTS
For ALT and AST, the E max of SGLT-2 inhibitors was -17.8% and -13.9%, respectively, and the ET 50 was 6.86 weeks and 10 weeks, respectively. Furthermore, the duration time to achieve 25%, 50%, 75%, and 80% E max were 2.3 weeks, 6.86 weeks, 20.6 weeks, 27.5 weeks in ALT, 3.4 weeks, 10 weeks, 30 weeks, 40 weeks in AST, respectively. Thus, to realize the plateau period (80% of E max ) of SGLT-2 inhibitors on ALT and AST in patients with NAFLD, 100 mg/day canagliflozin (or 10 mg/day dapagliflozin or 10 mg/day empagliflozin) needs to be taken for 20.6 weeks and 30 weeks, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
The present study explored the quantitative effects of SGLT-2 inhibitors on liver functions and recommends a therapeutic regimen in patients with NAFLD.</snippet>
<snippet id="36051336">Title: Impact of sodium glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors on liver steatosis/fibrosis/inflammation and redox balance in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
Authors: Bellanti, Francesco, Lo Buglio, Aurelio, Dobrakowski, Michał et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: World journal of gastroenterology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Sodium glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2-I) are the most recently approved drugs for type 2 diabetes (T2D). Recent clinical trials of these compounds reported beneficial cardiovascular (CV) and renal outcomes. A major cause of vascular dysfunction and CV disease in diabetes is hyperglycemia associated with inflammation and oxidative stress. Pre-clinical studies demonstrated that SGLT2-I reduce glucotoxicity and promote anti-inflammatory effects by lowering oxidative stress.
AIM
To investigate the effects of SGLT2-I on markers of oxidative stress, inflammation, liver steatosis, and fibrosis in patients of T2D with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).
METHODS
We referred fifty-two consecutive outpatients treated with metformin monotherapy and exhibiting poor glycemic control to our centre. We introduced the outpatients to an SGLT2-I (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, or canagliflozin; n = 26) or a different hypoglycemic drug [other glucose-lowering drugs (OTHER), n = 26]. We evaluated circulating interleukins and serum hydroxynonenal (HNE)- or malondialdehyde (MDA)-protein adducts, fatty liver index (FLI), NAFLD fibrosis score, aspartate aminotransferase (AST)/alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ratio, AST-to-platelet-ratio index (APRI), and fibrosis-4 on the day before (T0) and following treatment for six months (T1). We also performed transient elastography at T0 and T1.
RESULTS
Add-on therapy resulted in improved glycemic control and reduced fasting blood glucose in both groups. Of note, following treatment for six months, a reduction of FLI and APRI, as well as of the FibroScan result, was reported in patients treated with SGLT2-I, but not in the OTHER group; furthermore, in the SGLT2-I group, we reported lower circulating levels of interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, tumor necrosis factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, and higher levels of IL-4 and IL-10. We did not observe any modification in circulating interleukins in the OTHER group. Finally, serum HNE- and MDA-protein adducts decreased significantly in SGLT2-I rather than OTHER patients and correlated with liver steatosis and fibrosis scores.
CONCLUSION
The present data indicate that treatment with SGLT2-I in patients with T2D and NAFLD is associated with improvement of liver steatosis and fibrosis markers and circulating pro-inflammatory and redox status, more than optimizing glycemic control.</snippet>

<snippet id="29895557">Title: Effect of Empagliflozin on Liver Fat in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease: A Randomized Controlled Trial (E-LIFT Trial).
Authors: Kuchay, Mohammad Shafi, Krishan, Sonal, Mishra, Sunil Kumar et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Diabetes care
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors have been shown to reduce liver fat in rodent models. Data regarding the effect of SGLT-2 inhibitors on human liver fat are scarce. This study examined the effect of empagliflozin (an SGLT-2 inhibitor) on liver fat in patients with type 2 diabetes and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) by using MRI-derived proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF).
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS
Fifty patients with type 2 diabetes and NAFLD were randomly assigned to either the empagliflozin group (standard treatment for type 2 diabetes plus empagliflozin 10 mg daily) or the control group (standard treatment without empagliflozin) for 20 weeks. Change in liver fat was measured by MRI-PDFF. Secondary outcome measures were change in alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), and γ-glutamyl transferase (GGT) levels.
RESULTS
When included in the standard treatment for type 2 diabetes, empagliflozin was significantly better at reducing liver fat (mean MRI-PDFF difference between the empagliflozin and control groups -4.0%; P < 0.0001). Compared with baseline, significant reduction was found in the end-of-treatment MRI-PDFF for the empagliflozin group (16.2% to 11.3%; P < 0.0001) and a nonsignificant change was found in the control group (16.4% to 15.5%; P = 0.057). The two groups showed a significant difference for change in serum ALT level ( P = 0.005) and nonsignificant differences for AST ( P = 0.212) and GGT ( P = 0.057) levels.
CONCLUSIONS
When included in the standard treatment for type 2 diabetes, empagliflozin reduces liver fat and improves ALT levels in patients with type 2 diabetes and NAFLD.</snippet>
<snippet id="38536017">Title: Effects of empagliflozin on liver fat in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease without diabetes mellitus: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
Authors: Cheung, Ka Shing, Ng, Ho Yu, Hui, Rex Wan Hin et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.)
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS
We investigated whether empagliflozin reduces hepatic steatosis in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease without diabetes mellitus.
APPROACH AND RESULTS
This was an investigator-initiated, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial recruiting adult subjects from the community. Eligible subjects without diabetes mellitus (fasting plasma glucose < 7 mmol/L and HbA1c < 6.5%) who had magnetic resonance imaging-proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) ≥ 5% were randomly allocated to receive empagliflozin 10 mg daily or placebo (1:1 ratio) for 52 weeks (end of treatment, EOT). MRI-PDFF was conducted at baseline and EOT. The primary outcome was the difference in change of MRI-PDFF between the 2 groups at EOT. Secondary outcomes were hepatic steatosis resolution (MRI-PDFF < 5%), alanine aminotransferase drop ≥ 17 U/L, MRI-PDFF decline ≥ 30%, a combination of both, and changes of anthropometric and laboratory parameters at EOT. All outcomes were based on intention-to-treat analysis. Of 98 recruited subjects (median age: 55.7 y [IQR:49.5-63.4]; male:54 [55.1%]), 97 (empagliflozin:49, placebo:48; median MRI-PDFF:9.7% vs 9.0%) had MRI-PDFF repeated at EOT. The Empagliflozin group had a greater reduction in median MRI-PDFF compared to the placebo group (-2.49% vs. -1.43%; p = 0.025), with a nonsignificant trend of resolution of hepatic steatosis (44.9% vs. 28.6%; p = 0.094). There was no significant difference in alanine aminotransferase drop ≥ 17 U/L (16.3% vs. 12.2%; p = 0.564), MRI-PDFF drop ≥ 30% (49.0% vs. 40.8%; p = 0.417), and composite outcome (8.2% vs. 8.2%; p = 1.000). Empagliflozin group had a greater drop in body weight (-2.7 vs. -0.2 kg), waist circumference (-2.0 vs. 0 cm), fasting glucose (-0.3 vs. 0 mmol/L), and ferritin (-126 vs. -22 pmol/L) (all p < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS
Empagliflozin for 52 weeks reduces hepatic fat content in subjects with nondiabetic metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04642261).</snippet>
<snippet id="40085410">Title: The effect of SGLT2 inhibitors on hepatic steatosis detected by MRI-PDFF in patients with type 2 Diabetes mellitus and metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease.
Authors: Amin, Mona Ahmed, Sadik, Noha Adly, Saad, Hala Ahmed et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Internal and emergency medicine
Abstract: Sodium-glucose co-transporter type-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have been identified to have a crucial hepatoprotective role in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) and metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Thus, we aimed to assess the effect of SGLT2 inhibitors on hepatic steatosis in patients with T2DM and MASLD added to the standard of care (SOC) treatment. Our study was a single-arm clinical trial with trial no ISRCTN85961860. Thirty T2DM patients with MASLD were recruited from the outpatient endocrinology and diabetes clinic of the Internal Medicine Department at Kasr Al-Aini Hospital, Cairo University, Egypt. Our Patients received Empagliflozin 10 mg daily which was added to SOC treatment and followed up for 24 weeks. Magnetic resonance imaging proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) was done at baseline and after 24 weeks to assess the percentage change in hepatic fat mass. Also changes in Fib-4 and NAFLD fibrosis scores were calculated. Our study showed a statistically significant decrease in the mean MRI-PDFF measurement of hepatic steatosis after 24 weeks of adding empagliflozin to SOC treatment (13.297 ± 7.15) compared to the mean at baseline (15.288 ± 8.72), P = 0.006 with overall percentage decrease about 13.16% of liver steatosis. There were significant decreases in BMI, fasting blood glucose, and Alanine transaminase, (P < 0.001, 0.03, 0.01) respectively. There were no significant differences in Fib-4 or NAFLD fibrosis scores. Adding empagliflozin 10 mg to the standard treatment in patients with diabetes and MASLD could reduce hepatic fat mass significantly after 24 weeks of treatment. Thus, adding SGLT2 inhibitors to the clinical practice guidelines could be a therapeutic agent for patients with MASLD and T2DM.</snippet>
<snippet id="33593749">Title: Comparing the effects of tofogliflozin and pioglitazone in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (ToPiND study): a randomized prospective open-label controlled trial.
Authors: Yoneda, Masato, Honda, Yasushi, Ogawa, Yuji et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: BMJ open diabetes research & care
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
The treatment of diabetes has a significant impact on the pathogenesis of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). We compared the effectiveness of tofogliflozin, a selective sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, and pioglitazone for the treatment of NAFLD patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS
This open-label, prospective, single-center, randomized clinical trial recruited NAFLD patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a hepatic fat fraction of at least 10% as assessed based on the MRI-proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF). Eligible patients were stratified according to hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), alanine transaminase, and MRI-PDFF levels and randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either 20 mg tofogliflozin or 15-30 mg pioglitazone, orally, once daily for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was an absolute change in MRI-PDFF at 24 weeks. Efficacy and safety was assessed in all treated patients. This trial was registered in the Japan Registry of Clinical Trials.
RESULTS
Overall, 40 eligible patients were randomly assigned to receive tofogliflozin (n=21) or pioglitazone (n=19). Changes in hepatic steatosis after 24 weeks of treatment were evaluated by MRI-PDFF, which showed a significant decrease in both groups (-7.54% (p<0.0001) and -4.12% (p=0.0042) in the pioglitazone and tofogliflozin groups, respectively). Compared with baseline, the body weight decreased by 2.83±2.86 kg (-3.6%, p=0.0443) in the tofogliflozin group and increased by 1.39±2.62 kg (1.7%, p=0.0002) in the pioglitazone group after 24 weeks. No life-threatening events or treatment-related deaths occurred.
CONCLUSIONS
Tofogliflozin was well tolerated, and it reduced the MRI-PDFF levels in NAFLD patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

jRCTs031180159.</snippet>
<snippet id="37462748">Title: Impact of tofogliflozin on hepatic outcomes: a systematic review.
Authors: Pathak, Mani, Parveen, Rizwana, Khan, Parvej et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: European journal of clinical pharmacology
Abstract: PURPOSE
Studies have demonstrated a high prevalence of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) patients. The aim was to review the effect of tofogliflozin on hepatic outcomes in T2DM patients.
METHODS
A literature search in PubMed, Science Direct and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials was conducted for randomised clinical trials of tofogliflozin by applying predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria.
RESULTS
A total number of four randomised clinical trials, including 226 subjects, were included in the review. There was a significant decrease in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT) levels in the tofogliflozin group as compared to the control or active comparator groups. Additionally, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and magnetic resonance imaging proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) levels were also significantly decreased in the tofogliflozin group. However, no significant difference was observed in levels of adiponectin.
CONCLUSION
Overall, an improvement in levels of hepatic parameters was observed in T2DM patients with concurrent liver disorders. However, a large number of clinical trials are needed to prove the efficacy of tofogliflozin on hepatic outcomes in patients with T2DM.</snippet>

<snippet id="40959362">Title: Empagliflozin Treatment for Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease in Type 2 Diabetes Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
Authors: Alsarkhi, Loiy Naser, Eda, Sanjay, Mohammed Abdul, Rahman Hameed et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Cureus
Abstract: Empagliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, has emerged as a promising therapeutic option for patients with concurrent type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy of empagliflozin on liver enzymes and metabolic parameters in this dual-pathology population. A comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Web of Science databases from inception to July 2025. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing empagliflozin with placebo in adults with T2DM and NAFLD were included. Primary outcomes included changes in liver enzymes (alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)), while secondary outcomes comprised systolic blood pressure (SBP) and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels. Four studies met the inclusion criteria, encompassing 393 participants (206 empagliflozin, 187 control) with follow-up periods ranging from 20 to 24 weeks. Meta-analysis demonstrated significant reductions in ALT (mean difference (MD): -11.61; 95% confidence interval (CI): -19.18 to -4.04), AST (MD: -10.31; 95% CI: -15.41 to -5.21), and GGT levels (MD: -15.19; 95% CI: -18.13 to -12.25) with empagliflozin treatment compared to placebo. However, no statistically significant differences were observed for SBP (MD: -0.87; 95% CI: -7.93 to 6.20) or HbA1c (MD: -0.44; 95% CI: -1.10 to 0.22). Considerable heterogeneity was noted across studies for most outcomes. These findings suggest that empagliflozin offers hepatoprotective benefits in patients with concurrent T2DM and NAFLD, primarily through significant improvements in liver enzyme profiles. However, larger long-term studies with histological endpoints are needed to establish definitive clinical recommendations for this therapeutic approach.</snippet>
<snippet id="36931466">Title: Comparison of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors and thiazolidinediones for management of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
Authors: Hameed, Ishaque, Hayat, Javeria, Marsia, Shayan et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Clinics and research in hepatology and gastroenterology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
The pharmacologic treatment of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) remains unclear.
METHODS
Two reviewers searched PubMed, SCOPUS, Cochrane Central and clinicaltrials.gov for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of patients with NAFLD with or without type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) receiving TZDs vs SGLT2 inhibitors. The primary outcomes were change in alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) and improvement in steatosis and fibrosis. The secondary outcomes were changes in lipid profile, body weight and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). Random effects models with continuous outcomes as weighted mean differences (WMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were used.
RESULTS
Five studies (n = 311 NAFLD patients) were included. Patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors (n = 156) showed significant decrease in visceral fat area (VFA; WMD 23.45, p < 0.00001) and body weight (WMD 4.22, p < 0.00001) as compared to those treated with TZDs (n = 155). Patients from both groups showed improvement in AST (WMD 1.21, p = 0.40), ALT (WMD -0.46, p = 0.81), GGT (WMD -0.47, p = 0.84), hepatic fibrosis (WMD 0.11, p = 0.52), LDL (WMD 2.19, p = 0.35), HbA1c (WMD -0.16%, p = 0.20), HOMA-IR (WMD: -0.04, p = 0.91) and FPG (WMD -7.37, p = 0.28) which was equivalent and non-significant.
CONCLUSION
The improvement in liver enzymes, steatosis and fibrosis caused by SGLT2 inhibitors and TZDs was similar. SGLT2 inhibitors, however, resulted in a significant decrease in VFA and body weight. As weight loss is found to have a positive effect on the resolution of steatosis and fibrosis in NAFLD patients, SGLT2 inhibitors may have the potential to be considered for long-term management, however, further research needs to be conducted to determine the utility of SGLT2 inhibitor class of antidiabetic drugs for effectively treating NAFLD.</snippet>
<snippet id="39929274">Title: The efficacy of sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitors in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
Authors: Li, Hongsheng, Hou, Yanli, Xin, Wenyong et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Pharmacological research
Abstract: The efficacy of sodium-glucose transporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors for nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is unclear. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate SGLT-2 inhibitors efficacy for NAFLD treatment. We systematically searched major electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Embase) from inception until 11/2023, identifying randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of SGLT-2 inhibitors treatment for patients with NAFLD. The mean differences (MD or SMD) and 95 % confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated via random-effects models. Eleven articles (n = 805 patients with NAFLD) were included in this study. Of these, 408 participants received SGLT-2 inhibitors, while 397 participants were in the control group. SGLT-2 inhibitors significantly reduced liver enzyme levels, including aspartate alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (MD [95 % CI]; -9.31 U/L [-13.41, -5.21], p < 0.00001), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (MD [95 % CI]; -6.06 U/L [-10.98, -1.15], p = 0.02), and gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) (MD [95 % CI]; -11.72 U/L [-15.65, -7.80], p < 0.00001). SGLT-2 inhibitors intervention was also associated with significant reductions in body weight (MD [95 % CI]; -2.72 kg [-3.49, -1.95], p < 0.00001) and BMI (MD [95 % CI]; -1.11 kg/m 2 [-1.39, -0.82], p < 0.00001) and improvements in glycaemic indices, triglyceride (TG) and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C). However, no significant changes in total cholesterol (TC) or low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) were observed. The meta-analysis revealed a beneficial effect of SGLT-2 inhibitors on liver functions and body weight, BMI, TG, HDL-C, and glucose homeostasis in patients with NAFLD, indicating that SGLT-2 inhibitors might be a clinical therapeutic strategy for these patients, especially individuals with concurrent type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).</snippet>
<snippet id="36514450">Title: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors improve liver enzymes in patients with co-existing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
Authors: Amjad, Waseem, Malik, Adnan, Qureshi, Waqas et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Przeglad gastroenterologiczny
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is characterized by hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis. While sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors have been established to improve glycaemic control in type-2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), evidence of the beneficial effects in diabetics with coexisting NAFLD has yet to be quantitatively summarized.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We searched the PubMed, Medline, CINAHL, and Cochrane databases and ClinicalTrial.gov from database inception to July 2020. We included randomized controlled trials assessing the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on liver enzymes among patients with NAFLD. Our primary outcome included liver inflammation as measured using liver transaminase. Secondary outcomes included drug efficacy on hepatic steatosis and body mass index. Risk differences were calculated using a random model.
RESULTS
A total of 10,555 patients were included in this meta-analysis (SGLT2 inhibitor group: n = 7125; control group: n = 3430). The treatment duration ranged from 8 to 52 weeks. Patients with T2DM, who were treated with SGLT2 inhibitor had decrease in ALT (SMD = -0.22, 95% CI: -0.27 to -0.20) and AST levels (SMD = -0.20, 95% CI: -0.31 to -0.08). The SGLT-2 inhibitor did not cause statistically significant weight loss (SMD = -0.21, 95% CI: -0.47 to 0.06), fibrosis regression utilizing FIB-4 score (SMD = -0.12, 95% CI: -0.41 to 0.18), and hepatic steatosis by using MRI-PDFF (SMD = -0.31, 95% CI: -0.68 to 0.07), as compared to controls.
CONCLUSIONS
The SGLT2 inhibitor treatment may improve liver function, as demonstrated in the statistically significant reduction in transaminase levels. There were also notable trends in improved liver fibrosis and steatosis across the study periods.</snippet>

# Key Takeaways

- Long-term use of SGLT2 inhibitors in type 2 diabetes (T2D) with suspected NAFLD is associated with improvements in hepatic steatosis surrogates (MRI-PDFF, FLI/APRI/Fib-4) and favorable changes in liver enzymes (ALT/AST/GGT), with effects becoming more apparent over weeks to months of therapy and showing clearer benefits in steatosis-related markers than in fibrosis endpoints.<cite id="37462748">Studies have demonstrated a significant decrease in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels with tofogliflozin versus control, along with significant decreases in gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) and MRI-PDFF, indicating improved hepatic outcomes in T2D patients with liver disorders</cite><cite id="36051336">In T2D with NAFLD, adding an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, or canagliflozin) for six months reduced FLI and APRI and FibroScan compared with other glucose-lowering drugs, alongside reductions in circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress markers</cite><cite id="37669251">A modeling analysis in 4771 NAFLD patients estimated that canagliflozin 100 mg/day (or dapagliflozin 10 mg/day or empagliflozin 10 mg/day) would require about 20.6–30 weeks to approach 80% of maximal effect on ALT/AST, with earlier timepoints for 50% effect</cite>.

# Effects on Hepatic Steatosis (MRI-PDFF, elastography, noninvasive scores)

- Randomized trial evidence shows SGLT2 inhibitors reduce liver fat by MRI-PDFF in T2D with NAFLD over approximately 20 weeks. In the E-LIFT trial, empagliflozin reduced MRI-PDFF by 4.0% versus control (16.2% to 11.3% vs 16.4% to 15.5%), with a significant ALT improvement and nonsignificant AST/GGT changes.<cite id="29895557">Empagliflozin significantly reduced liver fat (MRI-PDFF mean difference −4.0%; P < 0.0001), lowered end-of-treatment MRI-PDFF (16.2% to 11.3% vs 16.4% to 15.5%), and improved ALT versus control, with nonsignificant effects on AST and GGT</cite>.
- Longer-duration and non-diabetic populations also show steatosis reductions. In a 52-week, placebo-controlled trial of empagliflozin in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) without diabetes, median MRI-PDFF decreased more in the treatment arm (−2.49% vs −1.43%), with a nonsignificant trend toward steatosis resolution; additional favorable changes included body weight, waist, fasting glucose, and ferritin.<cite id="38536017">Empagliflozin 10 mg daily for 52 weeks reduced median MRI-PDFF (−2.49% vs −1.43% vs placebo), with a nonsignificant increase in steatosis resolution and improvements in body weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, and ferritin</cite>.
- Single-arm experience supports steatosis improvement in T2D with MASLD over 24 weeks: empagliflozin reduced MRI-PDFF from 15.29 ± 8.72% to 13.30 ± 7.15% (≈13% relative decrease) with additional ALT reduction and modest BMI decrease.<cite id="40085410">Adding empagliflozin 10 mg to standard of care for 24 weeks decreased MRI-PDFF from 15.288 ± 8.72 to 13.297 ± 7.15 (P = 0.006; ~13.2% reduction), with significant decreases in BMI, fasting glucose, and ALT</cite>.
- Head-to-head against insulin-sensitizers suggests SGLT2 inhibitors may have comparable effects on liver enzymes and steatosis surrogates but with clearer benefits on visceral adiposity. A meta-analysis comparing SGLT2 inhibitors vs thiazolidinediones (TZDs) found similar improvements in AST/ALT/GGT and hepatic fibrosis, with SGLT2 inhibitors showing greater reductions in visceral fat area and body weight, potentially aiding NAFLD resolution via weight loss mechanisms.<cite id="36931466">Patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors showed significant decreases in visceral fat area and body weight compared to TZDs, while both groups had similar, non-significant improvements in AST, ALT, GGT, fibrosis, lipids, HbA1c, HOMA-IR, and fasting glucose</cite>.
- Across agents, longer-term data show trends toward improved steatosis/fibrosis indices in T2D with NAFLD. A 6‑month randomized trial of tofogliflozin versus pioglitazone demonstrated significant MRI-PDFF reductions in both groups, supporting class effects on steatosis, with tofogliflozin well tolerated.<cite id="33593749">In a 24-week randomized trial, MRI-PDFF decreased by −7.54% with tofogliflozin and −4.12% with pioglitazone, indicating significant reductions in hepatic steatosis in T2D with NAFLD</cite><cite id="37462748">A systematic review of tofogliflozin RCTs reported significant decreases in AST, ALT, GGT, and MRI-PDFF compared with controls</cite>.
- Modeling across NAFLD cohorts suggests SGLT2 inhibitors can reduce ALT/AST with time; estimated Emax for ALT/AST and time to reach 50–80% of maximal effect vary by agent and dose, implying a gradual, dose‑dependent approach to steatosis enzyme normalization over months.<cite id="37669251">Nonlinear mixed-effects modeling estimated Emax for ALT/AST at −17.8% and −13.9% with SGLT2 inhibitors and ET50 of 6.86–10 weeks; 25–80% Emax occurred over 2.3–27.5 weeks, suggesting ALT/AST reach plateau around 20.6–30 weeks with daily canagliflozin 100 mg or dapagliflozin/empagliflozin 10 mg</cite>.

# Effects on Liver Enzymes (ALT/AST/GGT)

- Meta-analyses consistently show SGLT2 inhibitors lower ALT/AST/GGT in T2D with NAFLD. A 2025 meta-analysis of empagliflozin RCTs (n=393) found significant reductions in ALT (MD −11.61; 95% CI −19.18 to −4.04), AST (MD −10.31; 95% CI −15.41 to −5.21), and GGT (MD −15.19; 95% CI −18.13 to −12.25), with heterogeneity across studies and no significant differences in SBP or HbA1c.<cite id="40959362">Empagliflozin significantly reduced ALT (MD −11.61), AST (MD −10.31), and GGT (MD −15.19) versus placebo across RCTs (n=393; 20–24 weeks), though heterogeneity was considerable and effects on SBP and HbA1c were not significant</cite>.
- Broader SGLT2 meta-analyses corroborate enzyme improvements. A 2025 pharmacological research review (11 RCTs; n=805) reported ALT (MD −9.31; 95% CI −13.41 to −5.21), AST (MD −6.06; 95% CI −10.98 to −1.15), and GGT (MD −11.72; 95% CI −15.65 to −7.80) reductions, alongside weight and BMI decreases and improved glycemic indices.<cite id="39929274">SGLT-2 inhibitors significantly reduced ALT (MD −9.31), AST (MD −6.06), and GGT (MD −11.72), and improved body weight, BMI, triglycerides, HDL-C, and glycemic indices in NAFLD patients</cite>.
- Another 2022 meta-analysis (10,555 patients; 8–52 weeks) found SGLT2 inhibitors significantly lowered ALT and AST (SMD −0.22 and −0.20, respectively), with trends toward improved fibrosis (FIB-4) and MRI-PDFF but without a statistically significant overall effect on steatosis by MRI-PDFF, underscoring heterogeneity and context dependence.<cite id="36514450">SGLT2 inhibitors decreased ALT (SMD −0.22) and AST (SMD −0.20), with trends toward improved FIB-4 and MRI-PDFF but no statistically significant change in MRI-PDFF overall compared to controls</cite>.
- Individual RCTs align with these pooled trends. The tofogliflozin systematic review reported significant AST/ALT/AST reductions versus controls, and a 24‑week tofogliflozin vs pioglitazone trial showed significant MRI-PDFF decreases, supporting class-level hepatoprotection beyond glycemic effects.<cite id="37462748">Studies of tofogliflozin showed significant decreases in AST, ALT, GGT, and MRI-PDFF compared with controls</cite><cite id="33593749">Tofogliflozin reduced MRI-PDFF by −7.54% at 24 weeks in T2D with NAFLD</cite>.

# Time Course, Dose, and Magnitude

- Effects on ALT/AST appear within weeks and may approach a plateau over months. Modeling across NAFLD cohorts estimated that achieving 50% of maximal ALT/AST effect occurs within roughly 2–6 weeks, with 80% of maximal effect by ~20–30 weeks on canagliflozin 100 mg/day or lower doses of dapagliflozin/empagliflozin, implying a gradual, sustained response with long-term use.<cite id="37669251">Time to 50% and 80% of maximal ALT/AST effect with SGLT2 inhibitors was estimated at 2.3–6.86–20.6–27.5 weeks for ALT and 3.4–10–30–40 weeks for AST, with dose–response alternatives (canagliflozin 100 mg/day or dapagliflozin/empagliflozin 10 mg/day)</cite>.
- In short-to-moderate duration RCTs (20–24 weeks), pooled analyses show clinically meaningful enzyme reductions (ALT/AST ~6–12 U/L decrease; GGT ~11–15 U/L), though heterogeneity in baseline severity and concurrent therapies may modulate effect size.<cite id="40959362">Empagliflozin RCTs showed ALT/AST/GGT reductions of ~11/10/15 U/L, with heterogeneity across studies</cite><cite id="39929274">Across SGLT2 RCTs, ALT/AST/GGT reductions of ~9/6/12 U/L were observed alongside weight and glycemic improvements</cite>.
- Longer-duration trials (52 weeks) confirm sustained reductions in MRI-PDFF and supportive improvements in NAFLD-related inflammatory markers, even when diabetes control is similar to controls, suggesting benefits beyond glycemia.<cite id="38536017">A 52-week empagliflozin trial reduced MRI-PDFF and improved multiple metabolic and inflammatory markers, even without diabetes-related benefit differences versus placebo</cite><cite id="36051336">Six months of SGLT2 inhibitor therapy in T2D with NAFLD improved FLI, APRI, and FibroScan and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress markers compared with other glucose-lowering drugs</cite>.

# Mechanisms and Associated Inflammation/Oxidative Stress

- Beyond steatosis and enzymes, SGLT2 inhibitors may reduce hepatic oxidative stress and inflammatory cytokines in T2D–NAFLD, aligning with preclinical data on anti‑glucotoxic and anti‑inflammatory effects. Clinical data show decreased serum protein adducts of oxidative stress markers and lower IL‑1β/IL‑6/TNF with SGLT2 inhibitors versus controls, alongside improved noninvasive fibrosis indices.<cite id="36051336">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced circulating IL‑1β, IL‑6, TNF, and monocyte chemoattractant protein‑1, increased IL‑4/IL‑10, and decreased HNE- and MDA‑protein adducts, with parallel improvements in FLI, APRI, and FibroScan</cite>.

# Practical Implications and Limitations

- For patients with T2D and suspected NAFLD, long-term SGLT2 inhibitor therapy can be expected to modestly but significantly improve liver enzymes and steatosis surrogates, with the most robust evidence for ALT/AST reductions and MRI-PDFF or noninvasive fibrosis score improvements over 20–52 weeks, especially with agents like empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and tofogliflozin.<cite id="29895557">Empagliflozin improved ALT and reduced MRI-PDFF over 20 weeks in T2D with NAFLD</cite><cite id="38536017">Empagliflozin over 52 weeks reduced MRI-PDFF and improved metabolic markers in MASLD without diabetes</cite><cite id="40959362">Empagliflozin meta-analysis showed significant ALT/AST/GGT reductions</cite><cite id="39929274">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced ALT/AST/GGT and improved weight/BMI and glycemic indices</cite><cite id="36514450">SGLT2 inhibitors decreased ALT/AST with trends toward improved fibrosis and steatosis surrogates</cite>.
- However, heterogeneity across trials, variable follow-up windows, and reliance on surrogate endpoints limit definitive conclusions on histologic fibrosis regression. Some meta-analyses report non-significant changes in fibrosis or MRI-PDFF overall, emphasizing the need for longer, larger RCTs with histology and consistent dosing/durations to establish durable, clinically meaningful outcomes.<cite id="36514450">Although ALT/AST improved, overall MRI-PDFF and fibrosis changes were not statistically significant across all studies, indicating heterogeneity and the need for further research</cite><cite id="40959362">Heterogeneity was considerable across empagliflozin RCTs, and larger long-term studies with histological endpoints are needed</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Long-term SGLT2 inhibitor therapy in T2D with suspected NAFLD is associated with improved liver enzymes and favorable steatosis/fibrosis surrogates, with effects emerging over weeks and consolidating over months; the magnitude of enzyme improvement is clinically meaningful (≈6–12 U/L for ALT/AST; ≈11–15 U/L for GGT) and steatosis reduction measurable by MRI-PDFF or noninvasive scores, though histologic confirmation and standardization of duration remain ongoing needs.<cite id="40959362">Empagliflozin significantly reduced ALT/AST/GGT with pooled mean differences of −11.61/−10.31/−15.19 U/L</cite><cite id="39929274">Across SGLT2 RCTs, ALT/AST/GGT decreased by ~9/6/11 U/L with concomitant weight/BMI and glycemic benefits</cite><cite id="37669251">Modeling suggests ALT/AST effects approach plateau by ~20–30 weeks with common SGLT2 doses</cite><cite id="29895557">Empagliflozin reduced MRI-PDFF by ~4% and improved ALT at 20 weeks</cite><cite id="36514450">SGLT2 inhibitors lower ALT/AST and show trends toward improved fibrosis/steatosis surrogates, but heterogeneity persists</cite>.
</answer>

data.title: Quantitative effects of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors on liver functions in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The present study aimed to explore the quantitative effects of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors on liver functions in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS
A total of 4771 patients with NAFLD were included for analysis by means of nonlinear mixed effect modeling, where the change rates of liver functions were taken as the evaluation indexes so as to eliminate the potential baseline effects.
RESULTS
For ALT and AST, the E max of SGLT-2 inhibitors was -17.8% and -13.9%, respectively, and the ET 50 was 6.86 weeks and 10 weeks, respectively. Furthermore, the duration time to achieve 25%, 50%, 75%, and 80% E max were 2.3 weeks, 6.86 weeks, 20.6 weeks, 27.5 weeks in ALT, 3.4 weeks, 10 weeks, 30 weeks, 40 weeks in AST, respectively. Thus, to realize the plateau period (80% of E max ) of SGLT-2 inhibitors on ALT and AST in patients with NAFLD, 100 mg/day canagliflozin (or 10 mg/day dapagliflozin or 10 mg/day empagliflozin) needs to be taken for 20.6 weeks and 30 weeks, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
The present study explored the quantitative effects of SGLT-2 inhibitors on liver functions and recommends a therapeutic regimen in patients with NAFLD.

data.title: Impact of sodium glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors on liver steatosis/fibrosis/inflammation and redox balance in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Sodium glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2-I) are the most recently approved drugs for type 2 diabetes (T2D). Recent clinical trials of these compounds reported beneficial cardiovascular (CV) and renal outcomes. A major cause of vascular dysfunction and CV disease in diabetes is hyperglycemia associated with inflammation and oxidative stress. Pre-clinical studies demonstrated that SGLT2-I reduce glucotoxicity and promote anti-inflammatory effects by lowering oxidative stress.
AIM
To investigate the effects of SGLT2-I on markers of oxidative stress, inflammation, liver steatosis, and fibrosis in patients of T2D with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).
METHODS
We referred fifty-two consecutive outpatients treated with metformin monotherapy and exhibiting poor glycemic control to our centre. We introduced the outpatients to an SGLT2-I (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, or canagliflozin; n = 26) or a different hypoglycemic drug [other glucose-lowering drugs (OTHER), n = 26]. We evaluated circulating interleukins and serum hydroxynonenal (HNE)- or malondialdehyde (MDA)-protein adducts, fatty liver index (FLI), NAFLD fibrosis score, aspartate aminotransferase (AST)/alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ratio, AST-to-platelet-ratio index (APRI), and fibrosis-4 on the day before (T0) and following treatment for six months (T1). We also performed transient elastography at T0 and T1.
RESULTS
Add-on therapy resulted in improved glycemic control and reduced fasting blood glucose in both groups. Of note, following treatment for six months, a reduction of FLI and APRI, as well as of the FibroScan result, was reported in patients treated with SGLT2-I, but not in the OTHER group; furthermore, in the SGLT2-I group, we reported lower circulating levels of interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, tumor necrosis factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, and higher levels of IL-4 and IL-10. We did not observe any modification in circulating interleukins in the OTHER group. Finally, serum HNE- and MDA-protein adducts decreased significantly in SGLT2-I rather than OTHER patients and correlated with liver steatosis and fibrosis scores.
CONCLUSION
The present data indicate that treatment with SGLT2-I in patients with T2D and NAFLD is associated with improvement of liver steatosis and fibrosis markers and circulating pro-inflammatory and redox status, more than optimizing glycemic control.

data.title: Effect of Empagliflozin on Liver Fat in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease: A Randomized Controlled Trial (E-LIFT Trial).
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors have been shown to reduce liver fat in rodent models. Data regarding the effect of SGLT-2 inhibitors on human liver fat are scarce. This study examined the effect of empagliflozin (an SGLT-2 inhibitor) on liver fat in patients with type 2 diabetes and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) by using MRI-derived proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF).
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS
Fifty patients with type 2 diabetes and NAFLD were randomly assigned to either the empagliflozin group (standard treatment for type 2 diabetes plus empagliflozin 10 mg daily) or the control group (standard treatment without empagliflozin) for 20 weeks. Change in liver fat was measured by MRI-PDFF. Secondary outcome measures were change in alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), and γ-glutamyl transferase (GGT) levels.
RESULTS
When included in the standard treatment for type 2 diabetes, empagliflozin was significantly better at reducing liver fat (mean MRI-PDFF difference between the empagliflozin and control groups -4.0%; P < 0.0001). Compared with baseline, significant reduction was found in the end-of-treatment MRI-PDFF for the empagliflozin group (16.2% to 11.3%; P < 0.0001) and a nonsignificant change was found in the control group (16.4% to 15.5%; P = 0.057). The two groups showed a significant difference for change in serum ALT level ( P = 0.005) and nonsignificant differences for AST ( P = 0.212) and GGT ( P = 0.057) levels.
CONCLUSIONS
When included in the standard treatment for type 2 diabetes, empagliflozin reduces liver fat and improves ALT levels in patients with type 2 diabetes and NAFLD.

data.title: Effects of empagliflozin on liver fat in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease without diabetes mellitus: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS
We investigated whether empagliflozin reduces hepatic steatosis in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease without diabetes mellitus.
APPROACH AND RESULTS
This was an investigator-initiated, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial recruiting adult subjects from the community. Eligible subjects without diabetes mellitus (fasting plasma glucose < 7 mmol/L and HbA1c < 6.5%) who had magnetic resonance imaging-proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) ≥ 5% were randomly allocated to receive empagliflozin 10 mg daily or placebo (1:1 ratio) for 52 weeks (end of treatment, EOT). MRI-PDFF was conducted at baseline and EOT. The primary outcome was the difference in change of MRI-PDFF between the 2 groups at EOT. Secondary outcomes were hepatic steatosis resolution (MRI-PDFF < 5%), alanine aminotransferase drop ≥ 17 U/L, MRI-PDFF decline ≥ 30%, a combination of both, and changes of anthropometric and laboratory parameters at EOT. All outcomes were based on intention-to-treat analysis. Of 98 recruited subjects (median age: 55.7 y [IQR:49.5-63.4]; male:54 [55.1%]), 97 (empagliflozin:49, placebo:48; median MRI-PDFF:9.7% vs 9.0%) had MRI-PDFF repeated at EOT. The Empagliflozin group had a greater reduction in median MRI-PDFF compared to the placebo group (-2.49% vs. -1.43%; p = 0.025), with a nonsignificant trend of resolution of hepatic steatosis (44.9% vs. 28.6%; p = 0.094). There was no significant difference in alanine aminotransferase drop ≥ 17 U/L (16.3% vs. 12.2%; p = 0.564), MRI-PDFF drop ≥ 30% (49.0% vs. 40.8%; p = 0.417), and composite outcome (8.2% vs. 8.2%; p = 1.000). Empagliflozin group had a greater drop in body weight (-2.7 vs. -0.2 kg), waist circumference (-2.0 vs. 0 cm), fasting glucose (-0.3 vs. 0 mmol/L), and ferritin (-126 vs. -22 pmol/L) (all p < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS
Empagliflozin for 52 weeks reduces hepatic fat content in subjects with nondiabetic metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04642261).

data.title: The effect of SGLT2 inhibitors on hepatic steatosis detected by MRI-PDFF in patients with type 2 Diabetes mellitus and metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease.
data.abstract: Sodium-glucose co-transporter type-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have been identified to have a crucial hepatoprotective role in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) and metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Thus, we aimed to assess the effect of SGLT2 inhibitors on hepatic steatosis in patients with T2DM and MASLD added to the standard of care (SOC) treatment. Our study was a single-arm clinical trial with trial no ISRCTN85961860. Thirty T2DM patients with MASLD were recruited from the outpatient endocrinology and diabetes clinic of the Internal Medicine Department at Kasr Al-Aini Hospital, Cairo University, Egypt. Our Patients received Empagliflozin 10 mg daily which was added to SOC treatment and followed up for 24 weeks. Magnetic resonance imaging proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) was done at baseline and after 24 weeks to assess the percentage change in hepatic fat mass. Also changes in Fib-4 and NAFLD fibrosis scores were calculated. Our study showed a statistically significant decrease in the mean MRI-PDFF measurement of hepatic steatosis after 24 weeks of adding empagliflozin to SOC treatment (13.297 ± 7.15) compared to the mean at baseline (15.288 ± 8.72), P = 0.006 with overall percentage decrease about 13.16% of liver steatosis. There were significant decreases in BMI, fasting blood glucose, and Alanine transaminase, (P < 0.001, 0.03, 0.01) respectively. There were no significant differences in Fib-4 or NAFLD fibrosis scores. Adding empagliflozin 10 mg to the standard treatment in patients with diabetes and MASLD could reduce hepatic fat mass significantly after 24 weeks of treatment. Thus, adding SGLT2 inhibitors to the clinical practice guidelines could be a therapeutic agent for patients with MASLD and T2DM.

data.title: Comparing the effects of tofogliflozin and pioglitazone in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (ToPiND study): a randomized prospective open-label controlled trial.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
The treatment of diabetes has a significant impact on the pathogenesis of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). We compared the effectiveness of tofogliflozin, a selective sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, and pioglitazone for the treatment of NAFLD patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS
This open-label, prospective, single-center, randomized clinical trial recruited NAFLD patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a hepatic fat fraction of at least 10% as assessed based on the MRI-proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF). Eligible patients were stratified according to hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), alanine transaminase, and MRI-PDFF levels and randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either 20 mg tofogliflozin or 15-30 mg pioglitazone, orally, once daily for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was an absolute change in MRI-PDFF at 24 weeks. Efficacy and safety was assessed in all treated patients. This trial was registered in the Japan Registry of Clinical Trials.
RESULTS
Overall, 40 eligible patients were randomly assigned to receive tofogliflozin (n=21) or pioglitazone (n=19). Changes in hepatic steatosis after 24 weeks of treatment were evaluated by MRI-PDFF, which showed a significant decrease in both groups (-7.54% (p<0.0001) and -4.12% (p=0.0042) in the pioglitazone and tofogliflozin groups, respectively). Compared with baseline, the body weight decreased by 2.83±2.86 kg (-3.6%, p=0.0443) in the tofogliflozin group and increased by 1.39±2.62 kg (1.7%, p=0.0002) in the pioglitazone group after 24 weeks. No life-threatening events or treatment-related deaths occurred.
CONCLUSIONS
Tofogliflozin was well tolerated, and it reduced the MRI-PDFF levels in NAFLD patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
jRCTs031180159.

data.title: Impact of tofogliflozin on hepatic outcomes: a systematic review.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
Studies have demonstrated a high prevalence of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) patients. The aim was to review the effect of tofogliflozin on hepatic outcomes in T2DM patients.
METHODS
A literature search in PubMed, Science Direct and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials was conducted for randomised clinical trials of tofogliflozin by applying predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria.
RESULTS
A total number of four randomised clinical trials, including 226 subjects, were included in the review. There was a significant decrease in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT) levels in the tofogliflozin group as compared to the control or active comparator groups. Additionally, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and magnetic resonance imaging proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) levels were also significantly decreased in the tofogliflozin group. However, no significant difference was observed in levels of adiponectin.
CONCLUSION
Overall, an improvement in levels of hepatic parameters was observed in T2DM patients with concurrent liver disorders. However, a large number of clinical trials are needed to prove the efficacy of tofogliflozin on hepatic outcomes in patients with T2DM.

data.title: Empagliflozin Treatment for Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease in Type 2 Diabetes Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
data.abstract: Empagliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, has emerged as a promising therapeutic option for patients with concurrent type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy of empagliflozin on liver enzymes and metabolic parameters in this dual-pathology population. A comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Web of Science databases from inception to July 2025. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing empagliflozin with placebo in adults with T2DM and NAFLD were included. Primary outcomes included changes in liver enzymes (alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)), while secondary outcomes comprised systolic blood pressure (SBP) and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels. Four studies met the inclusion criteria, encompassing 393 participants (206 empagliflozin, 187 control) with follow-up periods ranging from 20 to 24 weeks. Meta-analysis demonstrated significant reductions in ALT (mean difference (MD): -11.61; 95% confidence interval (CI): -19.18 to -4.04), AST (MD: -10.31; 95% CI: -15.41 to -5.21), and GGT levels (MD: -15.19; 95% CI: -18.13 to -12.25) with empagliflozin treatment compared to placebo. However, no statistically significant differences were observed for SBP (MD: -0.87; 95% CI: -7.93 to 6.20) or HbA1c (MD: -0.44; 95% CI: -1.10 to 0.22). Considerable heterogeneity was noted across studies for most outcomes. These findings suggest that empagliflozin offers hepatoprotective benefits in patients with concurrent T2DM and NAFLD, primarily through significant improvements in liver enzyme profiles. However, larger long-term studies with histological endpoints are needed to establish definitive clinical recommendations for this therapeutic approach.

data.title: Comparison of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors and thiazolidinediones for management of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The pharmacologic treatment of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) remains unclear.
METHODS
Two reviewers searched PubMed, SCOPUS, Cochrane Central and clinicaltrials.gov for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of patients with NAFLD with or without type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) receiving TZDs vs SGLT2 inhibitors. The primary outcomes were change in alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) and improvement in steatosis and fibrosis. The secondary outcomes were changes in lipid profile, body weight and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). Random effects models with continuous outcomes as weighted mean differences (WMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were used.
RESULTS
Five studies (n = 311 NAFLD patients) were included. Patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors (n = 156) showed significant decrease in visceral fat area (VFA; WMD 23.45, p < 0.00001) and body weight (WMD 4.22, p < 0.00001) as compared to those treated with TZDs (n = 155). Patients from both groups showed improvement in AST (WMD 1.21, p = 0.40), ALT (WMD -0.46, p = 0.81), GGT (WMD -0.47, p = 0.84), hepatic fibrosis (WMD 0.11, p = 0.52), LDL (WMD 2.19, p = 0.35), HbA1c (WMD -0.16%, p = 0.20), HOMA-IR (WMD: -0.04, p = 0.91) and FPG (WMD -7.37, p = 0.28) which was equivalent and non-significant.
CONCLUSION
The improvement in liver enzymes, steatosis and fibrosis caused by SGLT2 inhibitors and TZDs was similar. SGLT2 inhibitors, however, resulted in a significant decrease in VFA and body weight. As weight loss is found to have a positive effect on the resolution of steatosis and fibrosis in NAFLD patients, SGLT2 inhibitors may have the potential to be considered for long-term management, however, further research needs to be conducted to determine the utility of SGLT2 inhibitor class of antidiabetic drugs for effectively treating NAFLD.
