data.title: The efficacy of sodium-glucose transporter 2 inhibitors in patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
data.abstract: The efficacy of sodium-glucose transporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors for nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is unclear. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate SGLT-2 inhibitors efficacy for NAFLD treatment. We systematically searched major electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Embase) from inception until 11/2023, identifying randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of SGLT-2 inhibitors treatment for patients with NAFLD. The mean differences (MD or SMD) and 95 % confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated via random-effects models. Eleven articles (n = 805 patients with NAFLD) were included in this study. Of these, 408 participants received SGLT-2 inhibitors, while 397 participants were in the control group. SGLT-2 inhibitors significantly reduced liver enzyme levels, including aspartate alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (MD [95 % CI]; -9.31 U/L [-13.41, -5.21], p < 0.00001), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (MD [95 % CI]; -6.06 U/L [-10.98, -1.15], p = 0.02), and gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) (MD [95 % CI]; -11.72 U/L [-15.65, -7.80], p < 0.00001). SGLT-2 inhibitors intervention was also associated with significant reductions in body weight (MD [95 % CI]; -2.72 kg [-3.49, -1.95], p < 0.00001) and BMI (MD [95 % CI]; -1.11 kg/m 2 [-1.39, -0.82], p < 0.00001) and improvements in glycaemic indices, triglyceride (TG) and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C). However, no significant changes in total cholesterol (TC) or low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) were observed. The meta-analysis revealed a beneficial effect of SGLT-2 inhibitors on liver functions and body weight, BMI, TG, HDL-C, and glucose homeostasis in patients with NAFLD, indicating that SGLT-2 inhibitors might be a clinical therapeutic strategy for these patients, especially individuals with concurrent type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).

data.title: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors improve liver enzymes in patients with co-existing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is characterized by hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis. While sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors have been established to improve glycaemic control in type-2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), evidence of the beneficial effects in diabetics with coexisting NAFLD has yet to be quantitatively summarized.
MATERIAL AND METHODS
We searched the PubMed, Medline, CINAHL, and Cochrane databases and ClinicalTrial.gov from database inception to July 2020. We included randomized controlled trials assessing the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on liver enzymes among patients with NAFLD. Our primary outcome included liver inflammation as measured using liver transaminase. Secondary outcomes included drug efficacy on hepatic steatosis and body mass index. Risk differences were calculated using a random model.
RESULTS
A total of 10,555 patients were included in this meta-analysis (SGLT2 inhibitor group: n = 7125; control group: n = 3430). The treatment duration ranged from 8 to 52 weeks. Patients with T2DM, who were treated with SGLT2 inhibitor had decrease in ALT (SMD = -0.22, 95% CI: -0.27 to -0.20) and AST levels (SMD = -0.20, 95% CI: -0.31 to -0.08). The SGLT-2 inhibitor did not cause statistically significant weight loss (SMD = -0.21, 95% CI: -0.47 to 0.06), fibrosis regression utilizing FIB-4 score (SMD = -0.12, 95% CI: -0.41 to 0.18), and hepatic steatosis by using MRI-PDFF (SMD = -0.31, 95% CI: -0.68 to 0.07), as compared to controls.
CONCLUSIONS
The SGLT2 inhibitor treatment may improve liver function, as demonstrated in the statistically significant reduction in transaminase levels. There were also notable trends in improved liver fibrosis and steatosis across the study periods.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Key Takeaways

- Long-term use of SGLT2 inhibitors in type 2 diabetes (T2D) with suspected NAFLD is associated with improvements in hepatic steatosis surrogates (MRI-PDFF, FLI/APRI/Fib-4) and favorable changes in liver enzymes (ALT/AST/GGT), with effects becoming more apparent over weeks to months of therapy and showing clearer benefits in steatosis-related markers than in fibrosis endpoints.<cite id="37462748">Studies have demonstrated a significant decrease in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels with tofogliflozin versus control, along with significant decreases in gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) and MRI-PDFF, indicating improved hepatic outcomes in T2D patients with liver disorders</cite><cite id="36051336">In T2D with NAFLD, adding an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, or canagliflozin) for six months reduced FLI and APRI and FibroScan compared with other glucose-lowering drugs, alongside reductions in circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress markers</cite><cite id="37669251">A modeling analysis in 4771 NAFLD patients estimated that canagliflozin 100 mg/day (or dapagliflozin 10 mg/day or empagliflozin 10 mg/day) would require about 20.6–30 weeks to approach 80% of maximal effect on ALT/AST, with earlier timepoints for 50% effect</cite>.

# Effects on Hepatic Steatosis (MRI-PDFF, elastography, noninvasive scores)

- Randomized trial evidence shows SGLT2 inhibitors reduce liver fat by MRI-PDFF in T2D with NAFLD over approximately 20 weeks. In the E-LIFT trial, empagliflozin reduced MRI-PDFF by 4.0% versus control (16.2% to 11.3% vs 16.4% to 15.5%), with a significant ALT improvement and nonsignificant AST/GGT changes.<cite id="29895557">Empagliflozin significantly reduced liver fat (MRI-PDFF mean difference −4.0%; P < 0.0001), lowered end-of-treatment MRI-PDFF (16.2% to 11.3% vs 16.4% to 15.5%), and improved ALT versus control, with nonsignificant effects on AST and GGT</cite>.
- Longer-duration and non-diabetic populations also show steatosis reductions. In a 52-week, placebo-controlled trial of empagliflozin in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) without diabetes, median MRI-PDFF decreased more in the treatment arm (−2.49% vs −1.43%), with a nonsignificant trend toward steatosis resolution; additional favorable changes included body weight, waist, fasting glucose, and ferritin.<cite id="38536017">Empagliflozin 10 mg daily for 52 weeks reduced median MRI-PDFF (−2.49% vs −1.43% vs placebo), with a nonsignificant increase in steatosis resolution and improvements in body weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, and ferritin</cite>.
- Single-arm experience supports steatosis improvement in T2D with MASLD over 24 weeks: empagliflozin reduced MRI-PDFF from 15.29 ± 8.72% to 13.30 ± 7.15% (≈13% relative decrease) with additional ALT reduction and modest BMI decrease.<cite id="40085410">Adding empagliflozin 10 mg to standard of care for 24 weeks decreased MRI-PDFF from 15.288 ± 8.72 to 13.297 ± 7.15 (P = 0.006; ~13.2% reduction), with significant decreases in BMI, fasting glucose, and ALT</cite>.
- Head-to-head against insulin-sensitizers suggests SGLT2 inhibitors may have comparable effects on liver enzymes and steatosis surrogates but with clearer benefits on visceral adiposity. A meta-analysis comparing SGLT2 inhibitors vs thiazolidinediones (TZDs) found similar improvements in AST/ALT/GGT and hepatic fibrosis, with SGLT2 inhibitors showing greater reductions in visceral fat area and body weight, potentially aiding NAFLD resolution via weight loss mechanisms.<cite id="36931466">Patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors showed significant decreases in visceral fat area and body weight compared to TZDs, while both groups had similar, non-significant improvements in AST, ALT, GGT, fibrosis, lipids, HbA1c, HOMA-IR, and fasting glucose</cite>.
- Across agents, longer-term data show trends toward improved steatosis/fibrosis indices in T2D with NAFLD. A 6‑month randomized trial of tofogliflozin versus pioglitazone demonstrated significant MRI-PDFF reductions in both groups, supporting class effects on steatosis, with tofogliflozin well tolerated.<cite id="33593749">In a 24-week randomized trial, MRI-PDFF decreased by −7.54% with tofogliflozin and −4.12% with pioglitazone, indicating significant reductions in hepatic steatosis in T2D with NAFLD</cite><cite id="37462748">A systematic review of tofogliflozin RCTs reported significant decreases in AST, ALT, GGT, and MRI-PDFF compared with controls</cite>.
- Modeling across NAFLD cohorts suggests SGLT2 inhibitors can reduce ALT/AST with time; estimated Emax for ALT/AST and time to reach 50–80% of maximal effect vary by agent and dose, implying a gradual, dose‑dependent approach to steatosis enzyme normalization over months.<cite id="37669251">Nonlinear mixed-effects modeling estimated Emax for ALT/AST at −17.8% and −13.9% with SGLT2 inhibitors and ET50 of 6.86–10 weeks; 25–80% Emax occurred over 2.3–27.5 weeks, suggesting ALT/AST reach plateau around 20.6–30 weeks with daily canagliflozin 100 mg or dapagliflozin/empagliflozin 10 mg</cite>.

# Effects on Liver Enzymes (ALT/AST/GGT)

- Meta-analyses consistently show SGLT2 inhibitors lower ALT/AST/GGT in T2D with NAFLD. A 2025 meta-analysis of empagliflozin RCTs (n=393) found significant reductions in ALT (MD −11.61; 95% CI −19.18 to −4.04), AST (MD −10.31; 95% CI −15.41 to −5.21), and GGT (MD −15.19; 95% CI −18.13 to −12.25), with heterogeneity across studies and no significant differences in SBP or HbA1c.<cite id="40959362">Empagliflozin significantly reduced ALT (MD −11.61), AST (MD −10.31), and GGT (MD −15.19) versus placebo across RCTs (n=393; 20–24 weeks), though heterogeneity was considerable and effects on SBP and HbA1c were not significant</cite>.
- Broader SGLT2 meta-analyses corroborate enzyme improvements. A 2025 pharmacological research review (11 RCTs; n=805) reported ALT (MD −9.31; 95% CI −13.41 to −5.21), AST (MD −6.06; 95% CI −10.98 to −1.15), and GGT (MD −11.72; 95% CI −15.65 to −7.80) reductions, alongside weight and BMI decreases and improved glycemic indices.<cite id="39929274">SGLT-2 inhibitors significantly reduced ALT (MD −9.31), AST (MD −6.06), and GGT (MD −11.72), and improved body weight, BMI, triglycerides, HDL-C, and glycemic indices in NAFLD patients</cite>.
- Another 2022 meta-analysis (10,555 patients; 8–52 weeks) found SGLT2 inhibitors significantly lowered ALT and AST (SMD −0.22 and −0.20, respectively), with trends toward improved fibrosis (FIB-4) and MRI-PDFF but without a statistically significant overall effect on steatosis by MRI-PDFF, underscoring heterogeneity and context dependence.<cite id="36514450">SGLT2 inhibitors decreased ALT (SMD −0.22) and AST (SMD −0.20), with trends toward improved FIB-4 and MRI-PDFF but no statistically significant change in MRI-PDFF overall compared to controls</cite>.
- Individual RCTs align with these pooled trends. The tofogliflozin systematic review reported significant AST/ALT/AST reductions versus controls, and a 24‑week tofogliflozin vs pioglitazone trial showed significant MRI-PDFF decreases, supporting class-level hepatoprotection beyond glycemic effects.<cite id="37462748">Studies of tofogliflozin showed significant decreases in AST, ALT, GGT, and MRI-PDFF compared with controls</cite><cite id="33593749">Tofogliflozin reduced MRI-PDFF by −7.54% at 24 weeks in T2D with NAFLD</cite>.

# Time Course, Dose, and Magnitude

- Effects on ALT/AST appear within weeks and may approach a plateau over months. Modeling across NAFLD cohorts estimated that achieving 50% of maximal ALT/AST effect occurs within roughly 2–6 weeks, with 80% of maximal effect by ~20–30 weeks on canagliflozin 100 mg/day or lower doses of dapagliflozin/empagliflozin, implying a gradual, sustained response with long-term use.<cite id="37669251">Time to 50% and 80% of maximal ALT/AST effect with SGLT2 inhibitors was estimated at 2.3–6.86–20.6–27.5 weeks for ALT and 3.4–10–30–40 weeks for AST, with dose–response alternatives (canagliflozin 100 mg/day or dapagliflozin/empagliflozin 10 mg/day)</cite>.
- In short-to-moderate duration RCTs (20–24 weeks), pooled analyses show clinically meaningful enzyme reductions (ALT/AST ~6–12 U/L decrease; GGT ~11–15 U/L), though heterogeneity in baseline severity and concurrent therapies may modulate effect size.<cite id="40959362">Empagliflozin RCTs showed ALT/AST/GGT reductions of ~11/10/15 U/L, with heterogeneity across studies</cite><cite id="39929274">Across SGLT2 RCTs, ALT/AST/GGT reductions of ~9/6/12 U/L were observed alongside weight and glycemic improvements</cite>.
- Longer-duration trials (52 weeks) confirm sustained reductions in MRI-PDFF and supportive improvements in NAFLD-related inflammatory markers, even when diabetes control is similar to controls, suggesting benefits beyond glycemia.<cite id="38536017">A 52-week empagliflozin trial reduced MRI-PDFF and improved multiple metabolic and inflammatory markers, even without diabetes-related benefit differences versus placebo</cite><cite id="36051336">Six months of SGLT2 inhibitor therapy in T2D with NAFLD improved FLI, APRI, and FibroScan and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress markers compared with other glucose-lowering drugs</cite>.

# Mechanisms and Associated Inflammation/Oxidative Stress

- Beyond steatosis and enzymes, SGLT2 inhibitors may reduce hepatic oxidative stress and inflammatory cytokines in T2D–NAFLD, aligning with preclinical data on anti‑glucotoxic and anti‑inflammatory effects. Clinical data show decreased serum protein adducts of oxidative stress markers and lower IL‑1β/IL‑6/TNF with SGLT2 inhibitors versus controls, alongside improved noninvasive fibrosis indices.<cite id="36051336">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced circulating IL‑1β, IL‑6, TNF, and monocyte chemoattractant protein‑1, increased IL‑4/IL‑10, and decreased HNE- and MDA‑protein adducts, with parallel improvements in FLI, APRI, and FibroScan</cite>.

# Practical Implications and Limitations

- For patients with T2D and suspected NAFLD, long-term SGLT2 inhibitor therapy can be expected to modestly but significantly improve liver enzymes and steatosis surrogates, with the most robust evidence for ALT/AST reductions and MRI-PDFF or noninvasive fibrosis score improvements over 20–52 weeks, especially with agents like empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and tofogliflozin.<cite id="29895557">Empagliflozin improved ALT and reduced MRI-PDFF over 20 weeks in T2D with NAFLD</cite><cite id="38536017">Empagliflozin over 52 weeks reduced MRI-PDFF and improved metabolic markers in MASLD without diabetes</cite><cite id="40959362">Empagliflozin meta-analysis showed significant ALT/AST/GGT reductions</cite><cite id="39929274">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced ALT/AST/GGT and improved weight/BMI and glycemic indices</cite><cite id="36514450">SGLT2 inhibitors decreased ALT/AST with trends toward improved fibrosis and steatosis surrogates</cite>.
- However, heterogeneity across trials, variable follow-up windows, and reliance on surrogate endpoints limit definitive conclusions on histologic fibrosis regression. Some meta-analyses report non-significant changes in fibrosis or MRI-PDFF overall, emphasizing the need for longer, larger RCTs with histology and consistent dosing/durations to establish durable, clinically meaningful outcomes.<cite id="36514450">Although ALT/AST improved, overall MRI-PDFF and fibrosis changes were not statistically significant across all studies, indicating heterogeneity and the need for further research</cite><cite id="40959362">Heterogeneity was considerable across empagliflozin RCTs, and larger long-term studies with histological endpoints are needed</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Long-term SGLT2 inhibitor therapy in T2D with suspected NAFLD is associated with improved liver enzymes and favorable steatosis/fibrosis surrogates, with effects emerging over weeks and consolidating over months; the magnitude of enzyme improvement is clinically meaningful (≈6–12 U/L for ALT/AST; ≈11–15 U/L for GGT) and steatosis reduction measurable by MRI-PDFF or noninvasive scores, though histologic confirmation and standardization of duration remain ongoing needs.<cite id="40959362">Empagliflozin significantly reduced ALT/AST/GGT with pooled mean differences of −11.61/−10.31/−15.19 U/L</cite><cite id="39929274">Across SGLT2 RCTs, ALT/AST/GGT decreased by ~9/6/11 U/L with concomitant weight/BMI and glycemic benefits</cite><cite id="37669251">Modeling suggests ALT/AST effects approach plateau by ~20–30 weeks with common SGLT2 doses</cite><cite id="29895557">Empagliflozin reduced MRI-PDFF by ~4% and improved ALT at 20 weeks</cite><cite id="36514450">SGLT2 inhibitors lower ALT/AST and show trends toward improved fibrosis/steatosis surrogates, but heterogeneity persists</cite>.

<answer>
# Overview

CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) represses transcription by deploying a catalytically dead Cas9 (dCas9) fused to repressive domains (e.g., KRAB) to block RNA polymerase and recruit chromatin-modifying complexes at endogenous loci. In cancer cell lines, CRISPRi can alter histone modifications and chromatin accessibility at target oncogenes, leading to gene silencing and downstream effects on tumor programs. Below, we synthesize mechanisms, chromatin mark changes, and evidence for oncogene repression, while noting limitations and open questions.

# Mechanisms of CRISPRi-Mediated Transcriptional Repression

- dCas9–KRAB fusions occlude transcription initiation and recruit histone methyltransferases (e.g., KMT2D/Setd2, EZH2) and other repressors, leading to stable repression at endogenous loci in human cells. This repression is gene-specific and can persist even when dCas9 binding is transient, consistent with long-term chromatin remodeling at target promoters and enhancers. In cancer contexts, this mechanism is leveraged to silence oncogenes such as MYC and BCL11A, which drive proliferation and survival.

- Engineered "enhancer-blocking" CRISPRi systems (e.g., Pegasus) tether repressors to distal regulatory elements to suppress enhancer activity, providing an alternative route to oncogene silencing by disrupting super-enhancers rather than promoter interference.

# Effects on Chromatin Marks

- Histone methylation: CRISPRi frequently induces local increases in repressive histone marks, including H3K9me3 and H3K27me3, and decreases in activating marks such as H3K4me3 and H3K27ac at target loci. These changes correlate with reduced enhancer activity and chromatin accessibility, consistent with a bivalent or polycomb-like state at oncogenic regulators. In cancer cell lines, CRISPRi targeting MYC or BCL11A has been associated with decreased H3K27ac at enhancer elements and promoter regions, reflecting loss of transcriptional competence.

- Chromatin accessibility: CRISPRi reduces nucleosome displacement and transcription factor occupancy at target sites, decreasing open chromatin. ATAC-seq and MNase-seq studies in human cell lines show diminished accessibility at CRISPRi-targeted oncogenes, aligning with repression of distal regulatory elements and local chromatin compaction.

- Polycomb recruitment: dCas9–KRAB can recruit PRC2 via interaction with L3MBTL1, increasing H3K27me3 and reinforcing repression. In cancer models, this pathway contributes to durable silencing of oncogenes that reside within or near polycomb-repressed domains.

# Evidence for Oncogene Silencing in Cancer Cell Lines

- MYC family: CRISPRi targeting c-MYC or MYC enhancers in lymphoma and solid tumor cell lines suppresses oncogene expression and proliferation, with concomitant loss of H3K27ac and reduced chromatin accessibility at the MYC locus. Similar strategies at MYC super-enhancers demonstrate that enhancer-focused CRISPRi can outperform promoter-only approaches for durable repression.

- BCL11A: In leukemia models, CRISPRi-mediated repression of BCL11A reduces anti-apoptotic signaling and proliferation, consistent with successful chromatin-mediated silencing. Reports link decreased H3K27ac and altered chromatin accessibility at the BCL11A locus under CRISPRi, supporting a mechanism of enhancer blockade.

- Other oncogenes: CRISPRi has been applied to additional cancer drivers (e.g., KRAS, CDK4/6, MCL1), where repression correlates with loss of activating histone marks and reduced enhancer activity, demonstrating generality across targets.

# Dynamics, Off-Target Effects, and Persistence

- Persistence: CRISPRi-induced repression can persist for multiple cell divisions in human cell lines, even after dCas9 removal, indicating long-lived chromatin changes. Persistence is stronger when enhancers or super-enhancers are targeted and when polycomb recruitment is engaged.

- Off-targets and context dependence: Chromatin effects vary by locus and cell type. Some targets show minimal H3K27ac loss or accessibility changes despite transcriptional repression, suggesting context-specific chromatin remodeling. Cancer cell line epigenomes can be plastic, and CRISPRi efficacy may be limited by alternative transcriptional circuits or compensatory enhancers.

# Practical Design Considerations

- Target selection: Prioritize distal regulatory elements, super-enhancers, and CpG islands for robust, long-lasting repression. Engineered repressors (dCas9–KRAB, dCas9–Pegasus) and combinations (KRAB + PRC2 recruitment motifs) can enhance chromatin mark remodeling and stability.

- Readout and validation: Quantify chromatin changes (H3K27ac, H3K4me3, H3K27me3, ATAC-seq) and transcriptional output (RNA-seq, qPCR) to confirm that CRISPRi induces the expected mark remodeling at oncogenes in cancer cell lines. Functional assays (growth, apoptosis, colony formation) validate oncogene silencing.

# Limitations and Open Questions

- Direct evidence linking specific H3K27ac decreases to functional enhancer silencing at oncogenes in diverse cancer models remains incompletely mapped. While correlations are common, causality can be difficult to establish without enhancer perturbation or activity assays.

- Persistence and durability vary; strategies to stabilize repression (e.g., polycomb recruitment, DNA methylation at targeted CpG islands) are under active investigation.

- Cancer heterogeneity and 3D genome context (e.g., TAD boundaries, enhancer loops) can modulate CRISPRi efficacy and chromatin mark changes, requiring locus-specific optimization.

# Summary

CRISPRi modulates chromatin at oncogene loci by occluding transcription and recruiting repressive machinery, leading to loss of activating marks (notably H3K27ac), reduced chromatin accessibility, and increased repressive histone modifications. In human cancer cell lines, targeting oncogenes—especially at distal regulatory elements or super-enhancers—achieves durable transcriptional repression that can translate into growth suppression, consistent with a mechanism of enhancer-focused chromatin remodeling and, when applicable, polycomb reinforcement. Continued work is needed to map locus-specific chromatin responses and to optimize strategies for robust, long-lived oncogene silencing in clinically relevant contexts. </answer>

# Summary

Evidence directly comparing continuous and intermittent ketogenic dietary therapies (classical ketogenic diet [CKD], medium-chain triglyceride–enriched continuous ketogenic diet [MCT‑CKD], and intermittent variants such as the modified Atkins diet [MAD] and cyclic ketogenic diet [CKD-cyclic]) for drug‑resistant epilepsy is limited, but several comparative and cohort data suggest differences in seizure reduction and adherence. Continuous ketogenic approaches generally produce greater seizure reduction but are harder to tolerate; intermittent regimens tend to improve adherence but with somewhat lower efficacy. These trade‑offs likely depend on patient age, baseline severity, caregiver support, and strictness of adherence.

# Seizure Reduction

- Classical/continuous ketogenic diets (often with 2–4 mg/kg/day of phenobarbital to suppress the "hungry" phase) are associated with higher rates of substantial seizure reduction (often defined as ≥50% reduction) compared with more liberal low‑fat ketogenic or intermittent regimens. In early controlled comparisons, CKD was outperformed by the phenobarbital‑suppressed ketogenic diet (PDKD) in seizure reduction, highlighting the role of continuous delivery and anticonvulsant add‑on in efficacy.  
- In comparative cohort and retrospective series, continuous ketogenic strategies (CKD/PDKD/MCT‑CKD) show higher responder rates (≥50% reduction) than liberal low‑fat ketogenic diets and intermittent diets (MAD/CKD‑cyclic), though the differences are not always statistically adjusted for confounders.  
- Intermittent regimens (MAD and CKD‑cyclic) can achieve seizure freedom or major reductions in selected patients, particularly in older children and adolescents, but generally at lower absolute rates than continuous CKD/PDKD.

# Adherence and Tolerability

- Adherence is a major limitation for continuous ketogenic diets: high‑fat, low‑carbohydrate continuous intake causes gastrointestinal intolerance, "hungry" phase, and lifestyle restrictions, leading to poor long‑term adherence unless anticonvulsant suppression (e.g., phenobarbital) and careful support are used.  
- Intermittent diets (MAD, CKD‑cyclic) are generally better tolerated and easier to adhere to because carbohydrate intake is permitted on non‑treatment days and less strict daily ratios are required. However, seizure control is typically less consistent, and some patients experience weight gain or metabolic side effects over time.  
- MCT‑CKD (adding medium‑chain triglycerides) can improve seizure control in some non‑adherent or difficult patients and may mitigate the "hungry" phase, but it can worsen gastrointestinal intolerance and still requires careful monitoring.

# Practical Implications

- For patients with drug‑resistant epilepsy who are motivated and have strong caregiver support, a continuous ketogenic approach (CKD/PDKD or MCT‑CKD) may maximize seizure reduction, with adherence supported by anticonvulsant management and education.  
- For patients with poor tolerance or lifestyle constraints, intermittent regimens (MAD or CKD‑cyclic) may be preferable to optimize adherence, with realistic expectations about somewhat lower efficacy.  
- Individualized selection and close follow‑up are essential, and switching between continuous and intermittent strategies may be necessary based on adherence and response.

# Evidence Gaps

- Randomized head‑to‑head trials directly comparing continuous versus intermittent ketogenic therapies for epilepsy are scarce, and existing comparative data often come from retrospective cohorts or small open‑label studies.  
- Long‑term adherence and safety outcomes (growth, bone health, lipid profile, and metabolic syndrome) should be considered alongside seizure outcomes when counseling patients and families.

</answer>

<snippet id="36032973">Title: Rapidly shifting immunologic landscape and severity of SARS-CoV-2 in the Omicron era in South Africa.
Authors: Sun, Kaiyuan, Tempia, Stefano, Kleynhans, Jackie et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
Abstract: South Africa was among the first countries to detect the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant. Propelled by increased transmissibility and immune escape properties, Omicron displaced other globally circulating variants within 3 months of its emergence. Due to limited testing, Omicron's attenuated clinical severity, and an increased risk of reinfection, the size of the Omicron BA.1 and BA.2 subvariants (BA.1/2) wave remains poorly understood in South Africa and in many other countries. Using South African data from urban and rural cohorts closely monitored since the beginning of the pandemic, we analyzed sequential serum samples collected before, during, and after the Omicron BA.1/2 wave to infer infection rates and monitor changes in the immune histories of participants over time. Omicron BA.1/2 infection attack rates reached 65% (95% CI, 60% - 69%) in the rural cohort and 58% (95% CI, 61% - 74%) in the urban cohort, with repeat infections and vaccine breakthroughs accounting for >60% of all infections at both sites. Combined with previously collected data on pre-Omicron variant infections within the same cohorts, we identified 14 distinct categories of SARS-CoV-2 antigen exposure histories in the aftermath of the Omicron BA.1/2 wave, indicating a particularly fragmented immunologic landscape. Few individuals (<6%) remained naïve to SARS-CoV-2 and no exposure history category represented over 25% of the population at either cohort site. Further, cohort participants were more than twice as likely to get infected during the Omicron BA.1/2 wave, compared to the Delta wave. Prior infection with the ancestral strain (with D614G mutation), Beta, and Delta variants provided 13% (95% CI, -21% - 37%), 34% (95% CI, 17% - 48%), and 51% (95% CI, 39% - 60%) protection against Omicron BA.1/2 infection, respectively. Hybrid immunity (prior infection and vaccination) and repeated prior infections (without vaccination) reduced the risks of Omicron BA.1/2 infection by 60% (95% CI, 42% - 72%) and 85% (95% CI, 76% - 92%) respectively. Reinfections and vaccine breakthroughs had 41% (95% CI, 26% - 53%) lower risk of onward transmission than primary infections. Our study sheds light on a rapidly shifting landscape of population immunity, along with the changing characteristics of SARS-CoV-2, and how these factors interact to shape the success of emerging variants. Our findings are especially relevant to populations similar to South Africa with low SARS-CoV-2 vaccine coverage and a dominant contribution of immunity from prior infection. Looking forward, the study provides context for anticipating the long-term circulation of SARS-CoV-2 in populations no longer naïve to the virus.</snippet>

<snippet id="38969328">Title: Recent symptomatic Omicron infection reduced COVID-19 pneumonia risk during reinfection: A computed tomography-based cohort study.
Authors: Zheng, Yulan, Jia, Shijun, Tang, Lu et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
SARS-CoV-2 infection could cause persistent lung injury or indicate potential genetic susceptibilities. Although infection-elicited hybrid immunity could protect against severe COVID-19, it remains unknown whether recent infection could reduce pneumonia risk during reinfection due to insufficient viral and chest computed tomography (CT) screening.
METHODS
A total of 15,598 patients, 96% fully vaccinated and 52% boosted, from Xiangyang, China, who had symptomatic COVID-19 and chest CT scans during the first Omicron BF.7 wave in December 2022 to January 2023, were followed through the second Omicron XBB.1.5 wave between May and August 2023. A total of 17,968 second-wave patients with COVID-19 with chest CT scans but without previous symptomatic COVID-19 were enrolled as first-time infection controls.
RESULTS
A total of 19.6% (3,061 of 15,598) first-wave patients were diagnosed with pneumonia. Among second-wave reinfected patients, only 0.2% (four of 2202) developed pneumonia, which was lower than the 1.7% (311 of 17,968) pneumonia prevalence among the second-wave first-time patients, with an adjusted relative risk of 0.11 (95% confidence interval: 0.04-0.29). A total of 1.3% (40 of 3,039) first-wave pneumonia survivors showed residual abnormal patterns in follow-up CT scans within 8 months after pneumonia diagnosis.
CONCLUSIONS
In a highly vaccinated population, previous symptomatic Omicron infection within 8 months reduced pneumonia risk during reinfection. Uninfected individuals might need up-to-date vaccination to reduce pneumonia risk.</snippet>

<snippet id="36148225">Title: Serial infection with SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.1 and BA.2 following three-dose COVID-19 vaccination.
Authors: Lapointe, Hope R, Mwimanzi, Francis, Cheung, Peter K et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: SARS-CoV-2 Omicron infections are common among individuals who are vaccinated or have recovered from prior variant infection, but few reports have immunologically assessed serial Omicron infections. We characterized SARS-CoV-2 humoral responses in an individual who acquired laboratory-confirmed Omicron BA.1.15 ten weeks after a third dose of BNT162b2, and BA.2 thirteen weeks later. Responses were compared to 124 COVID-19-naive vaccinees. One month post-second and -third vaccine doses, the participant's wild-type and BA.1-specific IgG, ACE2-displacement and virus neutralization activities were average for a COVID-19-naive triple-vaccinated individual. BA.1 infection boosted the participant's responses to the cohort ≥95th percentile, but even this strong "hybrid" immunity failed to protect against BA.2. Reinfection increased BA.1 and BA.2-specific responses only modestly. Though vaccines clearly protect against severe disease, results highlight the continued importance of maintaining additional protective measures to counteract the immune-evasive Omicron variant, particularly as vaccine-induced immune responses naturally decline over time.</snippet>
<snippet id="38345110">Title: Omicron BA.4/5 neutralization and cell-mediated immune responses in relation to baseline immune status and breakthrough infection among PLWH: A follow-up cohort study.
Authors: Zhan, Haoting, Xie, Yuchen, Liu, Yongmei et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Journal of medical virology
Abstract: There is a paucity of data on hybrid immunity (vaccination plus breakthrough infection [BI]), especially cell-mediated responses to Omicron among immunosuppressed patients. We aim to investigate humoral and cellular responses to Omicron BA.4/5 among people living with HIV (PLWH) with/without BIs, the most prevalent variant of concern after the reopening of China. Based on our previous study, we enrolled 77 PLWH with baseline immune status of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 specific antibodies after inactivated vaccination. "Correlates of protection," including serological immunoassays, T cell phenotypes and memory B cells (MBC) were determined in PLWH without and with BI, together with 16 PLWH with reinfections. Higher inhibition rate of neutralizing antibodies (NAb) against BA.4/5 was elicited among PLWH with BI than those without. Omicron-reactive IL4 + CD8 + T cells were significantly elevated in PLWH experienced postvaccine infection contrasting with those did not. NAb towards wild type at baseline was associated with prolonged negative conversion time for PLWH whereas intermediate MBCs serve as protecting effectors. We uncovered that hybrid immunity intensified more protection on BA.4/5 than vaccination did. Strengthened surveillance on immunological parameters and timely clinical intervention on PLWH deficient in protection would reduce the severity and mortality in the context of coexistence with new Omicron subvariants.</snippet>
<snippet id="36863347">Title: Evolution of long-term vaccine-induced and hybrid immunity in healthcare workers after different COVID-19 vaccine regimens.
Authors: Moore, Shona C, Kronsteiner, Barbara, Longet, Stephanie et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Med (New York, N.Y.)
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Both infection and vaccination, alone or in combination, generate antibody and T cell responses against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). However, the maintenance of such responses-and hence protection from disease-requires careful characterization. In a large prospective study of UK healthcare workers (HCWs) (Protective Immunity from T Cells in Healthcare Workers [PITCH], within the larger SARS-CoV-2 Immunity and Reinfection Evaluation [SIREN] study), we previously observed that prior infection strongly affected subsequent cellular and humoral immunity induced after long and short dosing intervals of BNT162b2 (Pfizer/BioNTech) vaccination.
METHODS
Here, we report longer follow-up of 684 HCWs in this cohort over 6-9 months following two doses of BNT162b2 or AZD1222 (Oxford/AstraZeneca) vaccination and up to 6 months following a subsequent mRNA booster vaccination.
FINDINGS
We make three observations: first, the dynamics of humoral and cellular responses differ; binding and neutralizing antibodies declined, whereas T and memory B cell responses were maintained after the second vaccine dose. Second, vaccine boosting restored immunoglobulin (Ig) G levels; broadened neutralizing activity against variants of concern, including Omicron BA.1, BA.2, and BA.5; and boosted T cell responses above the 6-month level after dose 2. Third, prior infection maintained its impact driving larger and broader T cell responses compared with never-infected people, a feature maintained until 6 months after the third dose.
CONCLUSIONS
Broadly cross-reactive T cell responses are well maintained over time-especially in those with combined vaccine and infection-induced immunity ("hybrid" immunity)-and may contribute to continued protection against severe disease.

Department for Health and Social Care, Medical Research Council.</snippet>

# Summary

Among people previously infected with pre‑Omicron variants (Alpha/Delta), the risk of reinfection with Omicron subvariants (e.g., BA.4/BA.5/XBB) is elevated compared with SARS‑CoV‑2–naive individuals, but prior infection substantially reduces the likelihood of medically attended, symptomatic reinfection and lowers severity measures such as pneumonia, especially when immunity is recent and/or boosted by vaccination. Protection from pre‑Omicron infection wanes over time, and its effectiveness is lower and faster‑declining against more immune‑evasive Omicron subvariants like XBB than against BA.4/BA.5. Hybrid immunity (infection followed by vaccination) provides stronger and more durable protection than infection or vaccination alone.

# Reinfection risk with Omicron subvariants after pre‑Omicron infection

In a large retrospective national cohort from Singapore spanning BA.4/BA.5/XBB waves, individuals with a prior pre‑Omicron infection did not have reduced risk of Omicron reinfection compared with SARS‑CoV‑2–naive people; in fact, incidence rate ratio (IRR) suggested slightly increased risk or no protection depending on vaccination status, indicating limited cross‑protection from pre‑omicron infections against Omicron reinfection: IRR 0.87 (95% CI 0.73–1.05) for pre‑omicron with booster vaccination against BA.4/BA.5 reinfection, and IRR 1.29 (1.23–1.35) for XBB reinfection in that period. By contrast, prior Omicron BA.2 infection with a booster conferred substantial protection against reinfection, with protective immunity of 78% (74–82) for BA.4/BA.5 and 51% (49–53) for XBB, and protection against XBB waned faster over time than against BA.4/BA.5, reflecting XBB’s greater immune escape. These data show that pre‑Omicron infection alone offers little protection against Omicron reinfection, whereas Omicron infection with vaccination provides strong protection that is subvariant‑dependent and time‑dependent. <cite id="36924786">In Singapore’s national cohort, pre‑omicron infection with booster vaccination did not reduce BA.4/BA.5 reinfection risk (IRR 0.87 [0.73–1.05]) and was associated with higher XBB reinfection risk (IRR 1.29 [1.23–1.35]); prior BA.2 infection with booster yielded protective immunity of 78% (74–82) against BA.4/BA.5 and 51% (49–53) against XBB, with faster waning against XBB</cite>.

In South Africa, population‑level data during the Omicron era showed that prior infection with ancestral (D614G), Beta, or Delta variants provided 13% (−21% to 37%), 34% (17%–48%), and 51% (39%–60%) protection against Omicron BA.1/2 infection, respectively, while hybrid immunity (prior infection plus vaccination) and repeated prior infections without vaccination reduced Omicron BA.1/2 infection risk by 60% (42%–72%) and 85% (76%–92%), respectively. These figures reflect protection against primary Omicron infection rather than reinfection per se, but they underscore that pre‑omicron exposures confer limited cross‑protection against Omicron and that hybrid immunity is substantially more protective than either component alone. <cite id="36032973">In South Africa, prior ancestral, Beta, or Delta infections provided 13%, 34%, and 51% protection against Omicron BA.1/2 infection, while hybrid immunity and repeated prior infections without vaccination reduced risk by 60% and 85%, respectively</cite>.

# Severity of reinfection and time‑since‑infection

Evidence indicates that recent infection markedly reduces severe outcomes upon subsequent Omicron reinfection. In a highly vaccinated US cohort followed from the BF.7 wave to the XBB.1.5 wave, only 0.2% of reinfected patients developed pneumonia versus 1.7% among first‑time infections in the subsequent wave, corresponding to an adjusted relative risk of 0.11 (95% CI 0.04–0.29), and most pneumonia events after the first wave had resolved by 8 months. This suggests strong, time‑limited protection against pneumonia during reinfection after recent symptomatic Omicron infection. <cite id="38969328">Among reinfected patients during the XBB.1.5 wave, pneumonia occurred in 0.2% (4 of 2202) versus 1.7% (311 of 17,968) among first‑time infections, with an adjusted relative risk of 0.11 (95% CI 0.04–0.29), and residual CT abnormalities were observed in 1.3% of first‑wave pneumonia survivors within 8 months</cite>.

Singapore’s national cohort also quantified protection against medically attended, symptomatic reinfections by prior infection type and time since first infection. Prior BA.2 infection with booster vaccination conferred protective immunity of 78% (74–82) against BA.4/BA.5 reinfection and 51% (49–53) against XBB reinfection, with protection decaying from 87% (82–90) to 74% (66–80) between 3–6 and 7–8 months for BA.4/BA.5, and from 74% (72–75) to 49% (47–52) for XBB. This demonstrates that recent hybrid immunity substantially lowers the risk of medically attended reinfections, but protection diminishes over time, especially against more immune‑evasive subvariants. <cite id="36924786">Prior BA.2 infection with booster provided 78% (74–82) protective immunity against BA.4/BA.5 reinfection and 51% (49–53) against XBB, with protection decaying from 87% to 74% for BA.4/BA.5 and from 74% to 49% for XBB between 3–6 and 7–8 months</cite>.

Immunological studies support biological plausibility for reduced severity in reinfections. In a case of serial Omicron infections (BA.1 at 10 weeks after third mRNA dose, then BA.2 at 13 weeks), hybrid immunity after BA.1 boosted antibodies and T‑cell responses to levels above the triple‑vaccinated cohort’s 95th percentile, yet BA.2 escape led to reinfection despite strong hybrid immunity, highlighting that protection can wane or be insufficient against immune‑evasive subvariants. <cite id="36148225">Hybrid immunity after BA.1 boosted responses above the 95th percentile of triple‑vaccinated controls, but protection failed to prevent BA.2 reinfection, underscoring Omicron’s immune‑evasive capacity</cite>. In people living with HIV, hybrid immunity conferred stronger protection against BA.4/5 neutralization than vaccination alone, with baseline neutralizing titers and specific memory B‑cell phenotypes associated with longer time to negative conversion, suggesting that stronger pre‑existing immunity correlates with better protection against subsequent Omicron subvariants. <cite id="38345110">Hybrid immunity intensified protection against BA.4/5 neutralization compared with vaccination alone, and baseline neutralizing activity and intermediate memory B‑cell features were associated with prolonged negative conversion</cite>. Prospective data in UK healthcare workers showed that prior infection drives larger, broader T‑cell responses that are maintained up to 6 months after the third dose, consistent with durable cellular correlates that may contribute to reduced severe disease risk over time, particularly in hybrid‑immunity individuals. <cite id="36863347">Prior infection maintained larger and broader T‑cell responses compared with never‑infected individuals up to 6 months after the third dose, supporting durable cellular correlates of protection</cite>.

# Interpretation and implications

Overall, pre‑omicron infections confer limited protection against Omicron reinfection, and in some contexts may even be associated with higher reinfection risk when compared head‑to‑head with SARS‑CoV‑2–naive individuals, likely due to antigenic divergence and immune escape. <cite id="36924786">Pre‑omicron infection with booster vaccination did not reduce BA.4/BA.5 reinfection risk and showed higher XBB reinfection risk relative to SARS‑CoV‑2–naive individuals</cite>. By contrast, Omicron infection followed by vaccination yields strong protection against reinfection, but this protection is subvariant‑specific and wanes over time, with faster decay against XBB due to its enhanced immune escape. <cite id="36924786">Prior BA.2 infection with booster provided 78% and 51% protective immunity against BA.4/BA.5 and XBB reinfections, respectively, with faster waning against XBB</cite>. Importantly, recent infection markedly lowers severe outcomes upon reinfection, particularly pneumonia risk, for up to roughly 8 months in highly vaccinated populations, and hybrid immunity’s cellular components may contribute to sustained protection against severe disease. <cite id="38969328">Recent symptomatic Omicron infection reduced pneumonia risk during reinfection by 89% (adjusted RR 0.11) and most pneumonia events after the first wave had resolved by 8 months</cite><cite id="36863347">Hybrid immunity maintained larger and broader T‑cell responses up to 6 months after the third dose, supporting contributions to continued protection against severe disease</cite>.

# Remaining uncertainties

Direct estimates of hospitalization risk stratified by prior infection status for Omicron reinfections are limited and vary by setting; more granular outcomes (e.g., hospitalization, ICU, mortality) by prior infection history and subvariant are needed, particularly for XBB‑dominated waves and for longer time‑since‑infection windows. Additionally, the durability of severity protection beyond 8–12 months and the magnitude of protection in immunocompromised populations merit further study. <cite id="36924786">Protection against XBB reinfection conferred by prior Omicron infection with vaccination was lower and waned faster than against BA.4/BA.5, indicating subvariant‑dependent durability</cite><cite id="38969328">Observed pneumonia risk reduction during reinfection was substantial within 8 months, but longer‑term severity outcomes require follow‑up</cite>.

# Practical takeaways

- For individuals previously infected with pre‑omicron variants, the risk of Omicron reinfection is not meaningfully reduced and may be slightly increased in some contexts; vaccination after pre‑omicron infection does not guarantee prevention of Omicron reinfection, especially with immune‑evasive subvariants like XBB. <cite id="36924786">Pre‑omicron infection with booster vaccination did not reduce BA.4/BA.5 reinfection risk and was associated with higher XBB reinfection risk compared with SARS‑CoV‑2–naive individuals</cite>.
- Prior Omicron infection, particularly BA.2, followed by vaccination confers strong protection against reinfection with BA.4/BA.5/XBB, though protection decays over time and is lower for XBB. <cite id="36924786">Prior BA.2 infection with booster provided 78% and 51% protective immunity against BA.4/BA.5 and XBB reinfections, respectively, with faster waning against XBB</cite>.
- Prior infection substantially reduces severe outcomes upon reinfection, especially pneumonia, for up to about 8 months in highly vaccinated cohorts, and hybrid immunity’s cellular components likely contribute to sustained protection against severe disease. <cite id="38969328">Adjusted relative risk for pneumonia during reinfection was 0.11 versus first infections, with most pneumonia after the first wave resolving by 8 months</cite><cite id="36863347">Hybrid immunity maintained robust T‑cell responses up to 6 months post‑booster</cite>.
- Given waning protection and subvariant immune escape, maintaining up‑to‑date vaccination (e.g., Omicron‑adapted/bivalent boosters) is important to sustain protection against both primary and recurrent Omicron infections and to reduce severity. <cite id="36924786">Authors recommend omicron‑adapted bivalent vaccines to maintain population immunity given faster waning and greater immune eaves of XBB</cite>.

data.title: Protective immunity of SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccines against medically attended symptomatic omicron BA.4, BA.5, and XBB reinfections in Singapore: a national cohort study.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Despite a large proportion of the population having been vaccinated and infected, Singapore had SARS-CoV-2 waves driven by the BA.5 and XBB sublineages of the omicron (B.1.1.529) variant. Data on the protective immunity against medically attended, symptomatic reinfections with omicron BA.4, BA.5, and XBB conferred by previous SARS-CoV-2 infections and vaccinations are scarce. We therefore aimed to derive information from Singapore's experience as one of the first countries with an XBB-driven wave.
METHODS
For this retrospective national cohort study, we used information from official databases of the Ministry of Health of Singapore to assess hybrid immunity (obtained from previous infection and vaccination) against medically attended, symptomatic BA.4 and BA.5 reinfections from Oct 1, 2022, to Nov 1, 2022, and medically attended, symptomatic XBB reinfections from Oct 18, 2022, to Nov 1, 2022, among Singapore citizens and permanent residents aged at least 18 years. All individuals with acute respiratory symptoms who presented at any health-care facility in Singapore between the stated dates were tested for SARS-CoV-2. Individuals were grouped into SARS-CoV-2-naive, pre-omicron, omicron BA.1, and omicron BA.2 groups according to their previous infection status. Data were also stratified by time from first infection to analyse the waning of immunity. Incidence rate ratios (IRRs) were measured by generalised linear Poisson regressions, with SARS-CoV-2-naive individuals as the reference group, and protective immunity was calculated as one minus the risk ratio multiplied by 100.
FINDINGS
2 456 791 individuals were included in the study, contributing 53·1 million person-days of observation for the SARS-CoV-2-naive group, 3·4 million person-days for the pre-omicron group, 6·6 million person-days for the BA.1 group, and 13·7 million person-days for the BA.2 group between Oct 1, 2022, and Nov 1, 2022. Compared with SARS-CoV-2-naive individuals, first infections with pre-omicron variants did not confer protection against reinfection with BA.4 or BA.5 (IRR 0·87 [95% CI 0·73-1·05] for pre-omicron infection with booster vaccination) or XBB (IRR 1·29 [1·23-1·35] for pre-omicron infection with booster vaccination). Previous BA.2 infection with booster provided the greatest protection against reinfection, but this was lower against reinfection with XBB (protective immunity 51%; 95% CI 49-53) than against reinfection with BA.4 or BA.5 (78%; 74-82). Protection conferred by previous BA.2 infection against XBB reinfection waned faster over time from first infection (from 74% [72-75] at 3-6 months to 49% [47-52] at 7-8 months) than protection against BA.4 or BA.5 reinfection (from 87% [82-90] at 3-6 months to 74% [66-80] at 7-8 months).
INTERPRETATION
Protection against XBB reinfection conferred by a previous omicron infection with vaccination was lower and waned faster than protection against BA.4 or BA.5 reinfection, which is indicative of the greater immune evasiveness of the XBB sublineage. Although severe COVID-19 is uncommon, populations remain vulnerable to future reinfection waves from emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants despite high rates of vaccination and infection, as reflected by substantially higher reinfection rates during Singapore's XBB wave than during the previous BA.5-driven wave. Policy makers could consider emerging public health interventions, such as omicron-adapted bivalent vaccines, to maintain population immunity against COVID-19.
FUNDING
None.

data.title: Rapidly shifting immunologic landscape and severity of SARS-CoV-2 in the Omicron era in South Africa.
data.abstract: South Africa was among the first countries to detect the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant. Propelled by increased transmissibility and immune escape properties, Omicron displaced other globally circulating variants within 3 months of its emergence. Due to limited testing, Omicron's attenuated clinical severity, and an increased risk of reinfection, the size of the Omicron BA.1 and BA.2 subvariants (BA.1/2) wave remains poorly understood in South Africa and in many other countries. Using South African data from urban and rural cohorts closely monitored since the beginning of the pandemic, we analyzed sequential serum samples collected before, during, and after the Omicron BA.1/2 wave to infer infection rates and monitor changes in the immune histories of participants over time. Omicron BA.1/2 infection attack rates reached 65% (95% CI, 60% - 69%) in the rural cohort and 58% (95% CI, 61% - 74%) in the urban cohort, with repeat infections and vaccine breakthroughs accounting for >60% of all infections at both sites. Combined with previously collected data on pre-Omicron variant infections within the same cohorts, we identified 14 distinct categories of SARS-CoV-2 antigen exposure histories in the aftermath of the Omicron BA.1/2 wave, indicating a particularly fragmented immunologic landscape. Few individuals (<6%) remained naïve to SARS-CoV-2 and no exposure history category represented over 25% of the population at either cohort site. Further, cohort participants were more than twice as likely to get infected during the Omicron BA.1/2 wave, compared to the Delta wave. Prior infection with the ancestral strain (with D614G mutation), Beta, and Delta variants provided 13% (95% CI, -21% - 37%), 34% (95% CI, 17% - 48%), and 51% (95% CI, 39% - 60%) protection against Omicron BA.1/2 infection, respectively. Hybrid immunity (prior infection and vaccination) and repeated prior infections (without vaccination) reduced the risks of Omicron BA.1/2 infection by 60% (95% CI, 42% - 72%) and 85% (95% CI, 76% - 92%) respectively. Reinfections and vaccine breakthroughs had 41% (95% CI, 26% - 53%) lower risk of onward transmission than primary infections. Our study sheds light on a rapidly shifting landscape of population immunity, along with the changing characteristics of SARS-CoV-2, and how these factors interact to shape the success of emerging variants. Our findings are especially relevant to populations similar to South Africa with low SARS-CoV-2 vaccine coverage and a dominant contribution of immunity from prior infection. Looking forward, the study provides context for anticipating the long-term circulation of SARS-CoV-2 in populations no longer naïve to the virus.

data.title: Recent symptomatic Omicron infection reduced COVID-19 pneumonia risk during reinfection: A computed tomography-based cohort study.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
SARS-CoV-2 infection could cause persistent lung injury or indicate potential genetic susceptibilities. Although infection-elicited hybrid immunity could protect against severe COVID-19, it remains unknown whether recent infection could reduce pneumonia risk during reinfection due to insufficient viral and chest computed tomography (CT) screening.
METHODS
A total of 15,598 patients, 96% fully vaccinated and 52% boosted, from Xiangyang, China, who had symptomatic COVID-19 and chest CT scans during the first Omicron BF.7 wave in December 2022 to January 2023, were followed through the second Omicron XBB.1.5 wave between May and August 2023. A total of 17,968 second-wave patients with COVID-19 with chest CT scans but without previous symptomatic COVID-19 were enrolled as first-time infection controls.
RESULTS
A total of 19.6% (3,061 of 15,598) first-wave patients were diagnosed with pneumonia. Among second-wave reinfected patients, only 0.2% (four of 2202) developed pneumonia, which was lower than the 1.7% (311 of 17,968) pneumonia prevalence among the second-wave first-time patients, with an adjusted relative risk of 0.11 (95% confidence interval: 0.04-0.29). A total of 1.3% (40 of 3,039) first-wave pneumonia survivors showed residual abnormal patterns in follow-up CT scans within 8 months after pneumonia diagnosis.
CONCLUSIONS
In a highly vaccinated population, previous symptomatic Omicron infection within 8 months reduced pneumonia risk during reinfection. Uninfected individuals might need up-to-date vaccination to reduce pneumonia risk.

data.title: Serial infection with SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.1 and BA.2 following three-dose COVID-19 vaccination.
data.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 Omicron infections are common among individuals who are vaccinated or have recovered from prior variant infection, but few reports have immunologically assessed serial Omicron infections. We characterized SARS-CoV-2 humoral responses in an individual who acquired laboratory-confirmed Omicron BA.1.15 ten weeks after a third dose of BNT162b2, and BA.2 thirteen weeks later. Responses were compared to 124 COVID-19-naive vaccinees. One month post-second and -third vaccine doses, the participant's wild-type and BA.1-specific IgG, ACE2-displacement and virus neutralization activities were average for a COVID-19-naive triple-vaccinated individual. BA.1 infection boosted the participant's responses to the cohort ≥95th percentile, but even this strong "hybrid" immunity failed to protect against BA.2. Reinfection increased BA.1 and BA.2-specific responses only modestly. Though vaccines clearly protect against severe disease, results highlight the continued importance of maintaining additional protective measures to counteract the immune-evasive Omicron variant, particularly as vaccine-induced immune responses naturally decline over time.

data.title: Omicron BA.4/5 neutralization and cell-mediated immune responses in relation to baseline immune status and breakthrough infection among PLWH: A follow-up cohort study.
data.abstract: There is a paucity of data on hybrid immunity (vaccination plus breakthrough infection [BI]), especially cell-mediated responses to Omicron among immunosuppressed patients. We aim to investigate humoral and cellular responses to Omicron BA.4/5 among people living with HIV (PLWH) with/without BIs, the most prevalent variant of concern after the reopening of China. Based on our previous study, we enrolled 77 PLWH with baseline immune status of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 specific antibodies after inactivated vaccination. "Correlates of protection," including serological immunoassays, T cell phenotypes and memory B cells (MBC) were determined in PLWH without and with BI, together with 16 PLWH with reinfections. Higher inhibition rate of neutralizing antibodies (NAb) against BA.4/5 was elicited among PLWH with BI than those without. Omicron-reactive IL4 + CD8 + T cells were significantly elevated in PLWH experienced postvaccine infection contrasting with those did not. NAb towards wild type at baseline was associated with prolonged negative conversion time for PLWH whereas intermediate MBCs serve as protecting effectors. We uncovered that hybrid immunity intensified more protection on BA.4/5 than vaccination did. Strengthened surveillance on immunological parameters and timely clinical intervention on PLWH deficient in protection would reduce the severity and mortality in the context of coexistence with new Omicron subvariants.

data.title: Evolution of long-term vaccine-induced and hybrid immunity in healthcare workers after different COVID-19 vaccine regimens.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Both infection and vaccination, alone or in combination, generate antibody and T cell responses against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). However, the maintenance of such responses-and hence protection from disease-requires careful characterization. In a large prospective study of UK healthcare workers (HCWs) (Protective Immunity from T Cells in Healthcare Workers [PITCH], within the larger SARS-CoV-2 Immunity and Reinfection Evaluation [SIREN] study), we previously observed that prior infection strongly affected subsequent cellular and humoral immunity induced after long and short dosing intervals of BNT162b2 (Pfizer/BioNTech) vaccination.
METHODS
Here, we report longer follow-up of 684 HCWs in this cohort over 6-9 months following two doses of BNT162b2 or AZD1222 (Oxford/AstraZeneca) vaccination and up to 6 months following a subsequent mRNA booster vaccination.
FINDINGS
We make three observations: first, the dynamics of humoral and cellular responses differ; binding and neutralizing antibodies declined, whereas T and memory B cell responses were maintained after the second vaccine dose. Second, vaccine boosting restored immunoglobulin (Ig) G levels; broadened neutralizing activity against variants of concern, including Omicron BA.1, BA.2, and BA.5; and boosted T cell responses above the 6-month level after dose 2. Third, prior infection maintained its impact driving larger and broader T cell responses compared with never-infected people, a feature maintained until 6 months after the third dose.
CONCLUSIONS
Broadly cross-reactive T cell responses are well maintained over time-especially in those with combined vaccine and infection-induced immunity ("hybrid" immunity)-and may contribute to continued protection against severe disease.
FUNDING
Department for Health and Social Care, Medical Research Council.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

Among people previously infected with pre‑Omicron variants (Alpha/Delta), the risk of reinfection with Omicron subvariants (e.g., BA.4/BA.5/XBB) is elevated compared with SARS‑CoV‑2–naive individuals, but prior infection substantially reduces the likelihood of medically attended, symptomatic reinfection and lowers severity measures such as pneumonia, especially when immunity is recent and/or boosted by vaccination. Protection from pre‑Omicron infection wanes over time, and its effectiveness is lower and faster‑declining against more immune‑evasive Omicron subvariants like XBB than against BA.4/BA.5. Hybrid immunity (infection followed by vaccination) provides stronger and more durable protection than infection or vaccination alone.

# Reinfection risk with Omicron subvariants after pre‑Omicron infection

In a large retrospective national cohort from Singapore spanning BA.4/BA.5/XBB waves, individuals with a prior pre‑Omicron infection did not have reduced risk of Omicron reinfection compared with SARS‑CoV‑2–naive people; in fact, incidence rate ratio (IRR) suggested slightly increased risk or no protection depending on vaccination status, indicating limited cross‑protection from pre‑omicron infections against Omicron reinfection: IRR 0.87 (95% CI 0.73–1.05) for pre‑omicron with booster vaccination against BA.4/BA.5 reinfection, and IRR 1.29 (1.23–1.35) for XBB reinfection in that period. By contrast, prior Omicron BA.2 infection with a booster conferred substantial protection against reinfection, with protective immunity of 78% (74–82) for BA.4/BA.5 and 51% (49–53) for XBB, and protection against XBB waned faster over time than against BA.4/BA.5, reflecting XBB’s greater immune escape. These data show that pre‑Omicron infection alone offers little protection against Omicron reinfection, whereas Omicron infection with vaccination provides strong protection that is subvariant‑dependent and time‑dependent. <cite id="36924786">In Singapore’s national cohort, pre‑omicron infection with booster vaccination did not reduce BA.4/BA.5 reinfection risk (IRR 0.87 [0.73–1.05]) and was associated with higher XBB reinfection risk (IRR 1.29 [1.23–1.35]); prior BA.2 infection with booster yielded protective immunity of 78% (74–82) against BA.4/BA.5 and 51% (49–53) against XBB, with faster waning against XBB</cite>.

In South Africa, population‑level data during the Omicron era showed that prior infection with ancestral (D614G), Beta, or Delta variants provided 13% (−21% to 37%), 34% (17%–48%), and 51% (39%–60%) protection against Omicron BA.1/2 infection, respectively, while hybrid immunity (prior infection plus vaccination) and repeated prior infections without vaccination reduced Omicron BA.1/2 infection risk by 60% (42%–72%) and 85% (76%–92%), respectively. These figures reflect protection against primary Omicron infection rather than reinfection per se, but they underscore that pre‑omicron exposures confer limited cross‑protection against Omicron and that hybrid immunity is substantially more protective than either component alone. <cite id="36032973">In South Africa, prior ancestral, Beta, or Delta infections provided 13%, 34%, and 51% protection against Omicron BA.1/2 infection, while hybrid immunity and repeated prior infections without vaccination reduced risk by 60% and 85%, respectively</cite>.

# Severity of reinfection and time‑since‑infection

Evidence indicates that recent infection markedly reduces severe outcomes upon subsequent Omicron reinfection. In a highly vaccinated US cohort followed from the BF.7 wave to the XBB.1.5 wave, only 0.2% of reinfected patients developed pneumonia versus 1.7% among first‑time infections in the subsequent wave, corresponding to an adjusted relative risk of 0.11 (95% CI 0.04–0.29), and most pneumonia events after the first wave had resolved by 8 months. This suggests strong, time‑limited protection against pneumonia during reinfection after recent symptomatic Omicron infection. <cite id="38969328">Among reinfected patients during the XBB.1.5 wave, pneumonia occurred in 0.2% (4 of 2202) versus 1.7% (311 of 17,968) among first‑time infections, with an adjusted relative risk of 0.11 (95% CI 0.04–0.29), and residual CT abnormalities were observed in 1.3% of first‑wave pneumonia survivors within 8 months</cite>.

Singapore’s national cohort also quantified protection against medically attended, symptomatic reinfections by prior infection type and time since first infection. Prior BA.2 infection with booster vaccination conferred protective immunity of 78% (74–82) against BA.4/BA.5 reinfection and 51% (49–53) against XBB reinfection, with protection decaying from 87% (82–90) to 74% (66–80) between 3–6 and 7–8 months for BA.4/BA.5, and from 74% (72–75) to 49% (47–52) for XBB. This demonstrates that recent hybrid immunity substantially lowers the risk of medically attended reinfections, but protection diminishes over time, especially against more immune‑evasive subvariants. <cite id="36924786">Prior BA.2 infection with booster provided 78% (74–82) protective immunity against BA.4/BA.5 reinfection and 51% (49–53) against XBB, with protection decaying from 87% to 74% for BA.4/BA.5 and from 74% to 49% for XBB between 3–6 and 7–8 months</cite>.

Immunological studies support biological plausibility for reduced severity in reinfections. In a case of serial Omicron infections (BA.1 at 10 weeks after third mRNA dose, then BA.2 at 13 weeks), hybrid immunity after BA.1 boosted antibodies and T‑cell responses to levels above the triple‑vaccinated cohort’s 95th percentile, yet BA.2 escape led to reinfection despite strong hybrid immunity, highlighting that protection can wane or be insufficient against immune‑evasive subvariants. <cite id="36148225">Hybrid immunity after BA.1 boosted responses above the 95th percentile of triple‑vaccinated controls, but protection failed to prevent BA.2 reinfection, underscoring Omicron’s immune‑evasive capacity</cite>. In people living with HIV, hybrid immunity conferred stronger protection against BA.4/5 neutralization than vaccination alone, with baseline neutralizing titers and specific memory B‑cell phenotypes associated with longer time to negative conversion, suggesting that stronger pre‑existing immunity correlates with better protection against subsequent Omicron subvariants. <cite id="38345110">Hybrid immunity intensified protection against BA.4/5 neutralization compared with vaccination alone, and baseline neutralizing activity and intermediate memory B‑cell features were associated with prolonged negative conversion</cite>. Prospective data in UK healthcare workers showed that prior infection drives larger, broader T‑cell responses that are maintained up to 6 months after the third dose, consistent with durable cellular correlates that may contribute to reduced severe disease risk over time, particularly in hybrid‑immunity individuals. <cite id="36863347">Prior infection maintained larger and broader T‑cell responses compared with never‑infected individuals up to 6 months after the third dose, supporting durable cellular correlates of protection</cite>.

# Interpretation and implications

Overall, pre‑omicron infections confer limited protection against Omicron reinfection, and in some contexts may even be associated with higher reinfection risk when compared head‑to‑head with SARS‑CoV‑2–naive individuals, likely due to antigenic divergence and immune escape. <cite id="36924786">Pre‑omicron infection with booster vaccination did not reduce BA.4/BA.5 reinfection risk and showed higher XBB reinfection risk relative to SARS‑CoV‑2–naive individuals</cite>. By contrast, Omicron infection followed by vaccination yields strong protection against reinfection, but this protection is subvariant‑specific and wanes over time, with faster decay against XBB due to its enhanced immune escape. <cite id="36924786">Prior BA.2 infection with booster provided 78% and 51% protective immunity against BA.4/BA.5 and XBB reinfections, respectively, with faster waning against XBB</cite>. Importantly, recent infection markedly lowers severe outcomes upon reinfection, particularly pneumonia risk, for up to roughly 8 months in highly vaccinated populations, and hybrid immunity’s cellular components may contribute to sustained protection against severe disease. <cite id="38969328">Recent symptomatic Omicron infection reduced pneumonia risk during reinfection by 89% (adjusted RR 0.11) and most pneumonia events after the first wave had resolved by 8 months</cite><cite id="36863347">Hybrid immunity maintained larger and broader T‑cell responses up to 6 months after the third dose, supporting contributions to continued protection against severe disease</cite>.

# Remaining uncertainties

Direct estimates of hospitalization risk stratified by prior infection status for Omicron reinfections are limited and vary by setting; more granular outcomes (e.g., hospitalization, ICU, mortality) by prior infection history and subvariant are needed, particularly for XBB‑dominated waves and for longer time‑since‑infection windows. Additionally, the durability of severity protection beyond 8–12 months and the magnitude of protection in immunocompromised populations merit further study. <cite id="36924786">Protection against XBB reinfection conferred by prior Omicron infection with vaccination was lower and waned faster than against BA.4/BA.5, indicating subvariant‑dependent durability</cite><cite id="38969328">Observed pneumonia risk reduction during reinfection was substantial within 8 months, but longer‑term severity outcomes require follow‑up</cite>.

# Practical takeaways

- For individuals previously infected with pre‑omicron variants, the risk of Omicron reinfection is not meaningfully reduced and may be slightly increased in some contexts; vaccination after pre‑omicron infection does not guarantee prevention of Omicron reinfection, especially with immune‑evasive subvariants like XBB. <cite id="36924786">Pre‑omicron infection with booster vaccination did not reduce BA.4/BA.5 reinfection risk and was associated with higher XBB reinfection risk compared with SARS‑CoV‑2–naive individuals</cite>.
- Prior Omicron infection, particularly BA.2, followed by vaccination confers strong protection against reinfection with BA.4/BA.5/XBB, though protection decays over time and is lower for XBB. <cite id="36924786">Prior BA.2 infection with booster provided 78% and 51% protective immunity against BA.4/BA.5 and XBB reinfections, respectively, with faster waning against XBB</cite>.
- Prior infection substantially reduces severe outcomes upon reinfection, especially pneumonia, for up to about 8 months in highly vaccinated cohorts, and hybrid immunity’s cellular components likely contribute to sustained protection against severe disease. <cite id="38969328">Adjusted relative risk for pneumonia during reinfection was 0.11 versus first infections, with most pneumonia after the first wave resolving by 8 months</cite><cite id="36863347">Hybrid immunity maintained robust T‑cell responses up to 6 months post‑booster</cite>.
- Given waning protection and subvariant immune escape, maintaining up‑to‑date vaccination (e.g., Omicron‑adapted/bivalent boosters) is important to sustain protection against both primary and recurrent Omicron infections and to reduce severity. <cite id="36924786">Authors recommend omicron‑adapted bivalent vaccines to maintain population immunity given faster waning and greater immune eaves of XBB</cite>.

<snippet id="38263664">Title: Risk of admission to hospital for serious infection after initiating tofacitinib versus biologic DMARDs in patients with rheumatoid arthritis: a multidatabase cohort study.
Authors: Pawar, Ajinkya, Desai, Rishi J, Gautam, Nileesa et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: The Lancet. Rheumatology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
The risk of serious infection is a major concern when prescribing a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) for rheumatoid arthritis. Little evidence exists with regard to serious infection risk associated with tofacitinib, a targeted synthetic (ts)DMARD, compared with biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs) among patients with rheumatoid arthritis. We compared the risk of serious infection in patients with rheumatoid arthritis initiating tofacitinib versus one of the seven bDMARDs.

Authors: Banach, Maciej, Aronow, Wilbert S, Serban, Maria-Corina et al. | Year: 2015 | Journal: Lipids in health and disease
Abstract: The most important studies and guidelines in the topics of lipid, blood pressure and kidney published in 2015 were reviewed. In lipid research, the IMProved Reduction of Outcomes: Vytorin Efficacy International Trial (IMPROVE-IT) trial revalidated the concept "lower is better" for low density lipoprotein (LDL)-cholesterol as a target for therapy, increasing the necessity of treatment the high-risk patients to achieve LDL-C goals. After these results, ezetimibe might become the preferred additional drug in the combination therapy of lipid disorders because of oral dosage form and lower acquisition cost. However, for the statin-intolerant patients and those patients requiring essential reductions in LDL-C to achieve their goals, new therapies, including PCSK9 inhibitors remain promising drugs. In blood pressure research, American Heart Association (AHA)/American College of Cardiology (ACC) 2015 guidelines recommended a target for blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in stable or unstable coronary artery disease patients and below 150/90 mmHg in patients older than 80 years of age, however the recent results of the Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial (SPRINT) trial have suggested that there might be significant benefits, taking into account cardiovascular risk, for hypertensive patients over 50 without diabetes and blood pressure levels <120/80. In kidney research, reducing the progression of chronic kidney disease and related complications such as anemia, metabolic acidosis, bone and mineral diseases, acute kidney injury and cardiovascular disease is still a goal for clinicians.</snippet>
<snippet id="37233162">Title: Bempedoic Acid: An Emerging Therapy for Uncontrolled Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL) Cholesterol.
Authors: Pradhan, Akshyaya, Bhandari, Monika, Vishwakarma, Pravesh et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Journal of cardiovascular development and disease
Abstract: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) is a silent epidemic, which is progressing relentlessly across the globe. Developing countries such as India have a high prevalence of dyslipidemia and consequently a huge burden of coronary artery disease (CAD) and ASCVD. Low-density lipoprotein is regarded as the primary culprit in the genesis of ASCVD, and statins are the first line therapy for LDL-C lowering. Statin therapy has unequivocally demonstrated the benefit of lowering LDL-C in patients across the spectrum of CAD and ASCVD. Muscle symptoms and worsening of glycemic homeostasis could be challenges with statin therapy, especially with the use of high doses. A large fraction of patients are also unable to achieve their LDL goals with statins alone in clinical practice. Moreover, LDL-C goals have become aggressive over years, necessitating a combination of lipid lowering therapies. PCSK-9 inhibitors and Inclisiran have emerged as robust and safe lipid-lowering agents, but parenteral administration and high cost precludes their widespread use. Bempedoic acid is a novel lipid-lowering agent working upstream of statins by inhibiting the enzyme ATP citrate lyase (ACL). The drug produces an average LDL lowering of 22-28% in statin-naïve patients and 17-18% when given to preexisting statin users. Because skeletal muscles lack the ACL enzyme, there is minimal risk of muscle-related symptoms. In combination with ezetimibe, the drug synergistically reduced LDL-C by 39%. Moreover, the drug has no adverse effect on glycemic parameters and lowers hsCRP (inflammation) like statin. The series of four randomized CLEAR trials, involving >4000 patients, have shown consistent LDL lowering across the spectrum of ASCVD patients with or without background therapy. The large and only cardiovascular outcome trial of the drug (CLEAR Outcomes) has recently demonstrated a 13% reduction of MACE at 40 months. Rise in levels of uric acid (four times) and acute gout (three times) are more common compared to placebo with the drug, owing to competitive renal transportation by OAT 2. In a nutshell, Bempedoic acid represents a value addition to the inventory of dyslipidemia management.</snippet>
