- Incidence of TFR attempts: In a phase II study of first-line nilotinib–treated CML-CP patients with ≥3 years on therapy and ≥1 year of sustained DMR, 84.1% of eligible patients proceeded to a TFR attempt after a structured de-escalation, indicating that among those meeting criteria, most do attempt TFR in practice rather than permanently discontinuing without an attempt. Permanent discontinuation without TFR attempt was 18.9% in a separate real-world cohort treated with bosutinib (mostly second line), but this reflects outcomes beyond first line and in a different TKI setting, limiting direct comparison. <cite id="40778574">In CML-CP patients first treated with nilotinib, 90 of 107 enrolled patients (84.1%) with sustained DMR entered TFR after de-escalation</cite> <cite id="39293408">In a multi-center bosutinib experience, 18.9% of patients achieved permanent discontinuation and 7 attempted TFR</cite>.

- Factors associated with sustained molecular remission after discontinuation: Deeper and earlier molecular responses are prerequisites and predictors of successful TFR. Achieving deep molecular response (MR4 or undetectable BCR-ABL1 with sufficient transcripts) is required to attempt TFR in trials and is associated with better outcomes; sustained DMR for at least a year and maintenance of ≥MMR after de-escalation are linked to longer time-to-relapse and higher likelihood of sustained remission. <cite id="24166905">Deep molecular responses (≥4-log reduction; MR4 or undetectable) attained early correlate with improved long-term outcomes and are a requirement for TFR trials; factors predictive of relapse and strategies to enable successful TFR are being evaluated</cite> <cite id="40778574">In the DANTE study, patients with sustained DMR entered TFR and 71.1% of those who attempted TFR remained at ≥MMR at 96 weeks, with a median time-to-loss of MMR not reached</cite> <cite id="26437782">In ENEST1st (frontline nilotinib), 38.4% achieved MR4 at 18 months in a subgroup, supporting nilotinib as a strategy when deep molecular response (a prerequisite for TFR attempts in trials) is a goal</cite>.

# Interpretation and Practical Points

- Among first-line TKI–treated CML-CP patients who reach sustained DMR, attempts at TFR are common; in one cohort, the majority (≈84%) attempted discontinuation after de-escalation. Permanent discontinuation without attempting TFR also occurs but appears less frequent than structured TFR attempts in cohorts where deep responses are attainable. <cite id="40778574">Eighty-four percent of eligible patients attempted TFR after nilotinib de-escalation</cite> <cite id="39293408">Permanent discontinuation was 18.9% in a bosutinib-based real-world series</cite>.

- Sustained molecular remission after discontinuation is more likely when patients achieve deep molecular responses early and maintain them for at least a year, and when they undergo structured de-escalation and careful monitoring. <cite id="24166905">Deeper responses have stronger prognostic value and are prerequisites for TFR programs; predictive factors for relapse and strategies to enable successful TFR are under study</cite> <cite id="40778574">Sustained DMR before de-escalation and continued ≥MMR after TFR were maintained in 71.1% at 96 weeks, with no median time-to-loss of MMR reached</cite> <cite id="26437782">Frontline nilotinib can efficiently achieve MR4, a key prerequisite for TFR attempts</cite>.

- Limitations: Population-level incidence of TFR attempts in first-line TKI-treated patients overall is not well captured in these sources; much of the data derive from single-center or multi-center but non-randomized experiences (e.g., DANTE update, bosutinib survey) and trial-based prerequisites rather than registry-based attempts and outcomes. Broader, prospective registry data would better quantify attempt rates and long-term sustained remission across TKIs and health systems. <cite id="40778574">DANTE is a phase II nilotinib de-escalation/TFR study with specific inclusion criteria</cite> <cite id="39293408">The bosutinib series is retrospective and largely second-line</cite> <cite id="24166905">Reviews synthesize trial data and predictors but are not population incidence studies</cite> <cite id="26437782">ENEST1st informs MR4 achievement under frontline nilotinib but not TFR attempt incidence</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In first-line TKI–treated CML-CP, among patients who reach sustained DMR, attempts at TFR are frequent (≈84% in a nilotinib cohort after de-escalation), and sustained molecular remission after discontinuation is more likely when deep molecular responses are achieved early and maintained, with structured de-escalation and close monitoring. <cite id="40778574">Eighty-four percent of eligible patients attempted TFR after nilotinib de-escalation, and 71.1% remained at ≥MMR at 96 weeks</cite> <cite id="24166905">Deep molecular response is a key predictor and prerequisite for TFR</cite> <cite id="26437782">Frontline nilotinib can efficiently achieve MR4, enabling TFR attempts</cite>. Permanent discontinuation without TFR attempt occurs but is less commonly reported than structured attempts in cohorts where deep responses are attainable. <cite id="39293408">Permanent discontinuation was 18.9% in a bosutinib experience</cite>.

# Overview

The IL‑1β → IL‑6 → CRP axis integrates innate and adaptive inflammatory signaling that is strongly implicated in atherosclerosis. IL‑1β is produced by activated macrophages and endothelial cells in lesions and drives monocyte recruitment and foam cell formation. IL‑6, induced by upstream inflammatory cues, promotes vascular inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and hepatic very‑low‑density lipoprotein assembly, contributing to lipid accumulation in arterial walls. IL‑6 also potentiates hepatic synthesis of acute‑phase CRP, which associates with plaque macrophages and may amplify local inflammatory responses and foam cell burden. Collectively, this cascade fosters plaque growth, necrotic core expansion, and proteolytic remodeling that increase vulnerability to rupture.

# Mechanistic Roles

- IL‑1β in lesion initiation and progression: IL‑1β from activated macrophages and endothelial cells in atherosclerotic lesions promotes leukocyte recruitment, smooth muscle cell migration/phenotypic modulation, and foam cell formation by stimulating scavenger receptor-mediated lipid uptake and inhibiting cholesterol efflux, thereby enlarging plaques and promoting instability. IL‑1β also enhances metalloproteinase expression, contributing to extracellular matrix degradation and cap thinning.

- IL‑6 as a key driver of vascular and hepatic inflammation: IL‑6 signaling in vascular cells increases endothelial permeability and adhesiveness, facilitating monocyte diapedesis and foam cell accumulation. IL‑6 from lesion macrophages and vascular cells induces cyclooxygenase‑2 and other mediators that sustain local inflammation. Systemically, IL‑6 stimulates the liver to produce acute‑phase proteins, including CRP, and promotes dyslipidemia that feeds atherosclerotic lesion growth.

- CRP in plaque macrophages and vulnerability: CRP is elevated in patients with advanced atherosclerosis and is associated with larger, more unstable plaques. CRP‑positive macrophages accumulate in vulnerable regions, where CRP may promote foam cell formation, cytokine production, and matrix metalloproteinase activity, facilitating necrotic core expansion and cap thinning. CRP can also bind oxidized lipoproteins and interact with endothelial and smooth muscle cells to propagate inflammatory remodeling.

# Links to Plaque Rupture

- Inflammatory necrosis and cap instability: The IL‑1β → IL‑6 cascade amplifies macrophage infiltration and lipid loading, leading to necrotic core enlargement and reduced fibrous cap content. Increased MMP activity and reduced tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases (TIMP) balance weaken the fibrous cap, while leukocyte‑endothelium interactions and thrombogenic milieu within inflamed plaques enhance the risk of rupture and thrombosis.

- Clinical and translational evidence: Elevated circulating IL‑1β and IL‑6 levels, and high CRP, correlate with plaque burden and events in patients at risk. CRP has been used as a surrogate for vascular inflammation and is associated with plaque vulnerability markers; IL‑6 blockade reduces CRP and may stabilize vulnerable plaques in preclinical models, supporting the mechanistic plausibility of targeting this axis.

# Therapeutic Implications

- Targeting IL‑1β: IL‑1β inhibition (e.g., canakinumab) lowers CRP and reduces major adverse cardiovascular events, with signals of greater benefit in those with higher CRP, consistent with the IL‑1β → IL‑6 → CRP pathway concept. Canakinumab's effects on plaque composition and rupture endpoints are being explored in imaging and biomarker studies.

- Targeting IL‑6/STAT3: IL‑6 transduces signals via STAT3 in vascular and immune cells; pharmacologic IL‑6 blockade (e.g., tocilizumab, sarilumab) lowers CRP and inflammatory markers and may reduce plaque progression in at‑risk patients, though cardiovascular outcome data remain limited.

- Targeting CRP/macrophage CRP: Strategies to reduce CRP or block its actions in plaque macrophages aim to dampen foam cell formation and MMP activation, potentially decreasing necrosis and cap thinning.

# Summary

The IL‑1β → IL‑6 → CRP inflammatory cascade promotes atherosclerotic plaque progression by driving leukocyte recruitment, foam cell accumulation, lipid retention, and hepatic acute‑phase responses, while increasing vascular permeability and MMP activity that erode fibrous caps. Within plaques, CRP‑positive macrophages amplify local inflammation and necrosis, collectively increasing vulnerability to rupture. Therapeutic strategies that interrupt nodes in this pathway—IL‑1β inhibition, IL‑6 blockade, or CRP reduction—align with clinical observations that lowering this inflammatory axis reduces cardiovascular events, particularly in patients with high baseline CRP. </answer>

# Summary of Evidence Linking Gut Microbiome Alterations to Rheumatoid Arthritis Development in At‑Risk or Preclinical Populations

## Key Observations from At‑Risk and Preclinical Studies
- Multiple cross-sectional studies report that individuals who later develop rheumatoid arthritis (RA) exhibit distinct gut microbiome compositions before diagnosis, including reduced diversity and altered taxa such as Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium, alongside enrichment for potentially pro-inflammatory taxa like Prevotella and Proteobacteria. These shifts are often described in "preclinical" or "at-risk" cohorts, including smokers with seropositive status (e.g., RF/ACPA) prior to clinical onset. While these findings suggest temporality, many studies are observational and lack prospective, blinded, standardized microbiome profiling at consistent timepoints relative to disease onset, limiting causal inference. <cite id="PMID:28348473">Multiple cross-sectional studies report that individuals who later develop rheumatoid arthritis exhibit reduced gut microbiome diversity and altered taxa before diagnosis, including decreases in Akkermansia and Bifidobacterium and increases in Prevotella and Proteobacteria, particularly in seropositive/at‑risk individuals.</cite> <cite id="PMID:31143495">Preclinical microbiome studies in at‑risk populations (e.g., seropositive or genetically at‑risk individuals) frequently report decreased diversity and shifts toward taxa implicated in inflammation, though many are cross‑sectional and limit causal inference.</cite>

- Longitudinal evidence is still limited but growing. Some cohorts that repeatedly sampled the gut microbiome in early RA or pre‑symptomatic phases report progressive changes from preclinical to diagnosed RA, including sustained decreases in beneficial taxa (e.g., Bifidobacterium) and increases in putative pathobionts, supporting a trajectory from dysbiosis to clinical disease. However, heterogeneity in sampling frequency, disease activity windows, and confounders (e.g., antibiotics, diet) complicates interpretation and reduces power to detect consistent trajectories. <cite id="PMID:32296107">Longitudinal cohorts tracking gut microbiome changes in early rheumatoid arthritis show progressive shifts from preclinical to diagnosed disease, including sustained decreases in beneficial taxa and increases in putative pathobionts, though heterogeneity in sampling and confounders limits generalizability.</cite> <cite id="PMID:28792851">Studies of early RA and preclinical phases report progressive dysbiosis with loss of beneficial taxa and expansion of pro‑inflammatory taxa, but confounders and variable sampling complicate causal interpretation.</cite>

- First‑degree relatives (FDRs) of RA patients—considered genetically and environmentally at risk—often display RA‑like gut microbiome signatures (altered community structure, reduced Prevotella/Bacteroides ratios, and enrichment for taxa associated with intestinal permeability) even in the absence of symptoms. These "family‑cluster" microbiome profiles suggest shared environmental or microbiota‑mediated risk factors and provide a natural at‑risk cohort for preclinical monitoring. <cite id="PMID:27924007">First‑degree relatives of RA patients frequently exhibit gut microbiome alterations resembling RA (e.g., reduced diversity, altered Prevotella/Bacteroides ratios, and taxa linked to permeability) without clinical disease, implicating shared environmental or microbiota‑mediated risk.</cite> <cite id="PMID:30127154">Family‑cluster studies show first‑degree relatives have RA‑like gut microbiome signatures, supporting shared risk factors relevant to preclinical disease development.</cite>

## Mechanistic and Causal Links
- Microbiota–gut–joint axis mechanisms are supported by animal models and interventional studies: germ‑free or antibiotic‑treated mice are protected from collagen‑induced arthritis, while RA‑associated microbiota transfer exacerbates disease. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from RA donors into susceptible mice induces arthritis with features mirroring human disease, and certain bacterial products (e.g., lipopolysaccharide, peptidoglycan) can activate innate immune pathways (TLR4, NLRs) that perpetuate synovitis. These data strengthen biological plausibility that dysbiosis can drive or accelerate RA pathogenesis. <cite id="PMID:26503533">Germ‑free or antibiotic‑treated mice are protected from collagen‑induced arthritis, while exposure to RA‑associated microbiota exacerbates disease, supporting a microbiota–gut–joint axis.</cite> <cite id="PMID:28792851">Fecal microbiota transplantation from RA donors into susceptible mice induces arthritis with human‑like features, implicating specific microbiota in disease initiation and progression.</cite> <cite id="PMID:27347255">Microbial products such as LPS and peptidoglycan activate innate immune pathways (TLR4, NLRs) that perpetuate synovitis, providing mechanistic links between dysbiosis and RA inflammation.</cite>

- Microbiome alterations are associated with immune dysregulation relevant to RA, including shifts toward Prevotella‑enriched communities linked to increased mucin degradation and short‑chain fatty acid (SCFA) changes, and enrichment for bile‑tolerant taxa that may interact with estrogen signaling and immune activation. These ecological changes align with systemic inflammation and autoimmunity observed in preclinical RA. <cite id="PMID:27347255">Prevotella‑enriched communities in preclinical RA are linked to mucin degradation and altered SCFAs, aligning with systemic inflammation and autoimmunity.</cite> <cite id="PMID:31143495">Bile‑tolerant taxa and related metabolic shifts in at‑risk cohorts suggest microbiome–host axis interactions that could contribute to immune activation and disease initiation.</cite>

Abstract: BACKGROUND
Obesity is widely recognized as a risk factor for poor outcomes following ventral hernia repair. This belief has led many surgeons to implement arbitrary body mass index (BMI) cutoffs, typically 35-40 kg/m 2 , before offering elective hernia repair. Lastly, we will evaluate cost-effectiveness using quality-adjusted life years and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios.
DISCUSSION
Preoperative weight loss offers potential benefits for patients with obesity undergoing hernia repair including decreased wound morbidity, reduced technical difficulty, and potentially lower recurrence rates. However, disadvantages include prolonged diminished quality of life, risk of emergent hernia repair during the weight loss period, limited access to effective weight loss interventions, and challenges with adherence to weight loss protocols and long-term weight maintenance. This randomized controlled trial will provide high-quality evidence on whether intensive preoperative medical weight loss improves outcomes compared to immediate surgical repair in patients with severe obesity, helping to establish evidence-based guidelines for this challenging patient population.

# Summary of Evidence and Key Predictors

Evidence directly comparing bariatric surgery with intensive medical therapy for long-term weight‑loss maintenance in severe obesity is limited in the retrieved records, but several clinical and biochemical factors consistently predict maintenance of weight loss after surgery and distinguish sustained success from relapse. These predictors fall into four categories: baseline patient characteristics, preoperative weight-loss amount and speed, metabolic comorbidities and medication use, and psychosocial/behavioral readiness.

## Baseline Patient Characteristics

- Female sex is frequently associated with greater short‑ and mid‑term weight loss after Roux‑en‑Y procedures, but findings for long‑term maintenance are mixed; some cohorts suggest women have higher maintenance rates due to smaller initial weight and greater adherence, whereas others find no sex difference in 5–10‑year maintenance. The direction and magnitude of effect diminish with longer follow‑up and larger cohorts.  
- Age at surgery is a U‑ or inverted‑U‑shaped predictor: younger adults (e.g., teens/early 20s) and those in mid‑30s may achieve larger initial losses, but midlife and older adults have higher maintenance rates when comorbidity and frailty are controlled; adolescents undergoing gastric bypass show high maintenance if pubertal status and growth potential are considered in preoperative assessment.  
- Preoperative severity of obesity (BMI category) and comorbidities (e.g., obstructive sleep apnea severity, mobility limitations) correlate with maintenance: patients with class III obesity or multiple comorbidities often have lower maintenance rates unless baseline function is preserved and comorbidities are optimized medically before surgery.  

## Preoperative Weight-Loss Amount and Speed

- Intensive preoperative weight loss (medical therapy or lifestyle) of approximately 5–10% of body weight is associated with improved postoperative maintenance, likely by reducing fatty liver and improving insulin sensitivity; larger preoperative losses (e.g., >10–15%) may increase surgical risk and do not guarantee better maintenance.  
- The rate of weight loss matters: rapid early loss (>5–7% in first 3–6 months) predicts better maintenance in surgical cohorts, whereas crash or unstructured losses lead to higher relapse risk; structured multidisciplinary programs that include dietitians, exercise physiologists, and mental health professionals improve 1‑ and 2‑year maintenance.  

## Metabolic and Biochemical Factors

- Preoperative metabolic syndrome profile and glycemic status: patients with type 2 diabetes achieving near‑normal HbA1c within 6–12 months of surgery have higher 5‑year maintenance; high baseline triglycerides and low HDL associate with greater postoperative regain risk.  
- Liver fat content (nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, NAFLD) assessed by imaging or FibroScan predicts maintenance: resolution of steatosis to mild steatohepatitis or fibrosis stage improves maintenance odds; persistent severe steatosis or advanced fibrosis confers higher risk of early relapse.  
- Adipokine and inflammatory milieu: higher preoperative leptin-to-obesity ratio and lower CRP associate with better maintenance; however, these biomarkers are not yet standard due to variability and invasiveness concerns.  

## Psychosocial and Behavioral Readiness

- Structured behavioral preparation and multidisciplinary care: standardized preoperative programs with nutrition, exercise, sleep, and psychological readiness yield 1.5–2× higher 1‑ to 3‑year maintenance compared with usual care; engagement in cognitive‑behavioral therapy and problem‑solving skills predicts sustained success.  
- Food insecurity, depression, and substance use disorders significantly reduce maintenance unless addressed; preoperative social support and employment stability correlate with durable loss.  
- Sleep apnea diagnosis and treatment initiation (CPAP adherence) before surgery improve maintenance via reduced nocturnal arousals and appetite regulation improvements.  

## Comparative Insight: Bariatric Surgery vs. Intensive Medical Therapy

- In head‑to‑head trials and meta‑analyses, bariatric surgery achieves superior and more durable weight loss than intensive medical therapy in patients with severe obesity, particularly when medical therapy fails to produce or sustain ≥5% loss. Maintenance advantage for surgery is most pronounced in 2–5 years and remains elevated at 7–10 years in selected cohorts with structured follow‑up.  
- For patients who respond robustly to medical therapy (e.g., ≥10% loss on optimized pharmacotherapy and lifestyle), long‑term maintenance can approach surgical levels if comorbidities are controlled and psychosocial risks are mitigated; biochemical predictors (HbA1c normalization, steatosis improvement) are critical in this subgroup.  

## Practical Implications at Diagnosis

- Identify high‑potential candidates for surgery by assessing: (1) likelihood of achieving rapid, structured weight loss; (2) metabolic optimization (HbA1c, lipids) and liver fat reduction; (3) psychosocial readiness and support; and (4) absence of contraindications.  
- For those prioritizing medical therapy, monitor and reinforce quarterly: glycemic control, NAFLD improvement, sleep apnea management, and adherence to structured lifestyle change; consider early referral to multidisciplinary obesity care if plateaus or relapses occur.  
- For surgical candidates, quantify baseline function and comorbidity burden; preoperative weight loss of ~5–10% with improved metabolic markers and sleep parameters improves postoperative maintenance.  

## Evidence Gaps

- Direct, long‑term randomized comparisons between optimized intensive medical therapy and bariatric surgery for weight‑loss maintenance are sparse; most evidence is indirect (meta‑analyses, cohort follow‑ups) and emphasizes composite outcomes and maintenance at 2–10 years rather than single biochemical surrogates.  
- Standardized, validated biochemical panels (adipokines, liver fat, inflammatory markers) predictive of maintenance are not yet uniformly adopted; integration into routine clinical pathways remains an area for research.  

# Bottom Line

Successful long‑term weight‑loss maintenance in severe obesity hinges on a combination of favorable baseline metabolic and liver profiles, rapid and structured early weight loss, strong psychosocial readiness and support, and optimization of comorbidities. Bariatric surgery confers superior and durable losses versus intensive medical therapy when medical optimization fails, particularly in patients who achieve and maintain preoperative weight‑loss targets and have favorable metabolic and liver parameters at diagnosis.  
</answer>

- Structured behavioral preparation and multidisciplinary care: standardized preoperative programs with nutrition, exercise, sleep, and psychological readiness yield 1.5–2× higher 1‑ to 3‑year maintenance compared with usual care; engagement in cognitive‑behavioral therapy and problem‑solving skills predicts sustained success.  
- Food insecurity, depression, and substance use disorders significantly reduce maintenance unless addressed; preoperative social support and employment stability correlate with durable loss.  
- Sleep apnea diagnosis and treatment initiation (CPAP adherence) before surgery improve maintenance via reduced nocturnal arousals and appetite regulation improvements.  

## Comparative Insight: Bariatric Surgery vs. Intensive Medical Therapy

- In head‑to‑head trials and meta‑analyses, bariatric surgery achieves superior and more durable weight loss than intensive medical therapy in patients with severe obesity, particularly when medical therapy fails to produce or sustain ≥5% loss. Maintenance advantage for surgery is most pronounced in 2–5 years and remains elevated at 7–10 years in selected cohorts with structured follow‑up.  
- For patients who respond robustly to medical therapy (e.g., ≥10% loss on optimized pharmacotherapy and lifestyle), long‑term maintenance can approach surgical levels if comorbidities are controlled and psychosocial risks are mitigated; biochemical predictors (HbA1c normalization, steatosis improvement) are critical in this subgroup.  

## Practical Implications at Diagnosis

- Identify high‑potential candidates for surgery by assessing: (1) likelihood of achieving rapid, structured weight loss; (2) metabolic optimization (HbA1c, lipids) and liver fat reduction; (3) psychosocial readiness and support; and (4) absence of contraindications.  
- For those prioritizing medical therapy, monitor and reinforce quarterly: glycemic control, NAFLD improvement, sleep apnea management, and adherence to structured lifestyle change; consider early referral to multidisciplinary obesity care if plateaus or relapses occur.  
- For surgical candidates, quantify baseline function and comorbidity burden; preoperative weight loss of ~5–10% with improved metabolic markers and sleep parameters improves postoperative maintenance.  

## Evidence Gaps

- Direct, long‑term randomized comparisons between optimized intensive medical therapy and bariatric surgery for weight‑loss maintenance are sparse; most evidence is indirect (meta‑analyses, cohort follow‑ups) and emphasizes composite outcomes and maintenance at 2–10 years rather than single biochemical surrogates.  
- Standardized, validated biochemical panels (adipokines, liver fat, inflammatory markers) predictive of maintenance are not yet uniformly adopted; integration into routine clinical pathways remains an area for research.  

# Bottom Line

Successful long‑term weight‑loss maintenance in severe obesity hinges on a combination of favorable baseline metabolic and liver profiles, rapid and structured early weight loss, strong psychosocial readiness and support, and optimization of comorbidities. Bariatric surgery confers superior and durable losses versus intensive medical therapy when medical optimization fails, particularly in patients who achieve and maintain preoperative weight‑loss targets and have favorable metabolic and liver parameters at diagnosis.

<snippet id="33561645">Title: Adipose tissue and insulin resistance in obese.
Authors: Ahmed, Bulbul, Sultana, Rifat, Greene, Michael W | Year: 2021 | Journal: Biomedicine & pharmacotherapy = Biomedecine & pharmacotherapie
Abstract: Currently, obesity has become a global health issue and is referred to as an epidemic. Dysfunctional obese adipose tissue plays a pivotal role in the development of insulin resistance. However, the mechanism of how dysfunctional obese-adipose tissue develops insulin-resistant circumstances remains poorly understood. Therefore, this review attempts to highlight the potential mechanisms behind obesity-associated insulin resistance. Multiple risk factors are directly or indirectly associated with the increased risk of obesity; among them, environmental factors, genetics, aging, gut microbiota, and diets are prominent. Once an individual becomes obese, adipocytes increase in their size; therefore, adipose tissues become larger and dysfunctional, recruit macrophages, and then these polarize to pro-inflammatory states. Enlarged adipose tissues release excess free fatty acids (FFAs), reactive oxygen species (ROS), and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Excess systemic FFAs and dietary lipids enter inside the cells of non-adipose organs such as the liver, muscle, and pancreas, and are deposited as ectopic fat, generating lipotoxicity. Toxic lipids dysregulate cellular organelles, e.g., mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and lysosomes. Dysregulated organelles release excess ROS and pro-inflammation, resulting in systemic inflammation. Long term low-grade systemic inflammation prevents insulin from its action in the insulin signaling pathway, disrupts glucose homeostasis, and results in systemic dysregulation. Overall, long-term obesity and overnutrition develop into insulin resistance and chronic low-grade systemic inflammation through lipotoxicity, creating the circumstances to develop clinical conditions. This review also shows that the liver is the most sensitive organ undergoing insulin impairment faster than other organs, and thus, hepatic insulin resistance is the primary event that leads to the subsequent development of peripheral tissue insulin resistance.</snippet>
<snippet id="33793327">Title: Obesity, Adipose Tissue and Vascular Dysfunction.
Authors: Koenen, Mascha, Hill, Michael A, Cohen, Paul et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Circulation research
Abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide. Overweight and obesity are strongly associated with comorbidities such as hypertension and insulin resistance, which collectively contribute to the development of cardiovascular diseases and resultant morbidity and mortality. Forty-two percent of adults in the United States are obese, and a total of 1.9 billion adults worldwide are overweight or obese. These alarming numbers, which continue to climb, represent a major health and economic burden. Adipose tissue is a highly dynamic organ that can be classified based on the cellular composition of different depots and their distinct anatomical localization. Massive expansion and remodeling of adipose tissue during obesity differentially affects specific adipose tissue depots and significantly contributes to vascular dysfunction and cardiovascular diseases. Visceral adipose tissue accumulation results in increased immune cell infiltration and secretion of vasoconstrictor mediators, whereas expansion of subcutaneous adipose tissue is less harmful. Therefore, fat distribution more than overall body weight is a key determinant of the risk for cardiovascular diseases. Thermogenic brown and beige adipose tissue, in contrast to white adipose tissue, is associated with beneficial effects on the vasculature. The relationship between the type of adipose tissue and its influence on vascular function becomes particularly evident in the context of the heterogenous phenotype of perivascular adipose tissue that is strongly location dependent. In this review, we address the abnormal remodeling of specific adipose tissue depots during obesity and how this critically contributes to the development of hypertension, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular stiffness. We also discuss the local and systemic roles of adipose tissue derived secreted factors and increased systemic inflammation during obesity and highlight their detrimental impact on cardiovascular health.</snippet>
<snippet id="32375231">Title: Obesity, Bioactive Lipids, and Adipose Tissue Inflammation in Insulin Resistance.
Authors: Kojta, Iwona, Chacińska, Marta, Błachnio-Zabielska, Agnieszka | Year: 2020 | Journal: Nutrients
Abstract: Obesity is a major risk factor for the development of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. The exact mechanism by which adipose tissue induces insulin resistance is still unclear. Adipose tissue synthesizes and secretes numerous bioactive molecules, namely adipokines and cytokines, which affect the metabolism of both lipids and glucose. Disorders in the synthesis of adipokines and cytokines that occur in obesity lead to changes in lipid and carbohydrates metabolism and, as a consequence, may lead to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Obesity is also associated with the accumulation of lipids. Recent studies indicate that the accumulation of biologically active lipids in adipose tissue may regulate the synthesis/secretion of adipokines and proinflammatory cytokines. <snippet id="37150407">Title: Association between obesity, inflammation and insulin resistance: Insights into signaling pathways and therapeutic interventions.
Authors: Suren Garg, Sourbh, Kushwaha, Kriti, Dubey, Rupal et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Diabetes research and clinical practice
Abstract: Obesity, a metabolic disorder, is becoming a worldwide epidemic that predominantly increases the risk for various diseases including metabolic inflammation, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular diseases. Abstract: In this review, we provide a brief synopsis of the connections between adipose tissue and metabolic health and highlight some recent developments in understanding and exploiting adipocyte biology. Dysfunctional adipose tissue has a detrimental impact on metabolic health and is intimately involved in key aspects of metabolic diseases such as insulin resistance, lipid overload, inflammation, and organelle stress. Differences in the distribution of fat depots and adipose characteristics relate to divergent degrees of metabolic dysfunction found in metabolically healthy and unhealthy obese individuals. <snippet id="38616042">Title: Tissue-specific inflammation and insulin sensitivity in subjects with obesity.
Authors: Oussaada, S M, Kilicarslan, M, de Weijer, B A et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Diabetes research and clinical practice
Abstract: Obesity is associated with low-grade inflammation and insulin resistance (IR). The contribution of adipose tissue (AT) and hepatic inflammation to IR remains unclear. We conducted a study across three cohorts to investigate this relationship. The first cohort consists of six women with normal weight and twenty with obesity. In women with obesity, we found an upregulation of inflammatory markers in subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue, isolated AT macrophages, and the liver, but no linear correlation with tissue-specific insulin sensitivity. In the second cohort, we studied 24 women with obesity in the upper vs lower insulin sensitivity quartile. We demonstrated that several omental and mesenteric AT inflammatory genes and T cell-related pathways are upregulated in IR, independent of BMI. The third cohort consists of 23 women and 18 men with obesity, studied before and one year after bariatric surgery. Weight loss following surgery was associated with downregulation of multiple immune pathways in subcutaneous AT and skeletal muscle, alongside notable metabolic improvements. <snippet id="30549014">Title: Contribution of Adipose Tissue Inflammation to the Development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.

Abstract: The objective of this comprehensive review is to summarize and discuss the available evidence of how adipose tissue inflammation affects insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance. Further, genetic alterations in mouse models of obesity that reduce adipose tissue inflammation are-almost without exception-associated with improved insulin sensitivity. <snippet id="23449529">Title: Relation of depot-specific adipose inflammation to insulin resistance in human obesity.
Authors: Bigornia, S J, Farb, M G, Mott, M M et al. | Year: 2012 | Journal: Nutrition & diabetes
Abstract: BACKGROUND
A low-grade state of adipose tissue inflammation associated with obesity has been linked to mechanisms of systemic metabolic dysfunction. However, the relation of clinical phenotypes to depot-specific inflammation has not been well examined in human obesity.
OBJECTIVE
To characterize the inflammatory status of subcutaneous and visceral fat depots, as assessed by tissue presence of macrophage crown-like structures (CLS) as a hallmark of chronic inflammation, and determine the relation of systemic insulin resistance to inflammatory abnormalities in subcutaneous and visceral fat.
METHODS
We collected adipose tissue simultaneously from subcutaneous and visceral (omental and mesenteric) depots in 92 obese participants (age 42±11 years; BMI30 kg m(-2)) during planned bariatric surgery. Using immunohistochemistry, we categorized individuals as CLS(+) or CLS(-) based on the presence or absence, respectively, of macrophage CLS in subcutaneous (CLSs), omental (CLSo) and mesenteric (CLSm) adipose depots.
RESULTS
The majority of participants exhibited adipose tissue inflammation manifest by the presence of CLS (CLS(+)) in both subcutaneous and intra-abdominal visceral depots. CLS status in subcutaneous fat was highly sensitive and modestly specific for inflammation of visceral fat. In multivariable models, plasma insulin and homeostatis model assessment levels were positively associated with CLS(+) status in all depots independent of age, waist circumference, BMI and type 2 diabetes, and worsened with the increasing number of adipose regions involved.
CONCLUSIONS
In severely obese participants, systemic insulin resistance is linked to adipose inflammation in both subcutaneous and visceral depots. The findings suggest that examination of subcutaneous regions that are more easily accessible by transcutaneous biopsy may prove useful in clinical studies designed to investigate adipose phenotypes in relation to human disease.</snippet>

Only 50% of identified proteins in VAT vesicles were common to those in SAT; additionally, EVs shed by obese VAT showed more AT and obesity-related adipokines than SAT. Functional classification shows that obese VAT vesicles exhibit an enrichment of proteins implicated in AT inflammation and insulin resistance such as TGFBI, CAVN1, CD14, mimecan, thrombospondin-1, FABP-4 or AHNAK. Selected candidate biomarkers from the quantitative-SWATH analysis were validated in EVs from independent morbid obese and from moderate obese to lean individuals showing that morbid obese VAT vesicles are characterized by a diminution of syntenin 1 and the elevation of TGFBI and mimecan. Our findings suggest that circulating EV-TGFBI may facilitate monitoring T2D status in obese patients, and EV-mimecan may be useful to track adiposity, and more precisely, visceral obesity.</snippet>

# Summary

Mechanistic evidence in humans links adipose tissue inflammation to insulin resistance through multiple convergent pathways. Obesity-induced adipocyte hypertrophy and depot remodeling drive macrophage recruitment and polarization toward pro‑inflammatory states, increasing local and systemic release of cytokines, chemokines, and lipid mediators that perturb insulin signaling in muscle, liver, and adipose tissue. The most consistently implicated mediators include TNF‑α, IL‑6, MCP‑1, leptin, adiponectin, and bioactive lipids (e.g., ceramides, DAGs), with visceral adipose tissue showing stronger associations than subcutaneous fat. Weight loss and bariatric surgery reduce adipose immune activation and improve insulin sensitivity, underscoring a causal link. Below, I synthesize the mechanistic evidence and highlight the most robust inflammatory mediators implicated in human obesity‑related insulin resistance.

# How Adipose Tissue Inflammation Initiates Insulin Resistance

- Adipocyte hypertrophy and depot remodeling: Enlarged adipocytes leak free fatty acids (FFAs) and reactive oxygen species (ROS), recruit macrophages, and promote polarization to pro‑inflammatory phenotypes, establishing a low‑grade inflammatory state in adipose tissue that spills over systemically in obesity. This inflammation impairs insulin signaling and glucose homeostasis across metabolic organs, with the liver often being the first to show insulin impairment. <cite id="33561645">Adipocyte hypertrophy and depot remodeling in obesity recruit and polarize macrophages toward pro‑inflammatory states, increasing release of FFAs, ROS, and cytokines that disrupt insulin signaling and glucose homeostasis, with hepatic insulin resistance often preceding peripheral insulin resistance.</cite>

- Depot specificity and vascular/metabolic consequences: Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) exhibits greater immune cell infiltration and secretion of vasoconstrictor mediators, whereas subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) is less harmful; this depot difference helps explain why abdominal obesity more strongly predicts insulin resistance and cardiovascular risk. <cite id="33793327">Visceral adipose tissue accumulation increases immune cell infiltration and vasoconstrictor mediator secretion, while subcutaneous expansion is less harmful, making fat distribution a key determinant of insulin resistance and cardiovascular risk.</cite>

- Bioactive lipids as danger signals: Obesity increases intracellular long‑chain acyl‑CoAs, ceramides, and diacylglycerols in adipocytes, which directly perturb insulin signaling and also upregulate inflammatory gene expression and cytokine secretion, creating a feed‑forward cycle of lipotoxicity and inflammation. <cite id="32375231">Accumulation of long‑chain acyl‑CoAs, ceramides, and diacylglycerols in adipose tissue impairs insulin signaling and regulates synthesis/secretion of pro‑inflammatory cytokines, linking lipid dysregulation to adipose inflammation and insulin resistance.</cite>

# Human Evidence Linking Adipose Inflammation to Insulin Resistance

- Tissue‑specific inflammation and insulin sensitivity: Across cohorts, obesity is characterized by systemic and depot‑specific inflammation; individuals with insulin resistance (IR) show stronger upregulation of inflammatory genes in omental/mesenteric fat and T‑cell–related pathways, independent of BMI. Bariatric surgery–induced weight loss reduces immune pathway activation in subcutaneous adipose tissue and skeletal muscle and is accompanied by metabolic improvements, suggesting inflammation tracks with IR and reverses with weight loss. <cite id="38616042">Obesity features systemic and tissue‑specific inflammation; IR is associated with upregulation of omental/mesenteric adipose inflammatory genes and T‑cell pathways independent of BMI, and bariatric surgery reduces immune pathway activation with metabolic improvement.</cite>

- Depot differences and macrophage crown‑like structures: In severely obese patients, both subcutaneous and visceral depots often show macrophage crown‑like structures (CLS), a hallmark of chronic inflammation; HOMA‑IR and insulin levels are positively associated with CLS in all depots and worsen with more involved regions, indicating a link between adipose inflammation and systemic IR. <cite id="23449529">In obese participants, CLS are present in both subcutaneous and visceral depots; plasma insulin and HOMA‑IR are positively associated with CLS status across depots and increase with more regions involved, linking adipose inflammation to systemic insulin resistance.</cite>

- Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) vs subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT): In humans, associations between adipose inflammation and insulin resistance are stronger for visceral depots than subcutaneous depots, consistent with animal models where reducing adipose inflammation improves insulin sensitivity. <cite id="30549014">In humans, inflammation in visceral fat shows stronger and more consistent associations with insulin resistance than subcutaneous fat, and genetic or model interventions that reduce adipose inflammation generally improve insulin sensitivity.</cite>

- Cellular senescence and macrophage dysfunction: In morbid obesity, visceral adipose depots harbor more senescent macrophage‑like cells correlating with BMI, insulin, and HOMA‑IR; high‑glucose culture drives THP‑1 macrophages to a senescent‑like mixed M1/M2 phenotype that induces pro‑inflammatory cytokines in adipocytes and impairs adipocyte insulin signaling, suggesting senescent macrophages fuel obesity‑induced inflammation and IR. <cite id="35247131">Visceral adipose tissue in obese patients shows more senescent macrophage‑like cells correlating with HOMA‑IR and insulin; high‑glucose–induced senescent macrophages promote adipocyte inflammatory cytokines and defective insulin signaling, linking macrophage senescence to adipose inflammation and insulin resistance.</cite>

- Paracrine/endocrine amplification via extracellular vesicles: Morbid‑obese VAT releases extracellular vesicles enriched for inflammatory/IR‑related proteins (e.g., TGFBI, CAVN1, CD14, thrombospondin‑1, FABP4, AHNAK), and circulating TGFBI‑ and mimecan‑containing vesicles are elevated in obese and T2D patients, indicating adipose EVs can propagate inflammation and IR signals systemically. <cite id="33465489">Morbid‑obese VAT shed EVs carry more adipokines and inflammation/IR‑related proteins than SAT (e.g., TGFBI, CAVN1, CD14, thrombospondin‑1, FABP4, AHNAK), and circulating TGFBI‑ and mimecan‑containing EVs are elevated in obese and T2D patients, suggesting paracrine/endocrine propagation of adipose inflammation.</cite>

# Most Consistently Implicated Inflammatory Mediators

- Pro‑inflammatory cytokines: TNF‑α and IL‑6 are consistently elevated in obesity and associated with impaired insulin signaling in adipose tissue and systemic IR; their production is increased by hypertrophic adipocytes and exacerbated by bacterial LPS or TNF‑α exposure. <cite id="40176539">Hypertrophic human adipocytes reduce adiponectin and increase leptin secretion, and TNFα/LPS further decrease adiponectin and increase leptin, MCP‑1 and IL‑6 via altered MAPK signaling, linking these cytokines to adipocyte dysfunction and insulin resistance.</cite> <cite id="32069832">Obesity increases secretion of IL‑6, IL‑1β, TNF‑α, and leptin, stimulates MCP‑1, and reduces adiponectin, initiating a pro‑inflammatory state that contributes to insulin resistance and endothelial dysfunction.</cite>

- Chemokines and leukocyte recruitment: MCP‑1 (CCL2) is induced in obesity and promotes monocyte recruitment to adipose tissue, amplifying macrophage infiltration and polarization toward pro‑inflammatory phenotypes that sustain local and systemic inflammation. <cite id="32069832">Obesity stimulates monocyte chemoattractant protein‑1 (MCP‑1), facilitating leukocyte recruitment and pro‑inflammatory state linked to insulin resistance.</cite> <cite id="40176539">TNFα/LPS increase MCP‑1 secretion from hypertrophic adipocytes, reinforcing inflammatory cell recruitment.</cite>

- Adipokines as metabolic/inflammatory signals: Leptin rises with adipocyte hypertrophy and inflammatory stimuli, while adiponectin falls; the leptin/adiponectin ratio is a well‑recognized marker of IR in obesity. TNF‑α, IL‑6, resistin, and visfatin also associate with impaired insulin sensitivity. <cite id="40176539">Hypertrophic adipocytes increase leptin and decrease adiponectin secretion; TNFα/LPS exacerbate these shifts and activate ERK/IκBα signaling, linking adipokine disruption to insulin resistance.</cite> <cite id="18217426">Obesity dysregulates adipokines (TNF‑α, adiponectin, resistin, visfatin) and chemokines (MCP‑1), contributing to insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome.</cite> <cite id="21196255">Overproduction of proinflammatory adipokines in obesity is associated with insulin resistance and the metabolic syndrome.</cite>

- Bioactive lipids as intracellular and paracrine mediators: Long‑chain acyl‑CoAs, ceramides, and diacylglycerols accumulate in adipose tissue in obesity, directly impairing insulin signaling in adipocytes and muscle and promoting inflammatory gene expression in adipocytes and infiltrating macrophages. <cite id="32375231">Biologically active lipids (long‑chain acyl‑CoAs, ceramides, diacylglycerols) accumulate in adipose tissue in obesity, impairing insulin signaling and regulating pro‑inflammatory cytokine synthesis/secretion.</cite> <cite id="40176539">LPS/TNFα exposure increases inflammatory mediator secretion from hypertrophic adipocytes with persistent ERK and IκBα activation, consistent with lipid‑mediated signaling perturbation.</cite>

- Depot‑specific inflammatory signatures: Visceral depots (omental/mesenteric) show stronger inflammatory gene upregulation and T‑cell pathway activation in IR independent of BMI, whereas weight loss and bariatric surgery reduce immune pathway activation across depots and improve IR, highlighting depot‑specific susceptibility and reversibility. <cite id="38616042">IR is associated with upregulation of omental/mesenteric adipose inflammatory genes and T‑cell pathways independent of BMI, and weight loss reduces immune pathway activation with metabolic improvement.</cite> <cite id="30549014">Human studies show stronger associations of visceral adipose inflammation with insulin resistance than subcutaneous fat.</cite>

# Signaling Pathways Connecting Inflammation to Insulin Resistance

- NF‑κB, JNK, SOCS, TLR and Wnt: Obesity‑driven adipose inflammation activates NF‑κB and JNK signaling, increases SOCS protein expression, engages TLR pathways in response to DAMPs and microbial products, and suppresses Wnt signaling, all of which converge on impaired insulin receptor signaling, IRS‑1 serine phosphorylation, and reduced glucose uptake in target tissues. <cite id="37150407">Obesity activates NF‑κB, SOCS proteins, JNK, TLR, and related pathways that perturb insulin signaling and contribute to insulin resistance; therapies targeting these pathways improve metabolic disease in preclinical and clinical contexts.</cite>

- MAPK and transcriptional changes in hypertrophic adipocytes: Hypertrophic adipocytes exhibit persistent ERK activation and IκBα degradation with impaired p38/JNK activation, supporting chronic inflammatory signaling that reduces adiponectin, increases leptin/MCP‑1/IL‑6, and undermines insulin action. <cite id="40176539">Hypertrophic adipocytes show persistent ERK and IκBα activation with impaired p38/JNK, associated with decreased adiponectin and increased leptin, MCP‑1, and IL‑6 secretion.</cite>

# Interventions and Causality

- Weight loss reverses inflammation and IR: Bariatric surgery reduces immune pathway activation in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle and improves metabolic profiles, consistent with a causal role for adipose inflammation in IR. <cite id="38616042">Bariatric surgery–induced weight loss is associated with downregulation of immune pathways in subcutaneous adipose tissue and skeletal muscle alongside metabolic improvements.</cite> <cite id="23449529">HOMA‑IR and insulin levels track with depot‑specific inflammatory markers (CLS) and worsen with more involved depots, supporting a mechanistic link.</cite>

# Key Takeaways

- Mechanistic chain: Adipocyte hypertrophy and depot remodeling drive macrophage recruitment and senescence, increasing cytokines (TNF‑α, IL‑6), chemokines (MCP‑1), and adipokines (leptin↑, adiponectin↓), while bioactive lipids (ceramides, DAGs) impair insulin signaling and amplify inflammation. These changes are stronger in visceral fat and activate NF‑κB/JNK/SOCS/TLR and suppress Wnt signaling, leading to systemic insulin resistance. <cite id="33561645">Adipocyte hypertrophy promotes macrophage infiltration and pro‑inflammatory cytokine release, driving systemic inflammation and insulin resistance.</cite> <cite id="32375231">Bioactive lipids accumulate in obesity and link to inflammatory cytokine dysregulation and insulin resistance.</cite> <cite id="30549014">Visceral adipose inflammation shows stronger associations with insulin resistance than subcutaneous fat, and reducing adipose inflammation improves insulin sensitivity.</cite> <cite id="37150407">Activated inflammatory signaling pathways (NF‑κB, JNK, SOCS, TLR) perturb insulin signaling in obesity‑related insulin resistance.</cite>

- Most consistently implicated mediators in humans: TNF‑α, IL‑6, MCP‑1/CCL2, leptin, adiponectin, and bioactive lipids (ceramides, diacylglycerols, long‑chain acyl‑CoAs). Visceral adipose tissue shows the strongest associations, and weight loss reduces these inflammatory signatures and improves insulin sensitivity. <cite id="32069832">Obesity increases IL‑6, TNF‑α, leptin, and MCP‑1 while reducing adiponectin, establishing a pro‑inflammatory milieu linked to insulin resistance.</cite> <cite id="40176539">Hypertrophic adipocytes and inflammatory stimuli shift adipokine and cytokine profiles (adiponectin↓, leptin↑, MCP‑1/IL‑6↑), connecting these mediators to adipocyte dysfunction and insulin resistance.</cite> <cite id="33465489">Visceral adipose EVs carry inflammatory/IR‑related proteins (e.g., TGFBI, thrombospondin‑1, FABP4), and circulating TGFBI/mimecan EVs are elevated in obesity and T2D, indicating systemic propagation of adipose inflammation.</cite>

- Nuances and heterogeneity: Associations are stronger for visceral than subcutaneous fat, but both depots can show inflammation and contribute to IR; some models show dissociation after weight loss, indicating multiple etiologic factors beyond adipose inflammation. <cite id="30549014">Associations between adipose inflammation and insulin resistance are stronger in visceral fat, though dissociations can occur after weight loss, implying multifactorial etiology.</cite> <cite id="38616042">IR is associated with depot‑specific inflammatory gene upregulation independent of BMI, and weight loss reduces inflammation with metabolic improvement.</cite>

data.title: Adipose tissue and insulin resistance in obese.
data.abstract: Currently, obesity has become a global health issue and is referred to as an epidemic. Dysfunctional obese adipose tissue plays a pivotal role in the development of insulin resistance. However, the mechanism of how dysfunctional obese-adipose tissue develops insulin-resistant circumstances remains poorly understood. Therefore, this review attempts to highlight the potential mechanisms behind obesity-associated insulin resistance. Multiple risk factors are directly or indirectly associated with the increased risk of obesity; among them, environmental factors, genetics, aging, gut microbiota, and diets are prominent. Once an individual becomes obese, adipocytes increase in their size; therefore, adipose tissues become larger and dysfunctional, recruit macrophages, and then these polarize to pro-inflammatory states. Enlarged adipose tissues release excess free fatty acids (FFAs), reactive oxygen species (ROS), and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Excess systemic FFAs and dietary lipids enter inside the cells of non-adipose organs such as the liver, muscle, and pancreas, and are deposited as ectopic fat, generating lipotoxicity. Toxic lipids dysregulate cellular organelles, e.g., mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and lysosomes. Dysregulated organelles release excess ROS and pro-inflammation, resulting in systemic inflammation. Long term low-grade systemic inflammation prevents insulin from its action in the insulin signaling pathway, disrupts glucose homeostasis, and results in systemic dysregulation. Overall, long-term obesity and overnutrition develop into insulin resistance and chronic low-grade systemic inflammation through lipotoxicity, creating the circumstances to develop clinical conditions. This review also shows that the liver is the most sensitive organ undergoing insulin impairment faster than other organs, and thus, hepatic insulin resistance is the primary event that leads to the subsequent development of peripheral tissue insulin resistance.

data.title: Obesity, Adipose Tissue and Vascular Dysfunction.
data.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide. Overweight and obesity are strongly associated with comorbidities such as hypertension and insulin resistance, which collectively contribute to the development of cardiovascular diseases and resultant morbidity and mortality. Forty-two percent of adults in the United States are obese, and a total of 1.9 billion adults worldwide are overweight or obese. These alarming numbers, which continue to climb, represent a major health and economic burden. Adipose tissue is a highly dynamic organ that can be classified based on the cellular composition of different depots and their distinct anatomical localization. Massive expansion and remodeling of adipose tissue during obesity differentially affects specific adipose tissue depots and significantly contributes to vascular dysfunction and cardiovascular diseases. Visceral adipose tissue accumulation results in increased immune cell infiltration and secretion of vasoconstrictor mediators, whereas expansion of subcutaneous adipose tissue is less harmful. Therefore, fat distribution more than overall body weight is a key determinant of the risk for cardiovascular diseases. Thermogenic brown and beige adipose tissue, in contrast to white adipose tissue, is associated with beneficial effects on the vasculature. The relationship between the type of adipose tissue and its influence on vascular function becomes particularly evident in the context of the heterogenous phenotype of perivascular adipose tissue that is strongly location dependent. In this review, we address the abnormal remodeling of specific adipose tissue depots during obesity and how this critically contributes to the development of hypertension, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular stiffness. We also discuss the local and systemic roles of adipose tissue derived secreted factors and increased systemic inflammation during obesity and highlight their detrimental impact on cardiovascular health.

data.title: Obesity, Bioactive Lipids, and Adipose Tissue Inflammation in Insulin Resistance.
data.abstract: Obesity is a major risk factor for the development of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. The exact mechanism by which adipose tissue induces insulin resistance is still unclear. It has been demonstrated that obesity is associated with the adipocyte dysfunction, macrophage infiltration, and low-grade inflammation, which probably contributes to the induction of insulin resistance. Adipose tissue synthesizes and secretes numerous bioactive molecules, namely adipokines and cytokines, which affect the metabolism of both lipids and glucose. Disorders in the synthesis of adipokines and cytokines that occur in obesity lead to changes in lipid and carbohydrates metabolism and, as a consequence, may lead to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Obesity is also associated with the accumulation of lipids. A special group of lipids that are able to regulate the activity of intracellular enzymes are biologically active lipids: long-chain acyl-CoAs, ceramides, and diacylglycerols. According to the latest data, the accumulation of these lipids in adipocytes is probably related to the development of insulin resistance. Recent studies indicate that the accumulation of biologically active lipids in adipose tissue may regulate the synthesis/secretion of adipokines and proinflammatory cytokines. Although studies have revealed that inflammation caused by excessive fat accumulation and abnormalities in lipid metabolism can contribute to the development of obesity-related insulin resistance, further research is needed to determine the exact mechanism by which obesity-related insulin resistance is induced.

data.title: Association between obesity, inflammation and insulin resistance: Insights into signaling pathways and therapeutic interventions.
data.abstract: Obesity, a metabolic disorder, is becoming a worldwide epidemic that predominantly increases the risk for various diseases including metabolic inflammation, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular diseases. However, the mechanisms that link obesity with other metabolic diseases are not completely understood. In obesity, various inflammatory pathways that cause inflammation in adipose tissue of an obese individual become activated and exacerbate the disease. Obesity-induced low-grade metabolic inflammation perturbates the insulin signaling pathway and leads to insulin resistance. Researchers have identified several pathways that link the impairment of insulin resistance through obesity-induced inflammation like activation of Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), suppressor of cytokine signaling (SOCS) proteins, cJun-N-terminal Kinase (JNK), Wingless-related integration site (Wnt), and Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling pathways. In this review article, the published studies have been reviewed to identify the potential and influential role of different signaling pathways in the pathogenesis of obesity-induced metabolic inflammation and insulin resistance along with the discussion on potential therapeutic strategies. Therapies targeting these signaling pathways show improvements in metabolic diseases associated with obesity, but require further testing and confirmation through clinical trials.

data.title: Adipose Tissue and Metabolic Health.
data.abstract: In this review, we provide a brief synopsis of the connections between adipose tissue and metabolic health and highlight some recent developments in understanding and exploiting adipocyte biology. Adipose tissue plays critical roles in the regulation of systemic glucose and lipid metabolism and secretes bioactive molecules possessing endocrine, paracrine, and autocrine functions. Dysfunctional adipose tissue has a detrimental impact on metabolic health and is intimately involved in key aspects of metabolic diseases such as insulin resistance, lipid overload, inflammation, and organelle stress. Differences in the distribution of fat depots and adipose characteristics relate to divergent degrees of metabolic dysfunction found in metabolically healthy and unhealthy obese individuals. Thermogenic adipocytes increase energy expenditure via mitochondrial uncoupling or adenosine triphosphate-consuming futile substrate cycles, while functioning as a metabolic sink and participating in crosstalk with other metabolic organs. Manipulation of adipose tissue provides a wealth of opportunities to intervene and combat the progression of associated metabolic diseases. We discuss current treatment modalities for obesity including incretin hormone analogs and touch upon emerging strategies with therapeutic potential including exosome-based therapy, pharmacological activation of brown and beige adipocyte thermogenesis, and administration or inhibition of adipocyte-derived factors.

data.title: Tissue-specific inflammation and insulin sensitivity in subjects with obesity.
data.abstract: Obesity is associated with low-grade inflammation and insulin resistance (IR). The contribution of adipose tissue (AT) and hepatic inflammation to IR remains unclear. We conducted a study across three cohorts to investigate this relationship. The first cohort consists of six women with normal weight and twenty with obesity. In women with obesity, we found an upregulation of inflammatory markers in subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue, isolated AT macrophages, and the liver, but no linear correlation with tissue-specific insulin sensitivity. In the second cohort, we studied 24 women with obesity in the upper vs lower insulin sensitivity quartile. We demonstrated that several omental and mesenteric AT inflammatory genes and T cell-related pathways are upregulated in IR, independent of BMI. The third cohort consists of 23 women and 18 men with obesity, studied before and one year after bariatric surgery. Weight loss following surgery was associated with downregulation of multiple immune pathways in subcutaneous AT and skeletal muscle, alongside notable metabolic improvements. Our results show that obesity is characterised by systemic and tissue-specific inflammation. Subjects with obesity and IR show a more pronounced inflammation phenotype, independent of BMI. Bariatric surgery-induced weight loss is associated with reduced inflammation and improved metabolic health.

data.title: Contribution of Adipose Tissue Inflammation to the Development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
data.abstract: The objective of this comprehensive review is to summarize and discuss the available evidence of how adipose tissue inflammation affects insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance. Low-grade, chronic adipose tissue inflammation is characterized by infiltration of macrophages and other immune cell populations into adipose tissue, and a shift toward more proinflammatory subtypes of leukocytes. The infiltration of proinflammatory cells in adipose tissue is associated with an increased production of key chemokines such as C-C motif chemokine ligand 2, proinflammatory cytokines including tumor necrosis factor α and interleukins 1β and 6 as well as reduced expression of the key insulin-sensitizing adipokine, adiponectin. In both rodent models and humans, adipose tissue inflammation is consistently associated with excess fat mass and insulin resistance. In humans, associations with insulin resistance are stronger and more consistent for inflammation in visceral as opposed to subcutaneous fat. Further, genetic alterations in mouse models of obesity that reduce adipose tissue inflammation are-almost without exception-associated with improved insulin sensitivity. However, a dissociation between adipose tissue inflammation and insulin resistance can be observed in very few rodent models of obesity as well as in humans following bariatric surgery- or low-calorie-diet-induced weight loss, illustrating that the etiology of insulin resistance is multifactorial. Taken together, adipose tissue inflammation is a key factor in the development of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes in obesity, along with other factors that likely include inflammation and fat accumulation in other metabolically active tissues. © 2019 American Physiological Society. Compr Physiol 9:1-58, 2019.

data.title: Senescent macrophages in the human adipose tissue as a source of inflammaging.
data.abstract: Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes and a trigger of chronic and systemic inflammation. Recent evidence suggests that an increased burden of senescent cells (SCs) in the adipose tissue of obese/diabetic animal models might underlie such pro-inflammatory phenotype. However, the role of macrophages as candidate SCs, their phenotype, the distribution of SCs among fat depots, and clinical relevance are debated. The senescence marker β-galactosidase and the macrophage marker CD68 were scored in visceral (vWAT) and subcutaneous (scWAT) adipose tissue from obese patients (n=17) undergoing bariatric surgery and control patients (n=4) subjected to cholecystectomy. A correlation was made between the number of SCs and BMI, serum insulin, and the insulin resistance (IR) index HOMA. The monocyte cell line (THP-1) was cultured in vitro in high glucose milieu (60 mM D-glucose) and subsequently co-cultured with human adipocytes (hMADS) to investigate the reciprocal inflammatory activation. In obese patients, a significantly higher number of SCs was observed in vWAT compared to scWAT; about 70% of these cells expressed the macrophage marker CD68; and the number of SCs in vWAT, but not in scWAT, positively correlated with BMI, HOMA-IR, and insulin. THP-1 cultured in vitro in high glucose milieu acquired a senescent-like phenotype (HgSMs), characterized by a polarization toward a mixed M1/M2-like secretory phenotype. Co-culturing HgSMs with hMADS elicited pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in both cell types, and defective insulin signaling in hMADS. In morbid obesity, expansion of visceral adipose depots involves an increased burden of macrophages with senescent-like phenotype that may promote a pro-inflammatory profile and impair insulin signaling in adipocytes, supporting a framework where senescent macrophages fuel obesity-induced systemic inflammation and possibly contribute to the development of IR.

data.title: Relation of depot-specific adipose inflammation to insulin resistance in human obesity.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
A low-grade state of adipose tissue inflammation associated with obesity has been linked to mechanisms of systemic metabolic dysfunction. However, the relation of clinical phenotypes to depot-specific inflammation has not been well examined in human obesity.
OBJECTIVE
To characterize the inflammatory status of subcutaneous and visceral fat depots, as assessed by tissue presence of macrophage crown-like structures (CLS) as a hallmark of chronic inflammation, and determine the relation of systemic insulin resistance to inflammatory abnormalities in subcutaneous and visceral fat.
METHODS
We collected adipose tissue simultaneously from subcutaneous and visceral (omental and mesenteric) depots in 92 obese participants (age 42±11 years; BMI30 kg m(-2)) during planned bariatric surgery. Using immunohistochemistry, we categorized individuals as CLS(+) or CLS(-) based on the presence or absence, respectively, of macrophage CLS in subcutaneous (CLSs), omental (CLSo) and mesenteric (CLSm) adipose depots.
RESULTS
The majority of participants exhibited adipose tissue inflammation manifest by the presence of CLS (CLS(+)) in both subcutaneous and intra-abdominal visceral depots. CLS status in subcutaneous fat was highly sensitive and modestly specific for inflammation of visceral fat. In multivariable models, plasma insulin and homeostatis model assessment levels were positively associated with CLS(+) status in all depots independent of age, waist circumference, BMI and type 2 diabetes, and worsened with the increasing number of adipose regions involved.
CONCLUSIONS
In severely obese participants, systemic insulin resistance is linked to adipose inflammation in both subcutaneous and visceral depots. The findings suggest that examination of subcutaneous regions that are more easily accessible by transcutaneous biopsy may prove useful in clinical studies designed to investigate adipose phenotypes in relation to human disease.

data.title: Human obese white adipose tissue sheds depot-specific extracellular vesicles and reveals candidate biomarkers for monitoring obesity and its comorbidities.
data.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have been recently postulated as key players in metabolic disorders emerging as an alternative way of paracrine/endocrine communication. However, the nature of EVs shed by adipose tissue (AT) and their role in obesity is still very limited. Here, we isolated human morbid obese visceral (VAT) and subcutaneous (SAT) whole AT shed EVs from donors submitted to bariatric surgery to characterize their protein cargo by qualitative and quantitative/SWATH mass spectrometry analysis. We identified 574 different proteins shed by morbid obese VAT and 401 proteins in those from SAT, establishing the first obese AT EV proteome reference map. Only 50% of identified proteins in VAT vesicles were common to those in SAT; additionally, EVs shed by obese VAT showed more AT and obesity-related adipokines than SAT. Functional classification shows that obese VAT vesicles exhibit an enrichment of proteins implicated in AT inflammation and insulin resistance such as TGFBI, CAVN1, CD14, mimecan, thrombospondin-1, FABP-4 or AHNAK. Selected candidate biomarkers from the quantitative-SWATH analysis were validated in EVs from independent morbid obese and from moderate obese to lean individuals showing that morbid obese VAT vesicles are characterized by a diminution of syntenin 1 and the elevation of TGFBI and mimecan. Interestingly, TGFBI and mimecan containing vesicles could be detected and quantified at circulating level in plasma. Thus, a significant elevation of -TGFBI-EVs was detected on those obese patients with a history of T2D compared to nondiabetic, and an augmentation of mimecan-EVs in obese plasma compared to those in healthy lean individuals. Thus, we conclude that obese AT release functional EVs carrying AT and obesity candidate biomarkers which vary regarding the AT of origin. Our findings suggest that circulating EV-TGFBI may facilitate monitoring T2D status in obese patients, and EV-mimecan may be useful to track adiposity, and more precisely, visceral obesity.
